memory: Source article [PMC5462369]: A study compared Dihydroartemisin-piperaquine + primaquine (DHP + PQ) with Dihydroartemisin-piperaquine (DHP-only) on gametocyte carriage. Baseline gametocyte prevalence was 9% by microscopy and 46% by Pfs25 RT-PCR. Microscopic gametocytemia rose to 12% before primaquine administration on day 2. By day 7 post-treatment, the DHP + PQ group had a significantly lower gametocyte carriage rate (2.1%) compared to DHP-only (15%), with a prevalence ratio of 0.12 (95% CI 0.02–0.9, p = 0.03). In the DHP + PQ group, only 1 out of 4 participants with patent gametocytemia at day 2 remained positive at day 7, and all were gametocyte-free by day 14. These results indicate that adding primaquine to DHP significantly reduces gametocyte carriage, suggesting potential benefits in reducing malaria transmission.
text: Adding primaquine to dihydroartemisinin-piperaquine significantly reduces gametocyte carriage. By day 7, the DHP + PQ group had 2.1% gametocyte carriage versus 15% in DHP-only (prevalence ratio 0.12, 95% CI 0.02–0.9, p = 0.03), indicating reduced malaria transmission potential (PMC5462369).

memory: Source article [PMC5350209] found that "Visual warning (text)" significantly reduced the speed of alcohol consumption compared to "No warning" (p < .001). The study employed a between-subjects design with three conditions: "Visual warning (text)," "pictorial warning," and "No warning." Consumption speed was measured by the duration of drinking, with the "No warning" group drinking significantly faster than the "Visual warning (text)" group. No significant difference in consumption speed was observed between "Visual warning (text)" and "pictorial" warnings (p = .76). The presence of any warning slowed consumption compared to no warning. The effect of warning type on consumption speed was less pronounced than the effect of warning presence. Findings suggest that both text and pictorial warnings influence consumption speed, with text warnings being as effective as pictorial ones. The study highlights that the presence of a warning has a greater impact on slowing alcohol consumption than the specific format of the warning.
text: Visual warning (text) significantly reduced the speed of alcohol consumption compared to no warning (p < .001). The presence of any warning slowed consumption more than the warning type. Source: PMC5350209.

memory: Source article [PMC4171519] reports that Raloxifene improved femoral toughness in both diabetic and non-diabetic ZDSD rats compared to control (vehicle-treated) rats. The improvement was linked to increased energy absorption in the post-yield region of the stress-strain curve. Raloxifene also reduced the incidence of type 2 diabetes and lowered blood glucose levels in treated rats. Additional mechanical benefits included higher energy-to-failure, post-yield energy-to-failure, and post-yield displacement. These findings suggest that Raloxifene may protect against diabetes-induced deterioration of bone material properties. The study indicates that Raloxifene positively affects femoral toughness, potentially through enhanced mechanical properties and diabetes management. The results highlight the potential of Raloxifene in improving bone strength, particularly in diabetic conditions.
text: Raloxifene improves femoral toughness compared to control in both diabetic and non-diabetic rats (PMC4171519). This effect is linked to increased energy absorption and mechanical benefits, suggesting Raloxifene may protect against diabetes-induced bone deterioration.

memory: Source article [PMC3381083]: Compared alcohol-assisted epithelial removal (n=658 eyes) with mechanical epithelial removal (n=592 eyes) on mean spherical equivalent. The mean spherical equivalent was −4.37±2.3 D in the alcohol group and −3.8±1.3 D in the mechanical group (P = 0.78), indicating no significant difference between the two methods. These results suggest that both methods are similarly effective in terms of refractive outcomes and visual recovery.
text: A study (PMC3381083) found no significant difference in mean spherical equivalent between alcohol-assisted and mechanical epithelial removal (-4.37±2.3 D vs. -3.8±1.3 D, P=0.78). Both methods showed similar visual outcomes.

memory: A study compared the effect of proximal-release pellets versus distal-release pellets on plasma lithium levels. Proximal-release pellets significantly increased plasma lithium compared to distal-release pellets (P = 0.001), as measured by the AUC of plasma lithium concentrations over 7 hours post-administration. The release profiles indicated that proximal-release pellets resulted in higher lithium absorption. Additionally, proximal-release pellets with ATP showed significantly lower lithium AUC than those with placebo (P = 0.001). These findings suggest that the site of pellet disintegration in the gastrointestinal tract influences lithium absorption, with proximal sites leading to higher plasma lithium levels. Individual plasma lithium concentrations are detailed in Additional file 2: Figure S2. Source: [PMC3441280].
text: Administration via proximal-release pellets significantly increases plasma lithium levels compared to distal-release pellets (P = 0.001), as shown by higher AUC over 7 hours. This suggests that the site of pellet disintegration influences lithium absorption. Source: [PMC3441280].

memory: A study compared the effect of "Pap smear at enrollment" with "No intervention at enrollment" on "Levels of IL-10" in women. The control group (n=39) had no intervention but had cervical vault lavage (CVL) samples collected at enrollment and 2 weeks later. Inflammatory markers, including IL-10, were measured in CVL specimens. Following a Pap smear, levels of IL-8, IL-1β, and IL-6 remained unchanged, but markers of cell-mediated immunity (IL-12 p70 and TNF-α) and T cell regulation (IL-10) were significantly elevated. This suggests that the Pap smear may influence immune responses, particularly increasing IL-10, which is associated with T cell regulation. The study indicates that performing a Pap smear at enrollment may impact inflammatory and immune regulatory markers, including IL-10, compared to no intervention. Source: [PMC1868022] (Abstract section).
text: Performing a Pap smear at enrollment significantly increases IL-10 levels compared to no intervention, indicating enhanced T cell regulation. This effect was observed in a study comparing inflammatory markers in cervical vault lavage samples. Source: [PMC1868022].

memory: A randomized trial [PMC5264222] evaluated SB4 (etanercept biosimilar) versus etanercept (ETN) in 596 RA patients on methotrexate. At week 24, ACR20 response rates were 78.1% for SB4 and 80.3% for ETN, with a treatment difference of −2.2% (95% CI: −9.41% to 4.98%), which was within the −15% to 15% equivalence margin, confirming therapeutic equivalence. Efficacy and pharmacokinetics were comparable between SB4 and ETN. Adverse events occurred in 55.2% of SB4-treated patients and 58.2% of ETN-treated patients, with no significant difference. Antidrug antibodies were less frequent with SB4 (0.7%) compared to ETN (13.1%). These findings support the therapeutic equivalence of SB4 to ETN in RA patients on methotrexate.
text: SB4 (etanercept biosimilar) is therapeutically equivalent to etanercept (ETN) in RA patients on methotrexate, as shown by comparable ACR20 response rates (78.1% vs. 80.3%) within the equivalence margin (PMC5264222). Efficacy, pharmacokinetics, and safety were similar, with fewer antidrug antibodies in SB4.
outcome: therapeutic equivalence - Patients with moderate to severe rheumatoid arthritis (RA) despite methotrexate (MTX) treatment

memory: In the study [PMC3698010], Paracetamol 250 mg was evaluated against Control for its effect on "Activity" as an outcome. In infants, Paracetamol 250 mg was associated with significantly less frequent systemic reactions, including reduced activity, following at least one dose (all p < 0.05). In toddlers, where systemic reactions were more common, Paracetamol 250 mg showed a significant decrease in activity levels compared to Control (p = 0.005). These findings suggest that Paracetamol 250 mg may lead to reduced activity levels in comparison to the control group, particularly in toddlers. memory: In a crossover study with 24 infants, the effect of Nutrilon Omneo (new formula; NF) versus standard formula (SF) on soft stool frequency was examined. Weekly defecation frequency was not significantly different between NF (5.5/week) and SF (5.9/week), with a difference of -0.5 (95% CI: -1.6 to 0.6; p = 0.38). However, the frequency of soft stools was significantly higher during the NF period: 17% (n = 4) of infants had soft stools on NF, compared to 0% on SF (McNemar test, p = 0.046). No significant differences were observed in painful defecation or the presence of abdominal or rectal masses between the two periods. Although overall defecation frequency was similar, the study suggests that NF may improve stool consistency, which could enhance infant gastrointestinal comfort. This finding indicates a potential benefit of NF in promoting softer stools, despite comparable overall bowel movement frequency. Source: [PMC1852321].

memory: A study compared peramivir (Rapiacta) and oseltamivir (Tamiflu) in terms of the number of days required for the disappearance of influenza symptoms. The findings suggest that both peramivir and oseltamivir are similarly effective in reducing the duration of influenza symptoms. Source: [PMC5534217].

memory: A phase 2a trial evaluated the impact of synthetic amyloid-β peptide (Aβ42) (AN1792) versus placebo on the Dependence Scale. Among participants who developed anti-AN1792 antibodies, there was a statistically significant improvement compared to placebo (p=0.033). These findings suggest that the efficacy of AN1792 may be linked to the development of anti-AN1792 antibodies, though no differences in brain volume loss were observed between groups. memory: In a study [PMC4628236], cinaciguat (10 mg/kg/day) orally for 8 weeks was compared to placebo in diabetic subjects to assess its effect on nitro-oxidative stress. The study found that diabetes mellitus (DM) increased nitrotyrosine (NT) immunoreactivity in the left ventricular myocardium, indicating elevated nitro-oxidative stress. Cinaciguat treatment significantly reduced NT levels, suggesting a decrease in nitro-oxidative stress (Fig. 2a, b). Furthermore, DM was associated with increased expression of antioxidant enzymes, including HSP70a1, catalase, glutathione-reductase, and thioredoxin-1 (Fig. 2c). However, in the cinaciguat-treated diabetic group (DiabCin), mRNA expression of HSP70a1 and glutathione-reductase normalized to levels observed in healthy controls. These findings suggest that cinaciguat reduces nitro-oxidative stress in diabetic myocardium, potentially through the modulation of antioxidant enzyme expression. The study supports the potential of soluble guanylate cyclase (sGC) activation in mitigating oxidative damage in diabetes. The results highlight the therapeutic benefit of cinaciguat in reducing oxidative stress markers and restoring antioxidant enzyme expression in diabetic patients. This provides evidence for the use of sGC activators in managing oxidative stress-related complications in diabetes.

memory: Arformoterol demonstrated statistically significant improvements in quality of life, as measured by the overall St. George's Respiratory Questionnaire (SGRQ) and Clinical COPD Questionnaire (CCQ), compared to placebo (P < .05). However, a numerically higher percentage of patients on arformoterol (3.1%) experienced cardiac serious adverse events compared to those on placebo (2.4%), though the time-to-first cardiac serious adverse event was not significantly different between the two groups. These results highlight the potential benefits of arformoterol in improving both lung function and quality of life in COPD patients, while also indicating a need for careful monitoring of cardiac-related adverse events. The study supports arformoterol as a potential treatment option for COPD, though further research is needed to better understand the risk-benefit profile, particularly regarding cardiac safety. memory: A study compared bisoprolol with a combination of losartan, amlodipine, and hydrochlorothiazide, examining their effects on SNPs on chromosome 11 (rs2514036, rs948445, and rs2514037) associated with ASBP (systolic blood pressure) response. Source: [PMC4330076]. Results from Manhattan plots identified genome-wide associations of ~630,000 SNPs with antihypertensive responses to the drugs. Three SNPs on chromosome 11 reached genome-wide significance for ASBP response to bisoprolol (Figure 1C and Table 2). These SNPs are located in the coding and regulatory regions of ACY3, which encodes aminoacylase III. A total of 42 SNPs in 31 distinct regions were identified with at least one SNP associated with treatment response at P≤1×10−5 (Figure 1 and Tables 2 through 5). The findings suggest that specific genetic variants influence the response to bisoprolol in terms of systolic blood pressure reduction, highlighting potential genetic factors in drug response variability.

memory: Source article [PMC5101425] assessed the impact of Desmopressin versus Placebo on Thrombocytopenia rate. The study found no significant difference in post-surgery bleeding rates between Desmopressin and Placebo groups (359.3 ± 266.2 vs. 406.3 ± 341.6; P = 0.208). However, a significant difference in platelet changes was observed, with a higher thrombocytopenia rate in the Placebo group (P = 0.012). These results suggest that Desmopressin may offer a protective effect on platelet levels compared to Placebo, despite no significant difference in bleeding rates. The findings highlight the potential of Desmopressin in reducing the development of thrombocytopenia in surgical patients. This outcome underscores the possible role of Desmopressin in maintaining platelet levels in post-surgical care. The study supports the need for further research to explore the mechanisms through which Desmopressin influences platelet function and thrombocytopenia development. The evidence from this study contributes to the growing body of knowledge on the role of Desmopressin in post-surgical hemostasis and platelet preservation. These results suggest that while Desmopressin may not significantly reduce bleeding, it may help in preserving platelet counts, which could be clinically relevant in preventing thrombocytopenia. This calls for further investigation into its potential use in clinical settings where platelet preservation is a concern.
text: Desmopressin compared to Placebo showed a lower thrombocytopenia rate (P = 0.012) in surgical patients, suggesting a protective effect on platelet levels, though no significant difference in bleeding rates was observed (P = 0.208). Source: PMC5101425.

memory: A study evaluated the effect of a "Phlebotomy training programme" versus a "Control" on "Phlebotomy questionnaire score" among healthcare professionals (HCPs) at four centers (CHC A, CHC B, CDC C, CDC D). Pre-training scores ranged from 58% to 63% across centers. After the training programme, scores significantly improved at all centers: CHC A (63% to 96%, p = 0.039), CHC B (58% to 93%, p = 0.006), CDC C (60% to 97%, p = 0.001), and CDC D (63% to 97%, p = 0.001), with confidence intervals provided for each score. However, phlebotomy sample rejection rates before and after training were not significantly different (p > 0.05). The results suggest that the training programme enhanced HCPs' phlebotomy knowledge, as measured by the questionnaire, but did not significantly affect sample rejection rates. Source: PMC5419060.
text: The phlebotomy training programme significantly improved phlebotomy questionnaire scores across all centers (p < 0.05), indicating enhanced knowledge. However, it did not significantly affect sample rejection rates (p > 0.05). Source: PMC5419060.

memory: Source article [PMC4972969] reports that on-site support (OSS) significantly reduced the proportion of patients with negative malaria test results who were prescribed antimalarials in the IMID-MLP group compared to the Control. The relative risk reduction (aRRR) was 0.49 (99% CI: 0.26–0.92; p = 0.004), indicating a statistically significant effect. These findings were presented in the "Results > Outcomes > Facility Performance" section. The study suggests that OSS improves adherence to treatment guidelines by reducing inappropriate antimalarial prescriptions in patients with negative test results. This implies that on-site support enhances clinical decision-making and guideline implementation in resource-limited settings. The results highlight the importance of direct support in improving diagnostic accuracy and appropriate treatment practices among mid-level practitioners in integrated infectious disease management.
text: On-site support (OSS) significantly reduced the proportion of patients with negative malaria tests prescribed antimalarials in the IMID-MLP group compared to control (aRRR 0.49, 99% CI 0.26–0.92; p=0.004). This suggests OSS improves adherence to guidelines by reducing inappropriate prescriptions. Source: [PMC4972969].
outcome: proportion of patients with a negative malaria test result prescribed an antimalarial in integrated management of infectious diseases (IMID)- mid-level practitioners (MLP) group

memory: The study [PMC4497726] evaluated the impact of aerobic exercise (150 min/wk or 225 min/wk) compared to no exercise on VO2 peak (% change). Results showed a dose-response relationship, with greater improvements in VO2 peak observed at higher exercise volumes. Increased exercise duration was associated with a progressive increase in percent change in VO2 peak, suggesting that higher aerobic exercise volumes lead to more significant improvements in cardiorespiratory fitness. The study also reported cognitive outcomes, including visuospatial processing and simple attention, which showed a similar dose-response pattern. This supports the notion that aerobic exercise enhances both physiological and cognitive functions. The evidence indicates that aerobic exercise, regardless of specific duration, improves VO2 peak, with more pronounced benefits at higher exercise levels. The findings are relevant for understanding the physiological and cognitive benefits of regular aerobic exercise in clinical populations. The information is sourced from the Cognitive Outcomes section of the article.
text: Aerobic exercise (150 or 225 min/wk) significantly improves VO2 peak compared to no exercise, with greater % change at higher volumes (PMC4497726). This dose-response effect highlights enhanced cardiorespiratory fitness with increased exercise duration.

memory: Source article [PMC4144850] found that the Total Sanitation Campaign (TSC) significantly reduced daily open defecation compared to Control in intervention villages. Among adult men, open defecation was 75% versus 84% (mean difference 9.5%, p=0.001); adult women, 73% versus 83% (mean difference 10%, p<0.001); and children under 5, 84% versus 89% (mean difference 5%, p=0.014). Despite these reductions, the decline in open defecation was less than the increase in Improved Household Latrines (IHL) availability. In households with JMP-defined improved sanitation, 41% of intervention households still practiced open defecation, compared to 28% in control households. The TSC promoted latrines that safely contain feces, with most IHLs being improved facilities. However, a notable proportion of households with improved sanitation continued open defecation, indicating limited effectiveness in fully eliminating the behavior. The study suggests that while TSC reduced open defecation, latrine use alone may not be sufficient to eradicate the practice.
text: The Total Sanitation Campaign significantly reduced open defecation compared to control, with mean differences of 9.5% (p=0.001) in men, 10% (p<0.001) in women, and 5% (p=0.014) in children under 5. However, 41% of intervention households still practiced open defecation despite improved sanitation facilities (PMC4144850).

memory: In a study comparing the effect of "group III used hydrogen peroxide (H2O2) 1.5% followed by chlorhexidine (CHX)" with "group I rinsed with chlorhexidine (CHX) 0.2% alone" on the "amount of plaque formed at the end of week 3," group III showed significantly less plaque than group I after the first (P value, 0.000) and second week (P value, 0.017). memory: A 24-week multinational, randomized trial involving 132 patients across 24 sites compared prolonged-release fampridine (PR-fampridine) with placebo in terms of improvement in Timed Up and Go (TUG) speed. PR-fampridine showed greater median improvements in TUG speed from baseline compared to placebo. A significantly higher proportion of patients on PR-fampridine achieved at least 10% improvement (p = 0.0021) and 15% improvement (p = 0.0262) in TUG speed, indicating statistically significant benefits. These findings suggest that PR-fampridine may enhance functional mobility, as measured by TUG speed, over a 24-week period. The study supports the potential efficacy of PR-fampridine in improving mobility in patients, with significant outcomes observed at multiple improvement thresholds. The results are derived from a clinical trial published in [PMC4749757].
text: Prolonged-release fampridine significantly improved TUG speed compared to placebo over 24 weeks (p = 0.0021 for ≥10% improvement; p = 0.0262 for ≥15% improvement), suggesting enhanced functional mobility. Source: [PMC4749757].

memory: In a study comparing oral ibandronate 50 mg to placebo, the median time to first bone event was 90.3 weeks for ibandronate and 64.9 weeks for placebo (P=0.089). Multivariate Poisson's regression analysis showed a significant reduction in the risk of skeletal events with ibandronate 50 mg compared to placebo, with a hazard ratio of 0.62 (95% CI=0.48, 0.79, P<0.0001), indicating a 38% risk reduction. Additionally, patients on ibandronate 50 mg experienced a significant decrease in urinary CTx from baseline over 96 weeks (median change −77.3%) compared to a minimal change in the placebo group (+11.0%, P<0.001). These findings suggest that oral ibandronate 50 mg is associated with a lower risk of skeletal events and improved bone remodeling markers compared to placebo. Source: [PMC2409647]
text: Oral ibandronate 50 mg significantly reduces the risk of skeletal events compared to placebo, with a 38% risk reduction (HR 0.62, 95% CI 0.48–0.79, P<0.0001). This is supported by a longer median time to first bone event and improved bone remodeling markers. Source: [PMC2409647]
outcome: risk reduction for a skeletal event

memory: In a study [PMC5336430], the effect of "5-fluorouracil (5-FU) 0.5%/salicylic acid 10%" versus "vehicle" on "Treatment-emergent adverse events" was examined. The 5-FU/salicylic acid group experienced a significantly higher lesion clearance rate (69.5%) compared to the vehicle group (34.6%), with an odds ratio of 4.9 (95% CI 2.3, 10.5; P < 0.0001). However, treatment-emergent adverse events were more frequent in the 5-FU/salicylic acid group (99.1%) compared to the vehicle group (83.6%). These adverse events were primarily local and related to application-site reactions. The study highlights a trade-off between the enhanced efficacy of the combination treatment and the increased incidence of local adverse events compared to the vehicle. This information is drawn from the Abstract > Results section of the source article.
text: The combination of 5-FU 0.5%/salicylic acid 10% resulted in more treatment-emergent adverse events (99.1%) compared to vehicle (83.6%), primarily local reactions, despite higher efficacy (PMC5336430).

memory: The "FIFA 11 for Health" programme led to a significantly greater reduction in body fat percentage compared to the control group (−0.83% vs −0.04%, p<0.05) over 11 weeks. memory: A study examined the effect of Lactobacillus rhamnosus GG (LGG) versus placebo on Clostridium difficile et rel at 18 months of age. The placebo group had higher levels of Clostridium difficile et rel compared to the LGG group (1.19 ± 0.85% vs. 0.78 ± 0.60%, p=0.047), suggesting a potential reduction in Clostridium difficile et rel with LGG. The analysis was part of a broader investigation into intestinal microbiota composition and health status. Supporting data are provided in Additional file 7 and Additional file 8 of the source article [PMC3563445]. While the results are promising, further research is necessary to validate these findings and to explore the mechanisms underlying the observed effect. This study contributes to understanding the impact of probiotics on gut microbiota and early childhood health.

This finding supports the role of LGG in modulating gut microbiota in early childhood [PMC3563445].

memory: A study compared "Partial matrix excision" (Group I) and "Segmental phenolization" (Group II) in terms of postoperative complications. Three patients in Group I and two in Group II experienced moderate postoperative pain requiring analgesics for 3 days. No statistically significant difference was found between the groups in complication rates or recurrence (P = 0.688). However, patients in Group II returned to normal daily activities significantly faster than those in Group I (P < 0.05). Both procedures showed similar safety profiles, with no procedure leading to a significantly higher complication rate. Pain management was comparable between groups, with both requiring analgesics for a short duration. The findings suggest that while complication rates are similar, Segmental phenolization may offer a quicker recovery, which could be a clinically relevant factor in choosing between the two procedures. The study highlights the need for further research with larger patient populations to confirm these results. Source: PMC3726903.
text: A study found no significant difference in postoperative complication rates between "Partial matrix excision" and "Segmental phenolization" (P = 0.688). Both procedures had similar safety profiles and pain management. However, patients undergoing "Segmental phenolization" returned to normal activities faster (P < 0.05). Source: PMC3726903.

memory: Source article [PMC4312979] reports that kinetic oscillation stimulation (KOS) in the nasal cavity significantly reduced pain scores compared to placebo. Pain was assessed using the visual analog scale (VAS). Pre-treatment VAS scores were 5.5 for the KOS group and 4.9 for the placebo group. After 15 minutes, VAS scores decreased to 1.2 in the KOS group and 3.9 in the placebo group. The difference in pain score changes between KOS and placebo was 3.3 points (95% CI: 2.3, 4.4), P < .001. A significant difference was observed as early as 5 minutes into treatment (1.9 points, P = .007) and remained significant at 2 hours post-treatment (3.7 points, P < .001). These results suggest that KOS leads to a more pronounced and sustained reduction in pain compared to placebo. The study supports the efficacy of KOS as a pain relief intervention when compared to a placebo.
text: Kinetic oscillation stimulation (KOS) in the nasal cavity significantly reduced pain scores compared to placebo (P < .001). Pain, measured by VAS, decreased by 3.3 points more in the KOS group (95% CI: 2.3, 4.4). This effect was sustained up to 2 hours post-treatment. Source: [PMC4312979].
intervention: kinetic oscillation stimulation (KOS) in the nasal cavity

memory: A complete-case ANCOVA (n = 141) found no significant group difference in the SF-12 Physical Component Summary (PCS) at 6 months. However, the community-based intervention significantly improved the SF-12 Mental Component Summary (MCS) compared to usual care, with a mean difference of 2.74 (95% CI = 0.28–5.19, P = .03). Additionally, the intervention group showed significant improvements in the Summary of Diabetes Self-Care Activities (SDSCA), with a mean difference of 3.74 (95% CI = 0.9–6.57, P = .01). The SF-12 general health subdomain also improved significantly in the intervention group (mean difference = 3.11, 95% CI = 0.05–5.71, P = .02). No significant differences were observed for CES-D, GAD-7, or self-efficacy. Multiple imputation analyses confirmed the complete-case findings, reinforcing the benefits of the community-based intervention on mental health and diabetes self-care activities. These results suggest that while the primary physical health outcome was not significantly affected, the intervention had a positive impact on mental health and diabetes self-care behaviors. (Source: PMC5836873)
text: The community-based intervention significantly improved SF-12 MCS (mean diff 2.74, 95% CI 0.28–5.19, P = .03) and SDSCA (mean diff 3.74, 95% CI 0.9–6.57, P = .01) compared to usual care, but not SF-12 PCS. (Source: PMC5836873)
outcome: 12‐item Short‐Form Health Survey (SF‐12), Mental Component Summary (MCS), Summary of Diabetes Self‐Care Activities (SDSCA)

memory: A study evaluated the effect of bladder training plus tolterodine (Co) versus tolterodine only (To) on micturition frequency. Both Co and To groups showed significant improvements in micturition frequency and urgency scores compared to the bladder training (BT) group (p<0.05). Urgency scores improved significantly in both To (p=0.017) and Co (p=0.021) groups compared to BT. However, there was no significant difference in outcomes between the To and Co groups. Patient satisfaction scores at 12 weeks were similar across all groups, with the highest improvement rate in the Co group (71.0%), followed by To (63.0%) and BT (53.9%). The findings suggest that adding bladder training to tolterodine does not provide additional benefits over tolterodine alone in terms of micturition frequency or urgency improvement. Both Co and To interventions were more effective than BT alone. Tolterodine appears to be effective in managing symptoms, with combined therapy showing comparable results to monotherapy. Source: [PMC2721929]
text: Bladder training plus tolterodine (Co) did not significantly improve micturition frequency compared to tolterodine only (To) [PMC2721929]. Both Co and To showed greater improvement than bladder training alone.

memory: Source article [PMC4610927] evaluated the effect of Remifentanil 0.3 (Group RH) versus Remifentanil 0.3 + ketamine 0.5 (Group KRH) and Remifentanil 0.05 (Group RL) on the Touch-Test sensory evaluation after surgery. No significant differences were found in demographic and anesthetic parameters, except for end-tidal desflurane concentration. Group RH showed significantly higher additional analgesic consumption, higher NRS scores at 6 and 24 hours, and higher cumulative fentanyl dose compared to Groups KRH and RL. The Touch-Test sensory evaluation value was significantly more negative in Group RH, indicating more pronounced sensory changes post-surgery. This suggests that Remifentanil 0.3 alone caused greater sensory disturbance compared to Remifentanil 0.3 with ketamine or Remifentanil 0.05. The findings suggest that combining Remifentanil with ketamine or using a lower Remifentanil dose may reduce postoperative sensory disturbances, as measured by the Touch-Test. The study highlights the importance of anesthetic regimen selection in influencing postoperative sensory function.
text: Remifentanil 0.3 (Group RH) caused more pronounced sensory changes post-surgery compared to Remifentanil 0.3 + ketamine 0.5 (Group KRH) or Remifentanil 0.05 (Group RL), as indicated by more negative Touch-Test sensory evaluation values (PMC4610927).
comparator: Remifentanil 0.3 + ketamine 0.5 (group KRH) or remifentanil 0.05 (Group RL)

memory: A study comparing "Exercise training" with "Control" on "High density lipoprotein" (HDL) found no significant differences in HDL cholesterol level changes between the groups, as detailed in the "Changes In Cardiovascular Risk Factors" section of [PMC4724125]. Subgroup analyses based on the presence of carotid plaques also showed no differences in HDL changes between the exercise and control groups, regardless of plaque status. However, LDL cholesterol levels increased in the exercise group compared to controls, particularly in patients with carotid plaques, while this effect was not observed in those without plaques. These findings suggest that exercise training does not significantly alter HDL cholesterol levels compared to control conditions. The study highlights that, in this context, exercise training may not influence HDL cholesterol but could affect LDL cholesterol in specific subgroups. Source: [PMC4724125]

memory: Source article [PMC5380277] reported that heated infusions led to shorter consciousness recovery times compared to control. Patients receiving heated infusions had faster spontaneous breathing (4.06 ± 0.72 min vs 4.47 ± 0.84 min, P = 0.042), earlier eye opening (6.72 ± 1.73 min vs 8.66 ± 2.03 min, P < 0.001), and quicker consciousness recovery (9.91 ± 1.91 min vs 11.19 ± 1.49 min, P = 0.004) than those in the control group. Additionally, extubation times were shorter in the heated infusion group (10.09 ± 1.91 min vs 11.13 ± 1.34 min, P = 0.015). No significant difference was observed in hospital stay duration between the groups. These results suggest that heated infusions may enhance postoperative recovery by accelerating consciousness return and improving clinical outcomes.
text: Heated infusions significantly reduced consciousness recovery time compared to control (9.91 ± 1.91 min vs 11.19 ± 1.49 min, P = 0.004) [PMC5380277].

memory: Source article [PMC4365564] compared "Charité artificial disc" with "ALIF with BAK cages" regarding "Rate of superficial wound infection." The superficial wound infection rate was 6.3% in the Charité group versus 2.0% in the ALIF with BAK cages group, with no statistically significant difference (P = .103). The overall infection rate was higher in the Charité group (12.7%) than in the ALIF with BAK cages group (8.1%). No deep wound infections were reported in either group. In the ALIF with BAK cages group, 3.0% of cases had iliac crest donor site infections. The results suggest a trend toward higher infection rates with the Charité artificial disc, but the difference in superficial wound infection rates was not statistically significant. The study provides insights into the comparative infection risk of these two surgical approaches.

memory: Source article [PMC5330006] evaluated the effect of "receiving 1200 mg of cranberry extract for 6 weeks" compared to a "placebo group" on "Values of total antioxidant capacity (TAC)." Results indicated that TAC levels were significantly affected by both physical exercise (p < 0.001) and cranberry supplementation. In Trial I (before supplementation), both groups experienced significant post-exercise reductions in serum TAC. In Trial II (after supplementation), the cranberry group showed significantly higher resting, post-exercise, and post-recovery TAC levels compared to the placebo group. However, even with this improvement, cranberry-supplemented athletes still experienced a significant post-exercise drop in serum TAC during Trial II. The study suggests that cranberry supplementation modulates TAC levels in response to exercise, enhancing antioxidant capacity in supplemented individuals compared to controls. These findings are supported by Fig. 1, which illustrates TAC levels during exercise tests before and after supplementation (mean ± SD).

intervention: receiving 1200 mg of cranberry extract for 6 weeks

memory: A study compared "Propolis gel" with "No treatment" for "Pain" and found both groups experienced a statistically significant decrease in pain scores by the second follow-up (P = 0.000). However, no significant difference was observed between the groups in the magnitude of pain reduction (P = 0.255), suggesting similar effectiveness. These results imply that the pain reduction may be attributed to factors other than the intervention, such as natural healing or placebo effects. The study, based on data from [PMC5863413], does not support the use of "Propolis gel" over "No treatment" for pain relief due to the lack of a significant difference in outcomes. The findings highlight the need for further research to explore underlying mechanisms and potential influencing factors. Larger sample sizes or alternative study designs may be necessary to confirm these results and assess clinical applications of "Propolis gel." The results underscore the importance of considering non-interventional factors in pain management studies and suggest that additional evidence is required before concluding the efficacy of "Propolis gel" for pain relief.

memory: Source article [PMC5393542]: HA application significantly reduced salivary TF levels at 1 week post-treatment (T2) compared to baseline (T0) and the first measurement (T1), as determined by One-Way ANOVA for Repeated Measurements and LSD post-hoc test (p<0.05). memory: Source article [PMC4045368] evaluated the effect of locking plate fixation versus nonlocking plate fixation on mean knee scores at follow-up in 41 subjects. The locking plate group had a significantly higher mean knee score at follow-up compared to the nonlocking group (80.20 ± 10.21 vs. 72.52 ± 14.75, P = 0.039). Functional scores also favored the locking plate group (77.26 ± 9.95 vs. 69.55 ± 10.22, P = 0.026). A greater proportion of patients in the locking plate group achieved an excellent knee score (65.0% vs. 33.3%). No significant difference was observed in range of motion (ROM) between the groups (122.35 ± 12.93° vs. 115.71 ± 20.14°, P = 0.219). These results suggest that locking plate fixation may lead to improved knee function and higher scores at follow-up compared to nonlocking plate fixation. The study indicates a potential clinical benefit of locking plates in enhancing postoperative knee outcomes.
text: Locking plate fixation results in significantly higher mean knee scores at follow-up compared to nonlocking plate fixation (80.20 ± 10.21 vs. 72.52 ± 14.75, P = 0.039). Functional scores also favored locking plates (P = 0.026). This suggests locking plates may improve postoperative knee function. Source: [PMC4045368].

memory: Source article [PMC4687242] reported that Ashwagandha (Withania somnifera [L.] Dunal) significantly increased mean VO2 max from baseline compared to placebo after 8 weeks (4.91 vs. 1.42; P < 0.0001). The study involved 24 participants in the Ashwagandha group and 25 in the placebo group. Greater improvements were also noted at 12 weeks (5.67 vs. 1.86). Additionally, quality of life (QOL) scores across all subdomains improved significantly more in the Ashwagandha group at 12 weeks compared to placebo (P < 0.05). These findings suggest that Ashwagandha may enhance cardiorespiratory fitness and overall well-being more effectively than a placebo over 8 to 12 weeks. The study provides evidence supporting the potential of Ashwagandha in improving aerobic capacity and quality of life in participants over an extended period.

memory: In a study on acute ischemia-reperfusion injury in isolated rat hearts (PMC3637243), Lixisenatide was compared to a placebo in terms of its effect on left ventricular risk area. No significant difference was found between Lixisenatide-treated and control groups in left ventricular risk area (placebo: 306 ± 9 mm²; Lixisenatide: 288 ± 5 mm²; n=10-11, p > 0.05). However, Lixisenatide significantly reduced infarct size, with a 36% decrease in the infarct area to risk area ratio compared to the placebo group. Infarct area was 162 ± 12 mm² in the placebo group and 98 ± 9 mm² in the Lixisenatide group. No significant differences were observed in left ventricular total area (placebo: 543 ± 16 mm²; Lixisenatide: 505 ± 7 mm²) or in rate pressure product (LVP x HR) and coronary flow during reperfusion. The results suggest that while Lixisenatide does not impact left ventricular risk area, it may provide protective effects against infarct size in acute ischemia-reperfusion injury.

memory: Study [PMC4681902] compared the effects of 80% maximal voluntary isometric contraction (MVIC) and 10% MVIC on longus colli thickness during masticatory muscle interventions. Findings showed that longus colli thickness increased with higher contraction intensity, with 80% MVIC leading to a significant increase compared to deep cervical flexor training alone (p<0.05). In contrast, 10% MVIC did not produce a similar effect. This indicates that higher contraction intensity results in greater activation of the longus colli muscle. Although the exact section was not identified, the overall results support a significant effect of 80% MVIC on longus colli thickness relative to lower intensity conditions. These results highlight the importance of contraction intensity in influencing muscle engagement and thickness. The findings suggest that rehabilitation and training protocols targeting the longus colli muscle should consider intensity levels to optimize muscle activation. This research provides insights into the relationship between contraction intensity and muscle response, which could aid in developing therapeutic exercises aimed at improving muscle function and engagement. The study underscores the need for further investigation into optimal training parameters for the longus colli muscle, with potential applications in clinical and rehabilitative settings.
text: An 80% maximal voluntary isometric contraction significantly increases longus colli thickness compared to 10% MVIC (PMC4681902). Higher intensity leads to greater muscle activation, suggesting that contraction intensity strongly influences muscle engagement and thickness.

Understanding the impact of these antibiotics on hospitalization duration is important for evaluating clinical effectiveness and guiding treatment decisions. Results provide insights into real-world performance of these antibiotics in reducing hospital stays, though further research is needed to confirm findings and explore other potential differences between the two drugs.

memory: At 12 weeks, Dextromethorphan (DM60) demonstrated significantly improved treatment retention compared to Placebo, as reported in [PMC4540107]. The DM60 group also exhibited lower plasma morphine levels and a significant decrease in plasma TNF-α levels. No significant differences were found between the groups regarding changes in plasma cytokine levels, BDNF levels, or methadone dose requirements. These findings suggest that DM60 may enhance treatment retention and reduce inflammation, as indicated by the TNF-α reduction, without affecting other key biomarkers or methadone needs. The results support the potential of DM60 as an adjunct in strategies aimed at improving treatment retention.

memory: A study evaluated the effect of "Agave derived fructans" versus "Formula" on "C-Reactive Protein" (CRP) levels in infants. CRP was measured at baseline (approximately 20 days old) and at three months of age. No statistically significant differences were observed between the two groups in CRP levels (Wilcoxon test, p = 0.05). Furthermore, CRP levels were not significantly influenced by delivery type (cesarean vs. vaginal) or serum ferritin levels (Fisher Student T-Test: p > 0.05). The results, as presented in Table 3 of the source article, suggest that Agave derived fructans did not significantly alter CRP levels compared to formula. These findings imply that Agave derived fructans may not have a notable impact on inflammatory markers like CRP in this population. While the study aimed to explore the anti-inflammatory potential of Agave derived fructans in infants, the lack of statistical significance indicates the need for further research to clarify the effects of Agave derived fructans on inflammatory responses in infants. The study contributes to the understanding of feeding interventions and their potential influence on inflammatory markers. Future investigations should consider larger sample sizes, longer observation periods, and additional inflammatory markers to better evaluate the role of Agave derived fructans in modulating inflammation in infants.
text: A study found no statistically significant difference (p = 0.05) in C-Reactive Protein levels between infants fed Agave derived fructans versus formula. Thus, Agave derived fructans do not significantly affect CRP compared to formula.

memory: Source article [PMC4440033] evaluated the impact of "Vitamin D + Calcium" versus "Calcium" on "Serum interleukin-10" in diabetic CKD patients. Serum IL-10 levels remained stable in the Vitamin D + Calcium group (p = 0.06), whereas the Calcium-only group showed a significant decrease in IL-10 at weeks 6 and 12. These findings suggest that Vitamin D, likely calcitriol, may help maintain IL-10, an anti-inflammatory cytokine, potentially offering inflammatory benefits. The study implies that diabetic CKD patients may benefit from calcium supplementation with or without calcitriol, but non-diabetic patients may require calcitriol for similar benefits. A similar effect was observed in chronic heart failure patients treated with vitamin D3 and calcium [21], reinforcing the role of Vitamin D in maintaining anti-inflammatory responses in specific populations. The results highlight the importance of considering patient-specific factors when determining the optimal supplementation strategy for inflammatory outcomes.
text: In diabetic CKD patients, "Vitamin D + Calcium" maintained serum interleukin-10 levels (p = 0.06), while "Calcium" alone caused a significant decrease. This suggests Vitamin D may help preserve anti-inflammatory cytokine levels in this population (PMC4440033).

memory: The study compared Sevoflurane-fentanyl and Isoflurane-fentanyl anesthesia on MAC and SE values before fentanyl boluses. According to the source article [PMC2911596], MAC and SE values were not significantly different between the two groups prior to fentanyl administration, with values of 0.74 ± 0.12 vs. 0.77 ± 0.17 (P = .32) and 43.5 ± 8.1 vs. 45.2 ± 8.3 (P = .47), respectively. However, heart rate (HR) was significantly higher in the Sevoflurane group (70.6 ± 13.0) compared to the Isoflurane group (64.9 ± 11.8, P < .01). After fentanyl boluses, SE and HR changes were similar in both groups, and MAC values remained stable. SSI decreased similarly in both groups following fentanyl bolus, though SSI values during surgery were higher in the Sevoflurane group. The results indicate that MAC and SE values are comparable before fentanyl boluses, but hemodynamic responses, particularly HR, differ between the anesthetic regimens. These findings may inform clinical decisions regarding anesthetic choice based on desired hemodynamic stability during surgery.

outcome: MAC and SE values before fentanyl boluses

memory: Source article [PMC5986505] assessed the impact of Virgin olive oil (VOO), Optimized virgin olive oil (OVOO), and Functional olive oil (FOO) on fasting plasma triacylglycerol levels. Baseline triacylglycerol levels were 78 ± 5 mg/dL. Following intervention, FOO did not significantly alter triacylglycerol levels, whereas VOO and OVOO led to significant increases (p = 0.037 and p = 0.002, respectively). Additionally, FOO increased total cholesterol (p = 0.021) without affecting LDL cholesterol. In contrast, VOO reduced systolic blood pressure (SBP) (p = 0.019), while FOO increased SBP (p = 0.004). Diastolic blood pressure (DBP) and pulse pressure remained unchanged across all interventions. The study suggests that VOO and OVOO may elicit different metabolic and cardiovascular effects compared to FOO, particularly in terms of triacylglycerol levels and blood pressure responses. These results highlight the potential influence of olive oil type on lipid metabolism and cardiovascular health.

memory: Source article [PMC4007144] found that an "Intimate partner prevention intervention" significantly reduced hostility during conflict management compared to a control group (ARR 1.3, 95% CI 1.06-1.58). The intervention also showed reduced intentions to use physical IPV (ARR 0.83, 95% CI 0.66-1.06) and increased positive attitudes toward sexual IPV (ARR 1.21, 95% CI 0.77-1.91). Additionally, participants in the intervention group were more likely to take on gendered household tasks (ARR 2.47, 95% CI 1.24-4.90). These findings suggest that the intervention not only lessens hostility in conflict management but also influences broader attitudes and behaviors related to gender roles and IPV. The statistically significant confidence interval for hostility outcomes supports the effectiveness of the intervention in promoting healthier conflict resolution strategies. The study highlights the potential of such interventions in improving interpersonal dynamics and reducing hostile behaviors in intimate relationships. The results indicate that addressing hostility in conflict management may be a key component of broader efforts to prevent IPV and promote gender equity.

memory: In a study comparing Erlotinib with Placebo on Quality of Life (QoL), no significant differences were observed in QoL scores between the treatment groups at one or two months, even after adjusting for baseline scores (all P ≥ .40). These results are from the Results section on Quality Of Life in the source article [PMC4112798]. The findings suggest that Erlotinib does not significantly affect QoL compared to Placebo in the short term. Supplementary Table 2 from the referenced article provides detailed statistical analyses supporting these results. These findings are relevant for understanding the impact of Erlotinib on patient-reported outcomes and may influence clinical decisions regarding its use. The lack of significant differences implies that QoL may not be a distinguishing factor between Erlotinib and Placebo in this context. Further research may be needed to explore long-term effects or different patient populations. The evidence is based on a single study, and additional research would be necessary to confirm these findings or identify potential subgroups where differences might be observed. The study’s methodology and statistical approach should be considered when interpreting these results. Overall, the findings contribute to understanding Erlotinib’s effects on patient well-being and support the need for continued investigation into its clinical benefits and limitations.

memory: Source article [PMC4794540] found that combining yogic intervention with prescribed medication significantly improved positive well-being and vitality scores compared to medication alone. At six months, the intervention group showed statistically significant improvements in positive well-being (P<0.01) and vitality (P<0.02) relative to the control group. These results suggest that adding yogic practices to conventional medication may enhance outcomes related to well-being and vitality. The study assessed these outcomes as part of a broader evaluation of mental and physical health, including anxiety, depression, and general health. The findings highlight the potential benefits of integrating yogic intervention with standard medical treatment to improve vitality and overall well-being. The study supports the notion that complementary approaches, such as yoga, may enhance the effectiveness of prescribed medication in improving patient-reported outcomes. The improvements in vitality and well-being were observed in a clinical setting, indicating that such interventions could be valuable in holistic treatment strategies. The results are statistically significant and provide evidence for the role of yogic practices in enhancing the effects of medication on psychological and physical health domains. This study contributes to the growing body of evidence supporting integrative approaches in clinical care.

memory: A study evaluated the effect of "zhibitai 480 mg + atorvastatin 10 mg (ZA10 group)" compared with "atorvastatin 20 mg (A20 group)" and "atorvastatin 40 mg (A40 group)" on creatine kinase (CK) levels. memory: A study investigated the effect of p-synephrine (50 mg) alone versus a placebo on resting metabolic rates (RMR). Results indicated that p-synephrine significantly increased RMR by 65 kcal compared to the placebo. While the placebo group experienced a slight decrease in RMR due to an 8-10 hour fast, all treatment groups, including those receiving p-synephrine alone, showed increases in RMR. This suggests that p-synephrine (50 mg) alone has a positive effect on RMR relative to a placebo. The study also included groups receiving p-synephrine combined with other compounds, such as naringin and hesperidin, which showed even greater RMR increases. However, these combinations are not directly relevant to the comparison between p-synephrine alone and placebo. The findings support the potential thermogenic effect of p-synephrine on RMR, demonstrating that it can elevate RMR beyond that of a placebo. The observed increase of 65 kcal indicates a meaningful metabolic response to p-synephrine alone. Source: [PMC3085176]

memory: Study [PMC4085217] assessed the impact of an underwater treadmill and a control condition compared to baseline on anteroposterior, mediolateral, and total postural sway. The results may guide clinical practices by emphasizing the effectiveness of interventions in reducing postural sway. Further research is necessary to clarify the control condition and better assess the specific contribution of the underwater treadmill to balance improvement.

memory: Source article [PMC1618957] found that Lanreotide Autogel® 120 mg provided superior symptom control compared to lanreotide microparticles 30 mg in acromegaly patients. Symptom control was assessed by comparing the percentage of patients reporting symptoms at the selection visit and the final visit, using McNemar's test. Statistically significant improvements were observed in hyperhidrosis (P < 0·001) and headache (P < 0·001). Symptoms were generally mild or moderate in intensity. The results are presented in Fig. 2, which illustrates the presence and intensity of acromegaly symptoms after treatment with Lanreotide microparticles 30 mg or Lanreotide Autogel® 120 mg. memory: A study evaluated the effect of Perindopril versus Placebo on Flow-mediated vasodilatation (FMD) after 6 months. Baseline FMD was 2.6% in the Perindopril group and 2.8% in the Placebo group. After 36 months, FMD increased to 3.3% in the Perindopril group and 3.0% in the Placebo group. The change in FMD after 36 months was 0.55% (95% CI −0.36, 1.47; p = 0.23) higher in the Perindopril group, which was not statistically significant. However, the rate of change in FMD per 6 months was 0.14% (SE 0.05, p = 0.02) in the Perindopril group and 0.02% (SE 0.05, p = 0.74) in the Placebo group, with a 0.12% difference in rate of change (p = 0.07). This indicates a trend toward a more significant improvement in FMD over time in the Perindopril group, though not reaching statistical significance. The results suggest that Perindopril may have a beneficial effect on FMD over a prolonged period, but further research is needed to confirm these findings. Source: PMC2039813.

memory: Source article [PMC3489577] compared the effects of 100 grams of instant oat cereal versus 100 grams of wheat flour-based noodles on waist circumference over 6 weeks. memory: Excerpts from source article [PMC5358282]: Intervention: Diazepam + chlorpheniramine; Comparator: Control; Outcome: Local pain. memory: A study investigated the effect of two fasting protocols on REM sleep percentages. Participants were assigned to three groups: baseline fasting (BLF), where fasting occurred 4 weeks prior to Ramadan; Ramadan fasting, where fasting occurred during the second week of Ramadan; and a non-fasting baseline (BL) group, measured 1 week before Ramadan. REM sleep percentages were the primary outcome. Results indicated significantly lower REM sleep percentages in both the BLF (17.7 ± 8.1%) and Ramadan (18.6 ± 10.7%) groups compared to the BL group (25.6 ± 4.8%), with p < 0.05. No significant differences were observed in JDS scores or blink total duration among the groups. MRT remained unchanged across all study periods. The findings suggest that fasting, whether conducted before or during Ramadan, may reduce REM sleep percentages relative to a non-fasting baseline. These results imply that fasting may influence sleep architecture, particularly REM sleep, independently of the timing relative to Ramadan. Source: PMC3751553.

memory: In a study comparing high-dose aripiprazole to placebo, high-dose aripiprazole was associated with a significantly higher discontinuation rate (10 patients) compared to placebo (2 patients), with a hazard ratio of 5.51 (p = 0.0278). memory: Study [PMC4636858] assessed the impact of "Mitoxantrone + methylprednisolone" versus "No treatment" on "Multiple sclerosis plaques" in 28 men and 43 women. MRI data showed a minimal reduction in plaque numbers during treatment (2.29 vs. 2.17), but no significant difference between groups (P = 0.782). Six months post-treatment, plaque numbers increased slightly in both groups (0.72 vs. 0.77), with no significant difference (P = 0.611). The Expanded Disability Status Scale (EDSS) scores showed a slight reduction during treatment (0.79 vs. 0.53), but this was not statistically significant (P = 0.953). EDSS scores increased six months after treatment ended (0.35 vs. 0.43), with no significant difference (P = 0.624). These results suggest that "Mitoxantrone + methylprednisolone" did not significantly reduce MS plaques or improve EDSS compared to no treatment. The lack of significant differences between groups implies that the intervention may not offer a clear benefit over no treatment in this context. The study underscores the need for further research to evaluate the efficacy of this combination therapy in larger, more diverse populations or under different treatment protocols.

memory: A study compared artesunate monotherapy (2 or 4 mg/kg/day once daily) with quinine plus doxycycline TID for 7 days in terms of median fever clearance time (FCT). memory: In a study published in [PMC5079604], metformin 1,000 mg daily combined with sitagliptin 100 mg daily was compared with placebo for hyperglycemia relapse-free survival. The combination therapy showed a significantly higher relapse-free survival rate compared to placebo (P = 0.015). The 2-year failure rate was higher in the placebo group than in both the sitagliptin (77% vs. 44%, P = 0.113) and metformin (77% vs. 34%, P = 0.013) groups, suggesting the combination may be more effective in preventing hyperglycemia relapse. memory: A study evaluated the effect of a 1 litre saline enema versus no enema on puerperal and neonatal infection rates. Groups were well-balanced, with 86% follow-up at one month. Newborn infection rates were 20% in the enema group and 22% in the no-enema group (RR 1.12, 95% CI 0.76 to 1.66), while puerperal infection rates were 22% with enema and 14% without (RR 0.66, 95% CI 0.43 to 1.03). memory: A study evaluated the effect of 15-pulse anti-tachycardia pacing (ATP) versus eight-pulse ATP on syncope and near-syncope episodes as a secondary endpoint. memory: Source article [PMC4823408] evaluated the impact of using an 8 cm pillow versus a 4 cm pillow during tracheal intubation on patient discomfort scores. Discomfort scores were significantly higher in the 8 cm pillow group during sequence I (Table 2). No differences were observed between the groups in terms of laryngeal view or number of intubation attempts. Objective measurements revealed greater angles from the horizontal line to the laryngeal, pharyngeal, and oral axes in the 8 cm group; however, angular differences between adjacent axes were similar. One patient in the 8 cm group required two intubation attempts before successful placement with the 4 cm pillow. These results suggest that the 8 cm pillow may be associated with increased discomfort and potential difficulties during intubation, despite similar laryngeal visualization and attempt counts. The study underscores the role of pillow height in affecting patient discomfort during tracheal intubation.

memory: The study examined the effect of daily prednisone versus placebo on Procollagen type 1 N-propeptide (P1NP), a marker of bone formation. On Day 1, prednisone doses of 20 mg or higher significantly reduced P1NP levels compared to placebo (Figure 3c, PMC4947329). By Day 2, P1NP levels increased slightly relative to placebo but then decreased in a dose- and time-dependent manner until Day 8. These results indicate a dose-dependent suppression of P1NP by prednisone, with higher doses and longer exposure leading to greater reductions. As P1NP reflects bone formation activity, the findings suggest that prednisone inhibits collagen synthesis and bone formation. The effect is most pronounced with higher prednisone doses and persists throughout the study period. The study supports the understanding that glucocorticoids like prednisone negatively impact bone metabolism, contributing to the risk of osteoporosis and fractures in long-term users. These results align with the known adverse effects of glucocorticoids on bone density and remodeling. The inclusion of a placebo group and dose-dependent analysis strengthens the validity of these findings. The results may guide clinical strategies for managing patients on corticosteroid therapy, emphasizing the need for bone health monitoring and protective interventions.

This indicates prednisone suppresses bone formation by inhibiting collagen synthesis, highlighting its adverse effects on bone metabolism.

memory: Source article [PMC4737269] evaluated the effect of Intermediate progressive addition lenses (Intermediate PALs) versus Distance single vision lenses on Ascent vertical toe clearance. Results indicated no significant difference between the two lens types in Ascent vertical toe clearance (Wald χ2 = 0.4, p = 0.54) or its variability (Wald χ2 = 0.1, p = 0.93). Additional gait safety parameters, such as ascent duration, heel clearance on descent, and descent duration, also showed no significant differences. The study found that gait safety parameters with Intermediate PALs were comparable to those with participants' own spectacles. Intermediate bifocals performed worse than both Intermediate PALs and Distance single vision lenses. Participants were experienced PAL wearers, which may explain the similar performance of Intermediate PALs compared to Distance single vision lenses. These findings suggest that Intermediate progressive addition lenses do not significantly affect Ascent vertical toe clearance when compared to Distance single vision lenses. The study highlights that lens type may not impact certain gait safety parameters in experienced PAL users.
text: Intermediate progressive addition lenses (Intermediate PALs) had no significant effect on Ascent vertical toe clearance compared to Distance single vision lenses (Wald χ2 = 0.4, p = 0.54). Gait safety parameters were comparable between the two lens types.

memory: Source article [PMC3302141]: A study compared the effects of "Behavioral lifestyle intervention" with "Control" on "Waist circumference." The intervention group showed significant reductions in adiposity measures at both 3 months and 1-year follow-up. At 1-year follow-up, the intervention group had a 19% decrease in waist circumference standard deviation score (WC-SDS) from baseline, whereas the control group showed no significant changes in WC-SDS. Additionally, the intervention group experienced a 20% increase in VO2peak-SDS-kg, compared to an 18% decrease in the control group. Subjective exhaustion, measured by Borg scores, remained stable in both groups over time. The results indicate that the behavioral lifestyle intervention had a positive effect on reducing waist circumference compared to the control group, with sustained benefits observed at the 1-year follow-up. The study suggests that behavioral lifestyle interventions can lead to significant and lasting improvements in waist circumference and cardiovascular fitness.
text: A behavioral lifestyle intervention significantly reduced waist circumference compared to control, with a 19% decrease in WC-SDS at 1-year follow-up (PMC3302141). The control group showed no significant changes.

memory: In a study evaluating the effect of maintaining a 0.2 mg/day tamsulosin dose (nonescalators) versus increasing it to 0.4 mg/day (escalators) on IIEF-5 scores in patients with no improvement in LUTS, no significant difference was found between the groups (escalators: 1.2 vs. nonescalators: 0.8, p=0.859). In contrast, among 35 patients who experienced LUTS improvement, escalators had significantly greater IIEF-5 improvement (4.6) compared to nonescalators (1.7, p=0.002). These findings suggest that increasing the tamsulosin dose does not improve erectile function in patients without LUTS improvement. However, for patients who experienced LUTS improvement, dose escalation may be associated with better erectile function outcomes. The study indicates that tamsulosin dose escalation may not be beneficial for patients without LUTS improvement but could offer advantages for those who do experience LUTS improvement. Source: [PMC3580298].

memory: In a study comparing 1,800 mg and 1,000 mg doses of gepotidacin in healthy volunteers, the higher dose was linked to a greater frequency of adverse events. Specifically, 64% (34/54) of subjects experienced adverse events with 1,800 mg, compared to 46% (23/50) with 1,000 mg. Moderate adverse events were more commonly reported with the 1,800 mg dose, including vomiting (15%), nausea (8%), throat tightness (2%), and dizziness (2%). These moderate events occurred exclusively with the higher dose. Overall, adverse events were mild to moderate in severity and included nausea, abdominal pain, abdominal discomfort, vomiting, salivary hypersecretion, feeling hot, and oropharyngeal discomfort. Five subjects (9%) discontinued the study due to adverse events, which included one case of throat tightness, three positive tests for *Clostridium difficile*, and one case of *C. difficile* infection. These findings indicate that the 1,800 mg dose of gepotidacin is associated with a higher incidence of moderate adverse events compared to the 1,000 mg dose in healthy volunteers. Source: [PMC5404516].
text: The 1,800 mg dose of gepotidacin in healthy volunteers was associated with a higher incidence of moderate adverse events (15% vomiting, 8% nausea, etc.) compared to the 1,000 mg dose (PMC5404516).

memory: Source article [PMC5976307] reports that etomidate is linked to a significantly higher incidence of myoclonus (16.1%) compared to propofol based on midazolam (1.6%), with a P-value of .004. In contrast, propofol was associated with a higher rate of transient hypotension (41.9% vs. 24.2%, P = .036). Etomidate was also linked to more adverse events that disrupted the procedure (25.8% vs. 8.1%, P = .008). The findings suggest that etomidate increases the risk of myoclonus, while propofol is associated with greater hypotension but fewer procedure-disrupting adverse events. These results highlight the importance of anesthetic selection in influencing specific adverse event profiles during procedures.

Intervention: Ropivacaine-fentanyl-clonidine (RCF); Comparators: Ropivacaine-fentanyl (RF), Ropivacaine-clonidine (RC).  
Demographics and block characteristics were similar across all groups. RCF showed no significant differences (P>0.05) in analgesic properties or hemodynamic parameters compared to RF and RC. However, RCF significantly reduced side effects (P<0.05), improving patient comfort.  

Nausea/vomiting occurred in 40% of RF patients, 15% of RC, and 10% of RCF (P<0.05). Sedation was observed in 30% of RF, 10% of RC, and 5% of RCF (P<0.05). Dry mouth was more common in RC (P<0.05). Other side effects (shivering, headache, urinary retention, respiratory depression) were comparable and nonsignificant across groups.  

Figures 1-4 show intra- and post-operative MAP and HR comparisons. Table 5 summarizes side effects across groups. RCF demonstrated superior tolerability without compromising analgesia or hemodynamics.

memory: In a study comparing high glycemic index (HGI) and low glycemic index (LGI) interventions, LGI significantly reduced glycemic response (GR) after breakfast (p = 0.02), lunch (p = 0.02), and dinner (p = 0.05). LGI also reduced daily area under the curve (AUC) (p = 0.03) and showed a significant reduction in incremental AUC (IAUC) after breakfast compared to HGI (p = 0.03). Over 48 hours, HGI resulted in a significantly greater mean amplitude of glycemic excursion (MAGE) compared to LGI (p = 0.03). Daily total AUC was significantly higher for HGI than LGI (p = 0.03). On day 2, daily total AUC decreased for LGI (p = 0.03), while HGI showed a marked increase in GR IAUC overnight (p = 0.003). Fasting glucose at 0600 h on day 2 was significantly higher for HGI than LGI (p = 0.04). Energy intake at lunch was significantly lower after an LGI breakfast compared to HGI (t(10) = -2.662, p = 0.02), with HGI showing higher mean energy intake (1041.6 ± 258.9 kcal) compared to LGI (840.7 ± 404.8 kcal). MAGE values did not differ significantly between day 1 and day 2 for either intervention.

A study compared the transillumination-assisted technique (T group) and midline approach technique (R group) for intubation. Overall success rates and average intubation times were not significantly different between the groups (P > 0.05). Success rates at first, second, and third attempts were similar between the T and R groups. However, for patients who succeeded on the second attempt, intubation time was longer in the T group (P = 0.0006).

The T group had higher incidences of dry throat (52.2% vs. 40.4%, P = 0.020), sore throat (26.8% vs. 16.8%, P = 0.009), and hoarseness (14% vs. 8%, P = 0.045) compared to the R group. In the R group, intubation was successful at first, second, and third attempts in 78.0% (195/250), 14.4% (36/242), and 4.4% (11/242) of patients, respectively, with 3.2% (8/250) failing after three attempts, primarily due to difficulty visualizing the glottis.

These findings suggest that while both techniques have comparable success rates, the transillumination-assisted technique may be associated with increased post-intubation complications. Source: PMC5320759.
text: The intubation success rates at first, second, and third attempts were similar between the T group and R group (P > 0.05). Source: PMC5320759.
outcome: The intubation success rates at the first, second, and third attempt

memory: A study compared laryngeal mask airway (PLMA) and endotracheal intubation (ETT) in terms of stress response during CO2 insufflation. No significant differences were found between groups in age, BMI, gender, ASA status, or operation time (p > 0.05). Hemodynamic and respiratory parameters also showed no significant differences between or within groups (p > 0.05). Adrenalin, noradrenalin, and dopamine levels were not significantly different between or within groups. However, serum cortisol levels 20 minutes after CO2 insufflation were significantly lower in the PLMA group compared to the ETT group (p = 0.024). Within-group comparisons showed that cortisol levels 20 minutes after CO2 insufflation were significantly higher than cortisol levels after anesthesia induction in both groups (p = 0.001). These findings suggest that PLMA may induce a less pronounced stress response, as indicated by lower cortisol levels, compared to ETT during CO2 insufflation. Source: PMC3525032.

memory: In a clinical study comparing butoconazole nitrate 2% vaginal cream (Gynazole-1) with oral fluconazole 150 mg tablets (Diflucan), butoconazole demonstrated faster symptom relief. The median time to first symptom relief was 17.5 hours for butoconazole versus 22.9 hours for fluconazole (p < 0.001). At the 75th percentile, relief occurred at 24.5 hours for butoconazole and 46.3 hours for fluconazole (p < 0.001). By 12 and 24 hours post-treatment, 44.4% and 72.8% of butoconazole patients reported relief, compared to 29.1% and 55.7% of fluconazole patients (p = 0.044 and p = 0.024, respectively). Among patients with relief within 48 hours, the median time to relief was 12.9 hours for butoconazole versus 20.7 hours for fluconazole (p = 0.048). No significant differences were found in time to total relief of symptoms or reinfection rates within 30 days. Butoconazole showed fewer adverse events than fluconazole, with vulvovaginal pruritus and burning being the most common drug-related adverse events. Overall, butoconazole demonstrated faster symptom relief and a better safety profile compared to fluconazole.
text: Butoconazole nitrate 2% vaginal cream provides faster median time to first symptom relief (17.5 hours) compared to oral fluconazole 150 mg (22.9 hours; p < 0.001).

memory: A study compared lifestyle physical activity (LPA) with a fibromyalgia education (FME) control group. The LPA group engaged in 30 minutes of self-selected moderate-intensity activity five to seven days per week. Baseline measures of pain, fatigue, depression, tender points, BMI, and six-minute walk distance were comparable between groups. Post-intervention, the LPA group showed significant reductions in Fibromyalgia Impact Questionnaire (FIQ) scores (P = .032; Cohen's d = .53) and pain (P = .006; Cohen's d = .67) compared to the FME group. The six-minute walk test showed a trend toward improvement in the LPA group (P = .067; Cohen's d = .53). No significant differences were observed between groups in BMI, fatigue, depression, or tender points. The Center for Epidemiologic Studies Depression Scale (CES-D) showed a non-significant trend toward lower scores in the LPA group (P = .888). Fatigue severity scale scores did not differ significantly pre- or post-intervention. The study suggests that LPA may be beneficial in reducing pain and FIQ scores in fibromyalgia patients compared to education alone. Source: [PMC2888205]

memory: Green tea (GT) consumption increased post-exercise fat oxidation compared to placebo (p < 0.01) and also elevated resting fat oxidation (p < 0.05). memory: In Experiment 1, cursor color (red/blue) indicated specific curl field directions. During exposure, maximum perpendicular error (MPE) decreased significantly (F1,5 = 58.220; P = 0.001), but force compensation did not increase significantly (F1,5 = 0.223; P = 0.657). Postexposure, no trajectory deviations were observed, suggesting no learned compensation for opposing fields. In Experiment 2, without visual context, MPE decreased slightly (F1,5 = 12.560; P = 0.016), but force compensation did not increase significantly (F1,5 = 1.623; P = 0.259). Postexposure, no trajectory deviations were observed, indicating no learned compensation. In Experiment 3, field direction was determined by workspace location. During exposure, MPE decreased significantly (F1,5 = 82.295; P < 0.001), and force compensation increased significantly (F1,5 = 55.284; P = 0.001). Postexposure, strong trajectory deviations in the opposite direction were observed, indicating learned compensation for field directions. These findings suggest that visual context and workspace location influence the learning of force field compensation.
text: The initial trial showed greater MPE decrease compared to the final trial (Experiment 1: F1,5 = 58.220; P = 0.001). Visual context and workspace location (Experiment 3) enhanced MPE reduction and force compensation, suggesting that these factors influence learning. Source: Study experiments.
outcome: over the course of the exposure period maximum perpendicular error (MPE) decrease - cursor color (red or blue)

memory: In a study comparing regular activity breaks (RAB) to prolonged sitting (SIT), no significant differences were found in appetite scores or food consumption. Appetite area under the curve (AUC) did not differ between RAB and SIT on Day 1 (standardised effect: 0.11 S.D., 95% CI: −0.28, 0.06; p = 0.212) or Day 2 (0.04 S.D., 95% CI: −0.15, 0.24; p = 0.648). The quantity of food consumed at the ad libitum meal on Day 2 did not significantly differ between RAB and SIT (mean difference 17 g; 95% CI: −12, 46; p = 0.253). Appetite scores before the ad libitum lunch significantly predicted the amount consumed (β = −2.4 mm; 95% CI: 0.8 mm, 3.9 mm; p = 0.003). The study involved 35 participants, with average appetite scores across days and interventions shown in Figure 3. Regular activity breaks did not significantly alter appetite response compared to prolonged sitting (Table 3). The findings suggest that interrupting prolonged sitting with regular activity breaks does not acutely influence appetite or food consumption, despite potential increases in energy expenditure.
text: Regular activity breaks did not significantly affect appetite AUC on Day 1 compared to prolonged sitting (standardised effect: 0.11 S.D., 95% CI: −0.28, 0.06; p = 0.212). Appetite scores and food consumption were similar between groups.

memory: Source: [PMC1261533]. A study compared artemether-lumefantrine (ALN) and mefloquine-artesunate (MAS3) in 490 P. falciparum malaria patients. On admission, 12.3% were anaemic. At day 7, MAS3 showed a greater mean decrease in haematocrit (9.3%) compared to ALN (6.7%) (P = 0.023). PCR-adjusted cure rates at day 42 were 98.8% (ALN) vs. 96.3% (MAS3), not statistically significant (P = 0.08). New P. falciparum infections were 27 (ALN) vs. 24 (MAS3) (P > 0.05). Adverse events were more common in MAS3, though not statistically significant. P. vivax parasitaemia was detected in 26.3% of patients, with significantly fewer cases in MAS3 (29/227) vs. ALN (90/225) (P < 0.001), and a longer median time to appearance in MAS3 (40 days) vs. ALN (28 days) (P < 0.001). Both regimens were well-tolerated with no serious adverse events.
text: Artemether-lumefantrine (ALN) was associated with a higher incidence of P. vivax parasitaemia during follow-up compared to mefloquine-artesunate (MAS3) (P < 0.001). MAS3 showed significantly fewer cases and a longer median time to appearance of P. vivax parasitaemia. Source: [PMC1261533].

memory: A study compared three intubation techniques: lightwand only (LW), lightwand under direct laryngoscopy (DL), and lightwand with WEI JET under direct laryngoscopy (WEI). Intubation time was significantly longer in the WEI group (110.8±18.3 s) compared to the LW group (63.3±27.5 s, p = 0.000) and DL group (66.7±29.4 s, p = 0.000).
