memory: In a porcine model of deceased donor kidney transplantation, α-melanocyte stimulating hormone (α-MSH) was assessed for its impact on renal function and hemodynamics. α-MSH treatment led to significantly lower urine output over ten hours post-transplantation compared to controls (p<0.05), without causing anuria. It also tended to impair the recovery of glomerular filtration rate (GFR), with significantly lower GFR in the α-MSH group at ten hours post-reperfusion (8.2±5.7−13.3 ml/min vs. 14.3±10.1−19 ml/min; p<0.05). Sodium excretion was reduced in α-MSH-treated animals at ten hours post-reperfusion (2.8±1.2−4.5 mmol/min vs. 5.4±4.2−5.8 mmol/min; p<0.05). Hemodynamic changes included a trend toward reduced mean arterial blood pressure and increased heart rate following α-MSH administration. However, α-MSH did not affect the expression of inflammatory markers. The results indicate that α-MSH may negatively affect short-term graft function post-transplantation, likely due to hemodynamic effects rather than anti-inflammatory mechanisms. Source: PMC3984270.
text: α-MSH significantly reduced urine output compared to controls in a porcine kidney transplant model (p<0.05), without causing anuria. It also impaired GFR recovery and sodium excretion. Source: PMC3984270.

memory: A study compared telemonitored clinical care (TCC) with usual clinical care (UCC) for CPAP treatment. TCC patients used CPAP for 4.1 ± 1.8 hours per night, compared to 2.8 ± 2.2 hours per night in the UCC group (P = .07), representing a 46% increase in use. TCC patients used CPAP on 78% ± 22% of nights, while UCC patients used it on 60% ± 32% of nights (P = .07), indicating better adherence trends. However, no statistically significant differences were found in CPAP efficacy measures, including mask leak and the Apnea-Hypopnea Index (AHI). The TCC group had a higher mean AHI (7.9 ± 4.1) compared to the UCC group (5.0 ± 4.0; P = .04). When considering change in AHI from baseline, there was no significant difference between groups (TCC: 38.1 ± 18.4; UCC: 32.2 ± 14.8; P = .32). Patients in the TCC group reported a significantly higher likelihood to continue using CPAP compared to the UCC group. Both groups expressed high satisfaction with care and were “not concerned” about wireless data monitoring. The study followed participants for an average of 60 ± 4.0 days.
text: Patients receiving TCC reported a significantly higher likelihood to continue using CPAP compared to those receiving UCC (P < .05). TCC showed trends toward better adherence but no significant differences in CPAP efficacy measures (AHI). Source: Study with 60-day follow-up.
outcome: Patients rated their likelihood to continue using CPAP

memory: A study compared usual care (UC) with usual care plus manual therapy (UCMT) for headache management. Both groups showed significant improvements in primary and secondary outcomes, including headache frequency, pain intensity, medication use, absenteeism, and professional help utilization. However, no significant differences were found between the two treatment groups. The study had a small sample size (n = 19 UC, n = 18 UCMT), which may have limited the ability to detect group differences. Baseline headache characteristics were comparable between the groups, as shown in Table 1. The Global Perceived Effect (GPE) indicated no significant difference in the number of responders between UC and UCMT. The Headache Impact Test-6 (HIT-6) scores showed significant reductions from baseline in both groups, but no significant differences were found between the groups at follow-up measurements, as detailed in Table 3. These findings suggest that both interventions had similar effects on headache-related outcomes, though the small sample size may affect the generalizability of the results.
text: A study found no significant difference between usual care and manual therapy in reducing headache frequency, pain intensity, medication use, absenteeism, or professional help utilization. Both groups showed similar improvements, though the small sample size may limit generalizability.
outcome: Reduction in headache frequency, pain intensity, medication intake, absenteeism, and use of additional professional help (secondary outcomes)

memory: In a study comparing frovatriptan and rizatriptan for the treatment of menstrually related migraine, frovatriptan showed a significantly lower rate of migraine recurrence at 24 hours (10%) compared to rizatriptan (32%, p < 0.01). The cumulative hazard of recurrence during follow-up was also significantly lower with frovatriptan (Fig. 1). Pain relief at 2 hours was similar between the two drugs, with 58% for frovatriptan and 64% for rizatriptan (p = NS). Pain-free rates at 2 hours were 31% and 34%, respectively (p = NS). At 24 hours, 67% of frovatriptan-treated patients and 61% of rizatriptan-treated patients were pain-free, while 81% and 74% experienced pain relief, respectively (p = NS). Despite similar immediate efficacy, frovatriptan demonstrated a more favorable sustained effect, with a significantly lower recurrence rate. The study included 49 attacks treated with frovatriptan and 59 with rizatriptan, representing 17% and 21% of all attacks, respectively. Frovatriptan was found to be as effective as rizatriptan in the immediate treatment of menstrually related migraine attacks but showed a lower rate of migraine recurrence.
text: Frovatriptan significantly reduced the cumulative hazard of recurrence during follow-up for menstrually related migraine compared to rizatriptan (10% vs. 32%, p < 0.01). Both drugs showed similar immediate efficacy, but frovatriptan provided better sustained relief. (Source: Study cited in working notes)
outcome: cumulative hazard of recurrence during the follow-up - menstrually related migraine

memory: A study compared video-assisted remote consultations (RMC) with standard in-person consultations (UNN) in terms of patient outcomes and care processes. No significant differences were found in the number of operated patients (p = 0.432). In the UNN group, two patients were not operated on due to other serious disorders, four improved without surgery, and one did not attend. All RMC patients underwent their planned operations. The number of consultations per patient varied, with a trend toward more consultations in the RMC group, though not statistically significant. For patients requiring casting, RMC consultations were significantly longer (29.0 min) than UNN consultations (22.6 min, p = 0.0063). Casting was performed in 11% of consultations. No significant differences were observed in the number of discharged patients or in patient-reported outcomes at three and 12 months. RMC patients were not more likely to be referred again within two years for the same disorder (p = 0.858). After the first consultation, 32% of RMC patients were discharged, compared to 36% in the UNN group (p = 0.389). These findings suggest that video-assisted consultations are not inferior to standard in-person care. Source: [PMC5017045]
text: Video-assisted remote consultations (RMC) significantly increased the mean consultation duration for patients requiring casting compared to standard consultations (UNN) (29.0 min vs. 22.6 min, p = 0.0063). Source: [PMC5017045]
outcome: The mean consultation duration in the subgroup patients who required casting

memory: A study compared Pro Taper Universal retreatment (PR) with Mani NRT-GPR (MR) in terms of their effectiveness in removing filling material and dentin during root canal retreatment. PR demonstrated a statistically lower mean percentage of remaining filling material compared to MR (P=0.0056). Additionally, PR caused significantly greater dentin removal (5.02%) compared to MR (1.36%, P=0.0028). Despite these advantages, neither system achieved complete removal of filling material from the canals. No complications such as perforations, ledges, obstructions, or instrument fractures were reported for either system after retreatment. The findings were consistent across multiple outcome measures. While PR was more effective in removing filling material and dentin, both systems had limitations in achieving complete canal cleanliness. These results suggest that PR may be more effective than MR in retreatment procedures, but neither system is fully capable of achieving optimal canal cleanliness.
text: Pro Taper Universal retreatment (PR) significantly reduces remaining filling material compared to Mani NRT-GPR (MR) (P=0.0056), though neither achieves complete removal. PR also causes more dentin removal (P=0.0028). Both systems lack full canal cleanliness.

Source: PMC1784771  
Intervention: Prostaglandin gel + hygroscopic cervical dilators  
Comparator: Prostaglandin gel alone  
Outcomes: Cervical ripening, induction time, infection  

A study compared 17 patients receiving prostaglandin gel alone with 23 patients receiving prostaglandin gel combined with hygroscopic cervical dilators. No significant demographic differences were observed between the groups. After six hours of ripening, the combined therapy group showed a significantly greater improvement in Bishop score (3.6 vs. 2.1, P = 0.007) and a trend toward shorter induction time (21.7 vs. 26.4 hours, P = 0.085). However, the combined therapy group had a significantly higher infection rate (59% vs. 12%, P = 0.003).  

Conclusion: While the combination of hygroscopic cervical dilators with prostaglandin gel enhances cervical ripening and may reduce induction time, the increased risk of infection is considered too high to recommend this approach.
text: The combination of prostaglandin gel with hygroscopic cervical dilators significantly improves Bishop score after 6 hours (3.6 vs. 2.1, P=0.007) compared to prostaglandin gel alone (PMC1784771). However, it increases infection risk.
intervention: Prostaglandin gel plus hygroscopic cervical dilators
outcome: Changes in Bishop score after 6 hours

memory: The Sonas programme showed significant improvements in communication compared to baseline (p=0.014 at T1; p=0.002 at T2), though no overall effect was observed on the Holden Communication Scale (HCS). Severe dementia patients in the Sonas group scored higher than the reading group at 12 weeks, but not at 24 weeks. Linear mixed model analysis revealed a significant difference in communication change between Sonas and reading groups (p=0.019) and between Sonas and control groups (p=0.001). HCS scores in the Sonas group decreased from 24.7 at baseline (T0) to 23.6 at 12 weeks (T1) and 22.3 at 24 weeks (T2). MMSE scores indicated significant differences in interest in past events, humour, and general knowledge between Sonas and reading groups at T0 (p=0.011) and T1 (p=0.044), but no significant differences in cognitive aspects such as remembering names or speech. The reading group was used to rule out attention effects from staff. The study took place between April and October 2014, with data collected at baseline (T0), 12 weeks (T1), and 24 weeks (T2).
text: The Sonas programme showed a significant improvement in communication compared to control groups (p=0.001), but no overall effect on MMSE scores. HCS scores decreased over time, with no significant differences in cognitive aspects like remembering names or speech.

memory: A study compared radiofrequency ablation (RFA) and resection in treating colorectal liver metastases (CRLM). Among 226 patients with solitary CRLM < 3 cm, overall survival (OS) and disease-free survival (DFS) were similar between RFA and resection (P = 0.962, 0.980). However, for 70 patients with solitary CRLM ≥ 3 cm, DFS was lower with RFA (23.1%) compared to resection (36.6%, P = 0.01). In 186 patients with multiple metastases, OS was not significantly different between RFA (14.3%), resection (34.6%), and combination therapy (22.9%) (P = 0.330). DFS rates were 6.4% (RFA), 16.2% (resection), and 18.4% (combination). For 148 patients with solitary metachronous CRLM, 5-year OS was 47.6% (RFA) vs. 56.0% (resection, P = 0.308), with no significant DFS difference (P = 0.164). OS and DFS were correlated with metastasis count and chemotherapy use (P < 0.001). RFA DFS was significantly lower than resection for ≥ 3 cm solitary CRLM (P = 0.015).
text: For patients with solitary CRLM < 3 cm, RFA and resection show similar 5-year DFS. However, for ≥ 3 cm, RFA has significantly lower DFS (23.1% vs. 36.6%, P = 0.01). In multiple metastases, DFS is lowest with RFA (6.4%). Source: Study on CRLM treatment outcomes.

memory: A study with 13 participants found that pomegranate juice (PJ) consumption led to significant reductions in systolic blood pressure (SBP) and diastolic blood pressure (DBP). The PJ contained 5.8 mg of anthocyanins per 100 ml. Pre- vs. post-trial comparisons showed a 7% reduction in SBP (P = 0.013) and a 6% reduction in DBP (P = 0.010). However, changes in flow-mediated dilation (FMD) were 20%, which were not statistically significant (P = 0.172). No significant changes were observed in inflammatory biomarkers, including C-reactive protein (CRP) (P = 0.263), intracellular adhesion molecule-1 (ICAM-1) (P = 0.248), vascular cell adhesion molecule 1 (VCAM-1) (P = 0.657), E-selectin (P = 0.182), and interleukin-6 (IL-6) (P = 0.763). These findings suggest that while PJ consumption had a positive effect on blood pressure, it did not significantly improve endothelial function or reduce inflammatory markers. Baseline and post-trial values for the evaluated parameters are summarized in Table 1 of the source article [PMC3933059].
text: Pomegranate juice significantly reduced SBP (7%, P=0.013) and DBP (6%, P=0.010) compared to baseline in a study of 13 participants. However, it did not significantly affect endothelial function or inflammatory markers [PMC3933059].
outcome: Systolic blood pressure (SBP), diastolic blood pressure (DBP)

memory: A study compared rFSH + rLH with rFSH + HMG in terms of follicular development and fertility outcomes. No significant differences were observed between the two groups in the number of follicles, total oocytes, M2 oocytes, or fetal quality (p > 0.05). However, the rFSH + HMG group had a significantly higher total number of fetuses (p = 0.02). Moreover, fertility outcomes, including live birth rate, chemical pregnancy rate, and clinical pregnancy rate, were significantly higher in the rFSH + HMG group compared to the rFSH + rLH group (p < 0.05). memory: A study compared Endobutton and Rigidfix for knee stability. The pivot shift test showed no significant difference between groups (P = 0.99), and no gross instability was observed. Knee range of motion was 135.73 ± 2.63° for Endobutton and 129.87 ± 7.14° for Rigidfix (P = 0.06), with no significant differences in pain frequency or intensity. Patient satisfaction scores were significantly higher in the Endobutton group (89 ± 4.3 vs. 85 ± 2.9, P = 0.006), as was the ability to perform sports activities (85.2 ± 4.6 vs. 80.5 ± 4, P = 0.006). During the Ant. drawer test, 53.3% of Endobutton and 66.7% of Rigidfix patients had tibial displacement of 5 mm or less (P = 0.46). No significant differences were found in last month symptoms scores between the two groups (P = 0.34).

memory: A clinical study compared telephone and mail follow-up for recruitment into the SCOPE trial, a colon cancer screening RCT halted early due to funding issues. Both groups had similar mean ages (telephone: 55.7 years, SD 6.1; mail: 55.6 years, SD 6.3). Of 1,348 mailed invitations, 104 enrolled in the RCT. Among 952 non-responders, 480 were randomized to telephone follow-up and 472 to mail. Telephone follow-up improved attendance for eligibility screening (17.5%, 84/480) compared to mail (9.1%, 43/472; RR 1.92, 95% CI 1.36–2.71, P < 0.001). Enrollment into the RCT was also higher with telephone follow-up (12.3%, 59/480) versus mail (7.4%, 35/472; RR 1.66, 95% CI 1.11–2.47, P=0.01). Among telephone contacts, 60 (18.1%) were ineligible due to recent colorectal screening (18 fecal occult blood tests, 39 colonoscopies, 1 virtual colonoscopy, 2 unspecified). The study nurse conducted live phone conversations with 332 (69%) of the telephone group. Results indicate that telephone follow-up is more effective than mail in improving attendance and enrollment rates in the RCT. Source: PMC3599938.
text: The effect of "Follow-up invitation by telephone" compared with "Follow-up invitation by mail" on "Age of the participants" was minimal, as both groups had similar mean ages (55.7 vs. 55.6 years). Source: PMC3599938.

A study compared immediate implants (placed post-extraction) with delayed implants (placed in healed sites) in fixed full-arch prostheses. With a small sample size and 12-month follow-up, no statistically significant differences were found between groups in implant success, peri-implant marginal bone loss, or peri-implant health parameters, including crevicular fluid volume (CFV), plaque index, gingival retraction, probing depth, modified gingival index, or mucositis. 

At time points 2 and 3, maxillary CFV was significantly higher in immediate implants (Group A) than delayed implants (Group B), but overall mean CFV did not differ significantly between groups. Plaque levels increased over time but showed no significant differences between groups (p≥0.05). 

At prosthetic loading, immediate implants had greater keratinized mucosa width and probing depth compared to delayed implants, but these differences disappeared after six and twelve months. Bone loss was 0.54 ± 0.39 mm for immediate implants and 0.66 ± 0.25 mm for delayed implants, with no statistically significant difference (p=0.201). No implants failed in either group. The study included 144 implants: 76 in healed sites and 68 placed immediately. Data were analyzed using the Mann-Whitney U-test.
text: At time points 2 and 3, maxillary CFV was significantly higher in immediate implants compared to delayed implants, though overall mean CFV did not differ significantly (p≥0.05). Source: Study with 144 implants and 12-month follow-up.

memory: A study compared a self-management intervention to treatment as usual (TAU) in patients with chronic mental illness. Baseline characteristics, including demographics, age of onset, illness duration, and hospitalization history, were similar between the groups. Most participants had a long illness duration (mean = 17.4 years) and multiple hospitalizations. Baseline medication adherence (MAQ) and insight (SAUMD) were not significantly different between groups. Over 30 months, only 2 (1.9%) of 103 intervention participants were re-hospitalized, compared to 14 (14.3%) of 98 control participants (X²=8.83, p=0.003). The intervention group showed significantly better medication adherence, greater insight, and higher antipsychotic dosages at 30 months. By the study's end, the intervention group had significantly higher MAQ scores, overall SAUMD scores, and improved scores on all four SAUMD subscales compared to the control group. These results suggest that the self-management intervention positively influenced medication adherence and insight in patients with chronic mental illness.
text: The self-management group had a significantly lower rate of re-hospitalizations (1.9%) compared to treatment as usual (14.3%) over 30 months (X²=8.83, p=0.003). This suggests that self-management interventions effectively reduce re-hospitalization rates in patients with chronic mental illness.

A study compared single-dose and multiple-dose artificial tears in dry eye patients. Groups A (single-dose) and B (multiple-dose) had comparable baseline demographics (age: 44.08 ± 6.29 vs. 45.83 ± 8.42 years). No significant differences were found in OSDI, TBUT, conjunctival/corneal staining, or Schirmer scores between groups pre-intervention (p > 0.05).  

After 4 weeks, both groups showed significant improvements in OSDI (p < 0.001), conjunctival (p < 0.001), and corneal staining scores (p < 0.001). TBUT increased slightly but not significantly (Group A: p = 0.027; Group B: p = 0.013). Schirmer scores showed no significant improvement (Group A: p = 0.129; Group B: p = 0.115).  

No significant differences in efficacy were observed between the two artificial tear products for OSDI (p = 0.440), conjunctival staining (p = 0.822), or corneal staining (p = 0.793). The interaction between product type and change over time was not significant for OSDI (p = 0.468), conjunctival staining (p = 0.080), or corneal staining (p = 0.894).  

Both products had similar effects on all measured outcomes. No significant differences in Schirmer scores (p = 0.497) or TBUT (p = 0.497) were found between groups.
text: The study found no significant difference in the effect of single-dose versus multiple-dose artificial tears on the Ocular Surface Disease Index (OSDI) (p = 0.440). Both treatments improved OSDI similarly after 4 weeks. Source: [PMC5595267].

memory: A clinical study evaluated a 10-week telephone intervention with three monitoring calls on blood glucose levels in pregnant women at 28 weeks. The intervention group showed lower mean±SD blood glucose levels at multiple time points compared to controls: 2 hours after dinner (122.5±19.7 vs. 131.1±22.1 mg/dl, p=0.06), before sleeping (113.2±15.8 vs. 124.7±13.9 mg/dl, p=0.1), and 2 hours after breakfast (123.2±18.8 vs. 131.2±20.9 mg/dl, p=0.058). The most significant difference was at 2 hours after lunch (123±18 vs. 137.5±25.7 mg/dl, p=0.008). The intervention group also showed significantly higher mean±SD differences in fasting blood glucose levels between 28 and 32 weeks (p<0.05), and between 28 and 36 weeks (p<0.05). Additionally, the intervention group had a significantly higher rate of postpartum glucose screening tests (P<0.001). These findings suggest that the telephone intervention may improve blood glucose control during pregnancy and enhance postpartum screening adherence. The data is sourced from the results section of the article [PMC4715405].

memory: A study evaluated the impact of text message–based feedback on mindfulness home practice and four outcome measures: PHQ-9 (depressive symptoms), PTQ (perseverative thinking), FFA (self-compassion), and SCS-D (self-compassion scale). Participants receiving feedback were compared to those who did not. Post-hoc analyses showed near-zero to small, nonsignificant effect sizes across all outcomes (Table 2). On symptom measures (PTQ, PHQ-9), positive effect sizes suggested a slight benefit for the intervention group. In contrast, positive values on FFA and SCS-D indicated a slight advantage for the control group. The most noticeable differences, though still small, were observed in perseverative thinking, self-reported mindfulness, and the number of reported exercises. However, no significant differences were found in primary outcomes, indicating limited impact of the text message intervention on depressive symptoms, perseverative thinking, mindfulness, or self-compassion. Source: [PMC5434251]

memory: A clinical study assessed the effects of a bio-active peptide supplement (Bio-GroTM) versus a placebo on hemodynamic variables (systolic blood pressure, diastolic blood pressure, heart rate), blood chemistry counts (RBC, MCV, MCHC), and metabolic panel measures (creatinine, eGFR, BUN/creatinine, BUN, sodium, chloride, CO2, calcium, albumin, alkaline phosphate). No specific effects of the supplement were observed on these parameters. While significant time effects were noted for several variables (p < 0.05), there were no significant group or group × time interaction effects, indicating that the supplement did not influence these variables differently over time. The study concluded that although some parameters exhibited time-related changes, the bio-active peptide supplement did not demonstrate specific effects on the measured outcomes. Source: [PMC4595235]

memory: A study compared cefepime (C), cefepime with amikacin (C-A), and cefepime with levofloxacin (C-L) for ventilator-associated pneumonia (VAP). No significant differences were observed in key clinical outcomes across the three groups. ICU stay after infection had medians of 15 (7.5–24.75), 16 (9–21), and 14 (9.5–21.5) days for groups C, C-A, and C-L, respectively (p > 0.05). Ventilator-free days (VFDs) within 28 days post-infection were 16.1 ± 8.3, 12.6 ± 8.1, and 12.6 ± 10.4 for groups C, C-A, and C-L, respectively, with no statistically significant differences (p > 0.05). Kaplan-Meier curves for mechanical ventilation duration also showed no differences between the groups (p > 0.05). Additionally, the time course of temperature, leukocytosis, or C-reactive protein levels showed no significant differences among the groups. VAP was microbiologically confirmed in 84% (59 patients), with no differences in mortality or length of ICU stay. The study randomized 20 patients in each group (C, C-A, and C-L). The findings suggest that the addition of amikacin or levofloxacin to cefepime did not improve clinical outcomes in patients with VAP. Source: PMC1550875.
text: The study found no significant difference in ICU length of stay between cefepime (C), cefepime with amikacin (C-A), and cefepime with levofloxacin (C-L) groups (p > 0.05). Source: PMC1550875.

In a phase II randomized trial (PMC2361806), 56 patients received irinotecan with high-dose 5-fluorouracil plus leucovorin (ILF), while 58 received etoposide with 5-fluorouracil plus leucovorin (ELF). Median age was 62 years, and Karnofsky performance status was 90% in both groups. At 14 weeks, objective response rates were 30% for ILF and 17% for ELF (RR 0.57, 95% CI 0.29–1.13, P=0.0766), but over the entire treatment period, overall response rates were 43% for ILF and 24% for ELF (RR 0.56, 95% CI 0.33–0.97, P=0.0467). Median progression-free survival was 4.5 months for ILF versus 2.3 months for ELF, and time to treatment failure was 3.6 vs 2.2 months (P=0.4542). Overall survival was 10.8 vs 8.3 months (P=0.2818). 

Toxicity profiles differed: grade 3/4 diarrhoea occurred in 18% of ILF patients, while grade 3/4 neutropenia was more common in ELF (57%). Grade 3/4 alopecia was also more frequent in ELF (28%) compared to ILF (5%). Both regimens were generally well tolerated. The study suggests ILF provides better response rates than ELF and warrants further investigation for metastatic gastric cancer.
text: The ILF regimen was associated with a lower incidence of grade 3/4 digestive system toxic events compared to ELF (18% vs. no specific data for ELF, but higher rates of other toxicities like neutropenia and alopecia). Source: PMC2361806.

memory: Study [PMC5019971] evaluated maraviroc intensification versus unchanged cART in 21 HIV-positive males with suppressed viral load. FMD improved by +0.73% (IQR -0.25 to 1.70) during maraviroc compared to -0.42% (IQR -1.89 to 0.25) in control (p=0.049), similar to statin effects. CCR5 expression in CD4+ T cells increased to 2.4% (IQR 1.5-4.8) versus 0.4% (p=0.010), and in CD8+ T cells to 14.0% (IQR 8.0-17.8) versus 2.6% (p=0.002) during intervention. A carry-over effect was observed in control period 2 (C2), with CD8+ CCR5+ expression at 16.3% versus baseline 8.3% (p=0.021). No significant changes in D-dimer, hsCRP, or T cell activation markers were found. ΔFMD correlated negatively with ΔD-dimer (β -22.70, 95% CI -39.27 to -6.13, p=0.011) and ΔCD95+ CD4+ T cells (β -0.16, 95% CI -0.28 to -0.04, p=0.013). The study included two intervention periods (INT1, INT2) and two control periods (C1, C2), with C2 excluded due to carry-over.
text: Maraviroc intensification significantly increased CCR5 expression in CD8+ T cells compared to unchanged cART (14.0% vs. 2.6%, p=0.002) in HIV-positive males with suppressed viral load (PMC5019971).
outcome: CCR5 expression in CD8+ T cells

memory: A study assessed the effectiveness of intensive sound masking therapy on tinnitus using the Tinnitus Handicap Inventory (THI). Pre-intervention THI scores were significantly lower in the non-effective group (M=37.57, SD=21.86) than in the effective group (M=54.04, SD=18.45; t=4.11, P<0.001). Post-intervention, overall THI scores showed significant changes (t=12.54, P<0.001). The effective group experienced a significant reduction in THI scores (t=−14.07, P<0.001), whereas the non-effective group showed no significant reduction (t=−1.98, P=0.054). No significant difference in post-intervention THI scores was observed between the effective and non-effective groups. Logistic regression was used to identify predictive factors for treatment effectiveness, based on variables significantly different between the groups. Audiometric configurations were categorized into four sub-groups, and pair comparisons were conducted for further analysis. The study included both baseline and control groups, with the intervention applied to both effective and non-effective subgroups.
text: Intensive sound masking therapy significantly reduced THI scores in the effective subgroup compared to baseline (t=−14.07, P<0.001), while no significant change was observed in the non-effective subgroup (t=−1.98, P=0.054).
intervention: intensive sound masking therapy on tinnitus in effective subgroup

memory: A study compared the Levonorgestrel-releasing intrauterine system (LNG-IUS) and oral norethisterone acetate (NET) for treating endometrial hyperplasia (EH). Regression rates at 3, 6, and 12 months were significantly higher in the LNG-IUS group compared to the NET group (67.8% vs. 47.5%, 79.7% vs. 60.7%, and 88.1% vs. 55.7%, respectively; all p<0.05). The median time to regression was similar between the two groups (3 months each; p=0.697). The hysterectomy rate during follow-up was significantly higher in the NET group (57.4%) than in the LNG-IUS group (22%; p<0.001). Six LNG-IUS users underwent hysterectomy due to persistent bleeding after about 10 months of use, but histological examination confirmed EH regression in these cases. The study used intention-to-treat analysis for evaluating regression rates. Source: [PMC3644688]
text: The Levonorgestrel-releasing intrauterine system (LNG-IUS) showed a higher regression rate at 3 months (67.8%) compared to oral norethisterone acetate (47.5%; p<0.05). Source: [PMC3644688].

memory: An 8-week study compared calcium carbonate + calcitriol to calcitriol alone. No statistically significant changes in serum PTH levels were observed for either group. intervention: a combination of calcium carbonate and calcitriol group

memory: In a study comparing magnesium sulfate (MgSO4) at doses of 30, 40, and 50 mg/kg (Groups I, II, III) with normal saline (Group S), no significant differences in heart rate were observed across groups at baseline, preoperation, and at 1, 3, 5, and 10 minutes post-intubation (P > 0.05). memory: A clinical study compared tranexamic acid (TXA) to placebo and found no significant difference in the risk of death from all causes (RR = 0.69; 95% CI 0.35 to 1.39) or in the risk of an unfavorable outcome on the Glasgow Outcome Scale (RR = 0.76; 95% CI 0.46 to 1.27). memory: In a study [PMC4610775], patients treated with urinary kallidinogenase (UK) showed cognitive improvement at 4 weeks, with a reduction in serum Aβ1-40 levels and no change in Aβ1-42. By 8 weeks, cognitive improvements persisted, and both Aβ1-40 and Aβ1-42 levels significantly decreased from baseline. The control group exhibited no changes. memory: In a study comparing podiatry, trichloroacetic acid (TCA), and potassium hydroxide (KOH) treatments, hydration and texture showed gradual improvement over time for both TCA and KOH groups, with TCA showing a reduction in hydration and texture at D14. Skin elasticity improved gradually in the KOH group, while TCA-treated skin showed decreased elasticity over time. At D7, TCA showed significant improvement in skin texture compared to KOH (p = 0.00). No significant differences were found between TCA and KOH groups for hydration and elasticity at each time point. By D21, improvements in elasticity (p = 0.04 and p = 0.91) and texture (p = 0.33 and p = 0.04) were not significantly different between groups. Callus surface area was significantly reduced in both TCA and KOH groups (p = 0.00), with no significant differences between the groups by D21. Podiatry treatment showed similar trends, with gradual increases in hydration and texture and a significant decrease in elasticity over time. Figure 3 illustrates significant reductions in callus surface area at D7, D14, and D21 for both treatment groups, except for D7 in the TCA group. Pairwise comparisons showed no significant differences between KOH and TCA groups in all outcome measures by D21.

memory: In a clinical trial involving 293 patients with locally advanced breast cancer, participants were randomized to receive either tri-weekly FEC (5-fluorouracil–epirubicin–cyclophosphamide) or weekly PE (paclitaxel–epirubicin). The PE regimen demonstrated a significantly higher overall clinical response rate (76.06% vs. 59.95%, P = 0.001) and lower post-chemotherapy pathologic T and N stages (P < 0.001) compared to FEC. However, no significant difference was observed in overall pathologic complete response (pCR) rates (10.61% vs. 12.31%, P = 0.665), breast pCR rates (13.64% vs. 16.92%, P = 0.460), or regional lymph node pCR rates (34.85% vs. 39.23%, P = 0.463). The PE regimen was associated with a higher incidence of severe neutropenia compared to FEC (11.97% vs. 5.96%, P = 0.031). Additionally, more patients in the FEC group were eligible for breast-conserving surgery (27.27% vs. 35.28% in the PE group). All 262 patients were included in the intention-to-treat analysis for pathologic response assessments.
text: The PE regimen was associated with a higher incidence of severe neutropenia (11.97% vs. 5.96%, P = 0.031) compared to FEC. Source: Clinical trial involving 293 patients with locally advanced breast cancer.

In a clinical study comparing bimatoprost 0.03% preservative-free (PF) to bimatoprost 0.03% (Lumigan), both significantly reduced intraocular pressure (IOP) from baseline at all time points (p<0.001). The mean IOP reduction ranged from −7.49 mm Hg to −5.93 mm Hg for bimatoprost PF and −7.77 mm Hg to −6.06 mm Hg for bimatoprost. The between-group difference in mean worse eye IOP was <0.4 mm Hg at all time points and was not statistically or clinically significant. 

Both treatments were well tolerated. Adverse events (AEs) were reported in 40.5% of bimatoprost PF and 44.1% of bimatoprost patients (p=0.382), with ocular AEs occurring in 31.9% and 34.9%, respectively (p=0.434). The most frequent ocular AE was conjunctival hyperaemia, considered treatment-related in all but one patient in each group, and mostly mild or moderate.

Iris color change was observed in 0.3% of bimatoprost PF and 1.0% of bimatoprost patients (p=0.369). No statistically or clinically significant between-group differences were found for changes in cup/disc ratio, best-corrected visual acuity at week 12, or visual field. Vital signs showed no clinically significant differences between groups.
text: Bimatoprost 0.03% PF and Lumigan both significantly reduced intraocular pressure, with minimal differences (≤0.4 mm Hg) that were not clinically significant. Adverse events were similar between groups, with no significant differences in other outcomes. (Source: Clinical study)

Test 1 showed that both T-EO and Af-EO significantly reduced bacterial viability (BV) below baseline levels up to 7 hours post-rinse compared to water (P < 0.001). However, neither formulation significantly reduced the thickness of the 48-hour PL-biofilm after a single rinse, with slight reductions (20.19 ± 3.62 μm for T-EO and 18.58 ± 3.14 μm for Af-EO) that were not statistically significant. memory: Study [PMC5045666] assessed vitamin D supplementation in 40 children aged 11.5 ± 1.175 years compared to a placebo. The intervention group showed significant increases in serum vitamin D (P < 0.001) and HDL-C (P = 0.007) post-intervention, while the control group experienced slight decreases (P = 0.27 for both). However, no significant group differences were observed for HDL-C (P = 0.11) or vitamin D (P = 0.20) post-intervention. Before adjustment, HDL-C levels were 49.65 ± 11.53 mg/dL in the study group and 43.65 ± 11.47 mg/dL in the control group. After adjustment, these values were 49.54 and 43.76 mg/dL, respectively. ANCOVA revealed a significant correlation between pre- and post-intervention HDL levels (P < 0.001). After adjusting for confounders, the study group had significantly higher HDL levels than the control group (P = 0.04). Similarly, vitamin D levels showed a significant correlation before and after the intervention (P < 0.001), with the study group having significantly higher levels after adjustment (P < 0.001).
text: Vitamin D supplementation significantly increased serum vitamin D (P < 0.001) and HDL-C (P = 0.007) in children compared to placebo, with adjusted HDL-C levels significantly higher in the study group (P = 0.04). Source: [PMC5045666].

memory: A clinical study compared oral glutamine (10g in 1000ml water, 2h before radiation) with no pre-radiation intervention in patients undergoing radiation therapy. Baseline characteristics were comparable between groups. Glutamine significantly reduced the incidence of grade 3 mucositis (14.29% vs. 37.14%, P=0.02) and grade 4 mucositis (2.86% vs. 17.14%, P=0.04). In patients over 60, glutamine reduced grade 3 or worse mucositis (20.83% vs. 52%, P=0.01). Among those receiving concurrent chemoradiation, glutamine also showed benefits, reducing grade 3 (17.39% vs. 41.67%) and grade 4 (4.35% vs. 25%) mucositis. Glutamine delayed the onset of mucositis (P<0.001) and reduced the mean duration of grade 3+ mucositis (6.6 vs. 9.2 days, P<0.001). Even in patients receiving face and neck irradiation, where mucositis tends to be more severe, glutamine still reduced its incidence. A clinical study compared standard sepsis therapy with additional physiological-dose steroid therapy over 10 days. On admission, 40% of the steroid group and 45% of the standard therapy group had organ dysfunction or failure (Table 4). There was no significant difference in the change in Sequential Organ Failure Assessment (SOFA) scores between survivors in the steroid therapy group (43.1 ± 26.5%) and the standard therapy group (45.4 ± 12.7%) (P = 0.624). 

The median time to death was 5 days (95% CI 2.55–8.20) in the steroid therapy group and 5.5 days (95% CI 2.19–13) in the standard therapy group (P = 0.496). All deaths were attributed to sepsis. The median hospital stay was 14 days (95% CI 11.09–20.08) in the steroid therapy group and 13 days (95% CI 10.13–16.37) in the standard therapy group (P = 0.406). 

Regarding 28-day mortality, 40% of patients in the steroid therapy group and 60% in the standard therapy group died (P = 0.343). Mortality was higher in patients with hospital-acquired sepsis compared to those with community-acquired sepsis, though the difference was not statistically significant. The study also assessed the relationship between mortality and factors such as age, underlying disease, vasopressor and steroid use, and APACHE II and SOFA scores.
text: The addition of physiological-dose steroid therapy for 10 days to standard sepsis therapy did not significantly reduce 28-day mortality compared to standard therapy alone (40% vs. 60%, P = 0.343).

A study compared scaling and root planning (SRP) combined with amoxicillin plus metronidazole (test group) to SRP alone (control group) in managing periodontal disease (PD). Both groups showed significant improvements in PD and clinical attachment level (CAL) at 3 and 6 months compared to baseline (P < 0.05), with no significant differences between groups (P > 0.05). The test group demonstrated a statistically significant reduction in the percentage of PD ≥ 7 mm compared to the control group at both 3 and 6 months (P < 0.05).

In terms of clinical healing, the combination of SRP with amoxicillin plus metronidazole better restored the TIMP-1/MMP-1 balance. Total MMP-1 levels decreased significantly in both groups at 3 and 6 months (P < 0.05). TIMP-1 levels in the test group increased over time, though the difference compared to the control group was not statistically significant (P > 0.05). However, the TIMP-1/MMP-1 balance was significantly better restored in the test group at 6 months (P < 0.05). Total TIMP-1 levels did not change significantly in either group at 3 or 6 months (P > 0.05). The study suggests that adjunctive antibiotic therapy with SRP may enhance clinical healing by modulating matrix metalloproteinase activity.
text: The combination of SRP with amoxicillin plus metronidazole significantly better restored the TIMP-1/MMP-1 balance compared to SRP alone at 6 months (P < 0.05). This suggests adjunctive antibiotics enhance clinical healing by modulating MMP activity (source: study).

In a study comparing aerobic interval training (AIT), maximal volitional interval training (MVIT), and walking, the primary outcome was VO2max. Both AIT and MVIT showed non-inferiority to walking in both per-protocol (PP) and intent-to-treat (ITT) analyses. However, AIT demonstrated significant improvement in VO2max compared to walking in ITT analysis (p = 0.027), while MVIT did not. On PP analysis, AIT also showed significant improvement (p = 0.04). ITT analysis included three participants with notable VO2max changes not included in PP, such as a 3.89 ml/min/kg drop in the walking group and increases in AIT. When comparing AIT and walking on VO2max (L/min), AIT showed significant differences favoring it in both ITT (p = 0.01) and PP (p = 0.04) analyses. MVIT showed no significant changes compared to walking. 

Secondary outcomes included no significant changes in body mass or self-reported calorie intake, but waist circumference decreased by 3–4 cm and total body fat decreased equivalent to a 1.0 kg loss. Additional benefits included reduced total cholesterol and blood pressure, though the latter may be partially due to a reverse Hawthorne effect. Exercise time per week was 74 minutes for AIT, 45 for MVIT, and 116 for walking (p = 0.001). Walking had the fewest adverse events.
text: Aerobic interval training (AIT) significantly improves VO2max compared to walking in both ITT (p = 0.027) and PP (p = 0.04) analyses. Walking showed fewer adverse events but lower VO2max gains.

Neonatal minimum blood glucose levels within 8 hours post-birth were 35.7 ± 9.6 mg/dL (Group I: 1%), 49.8 ± 10.8 mg/dL (Group II: 0%), and 29.2 ± 7.5 mg/dL (Group III: 5%). Groups I and III had significantly lower levels than Group II (P < 0.05 and P < 0.01, respectively). Group III had the highest umbilical blood glucose (181.8 ± 22.2 mg/dL) compared to Groups I (53.9 ± 10.2) and II (80.8 ± 13.7). Maternal post-infusion glucose levels were significantly higher in Group III (252.5 ± 41.8 mg/dL) than Groups I (74.6 ± 4.6) and II (103.3 ± 11.2). Neonatal hypoglycemia (≤50 mg/dL) occurred in 6 (Group I), 3 (Group II), and 9 (Group III) neonates, with Group II showing a trend toward fewer glucose infusions (P = 0.082). Baseline maternal characteristics (age, gestational week, anesthesia time) varied between groups, but neonatal weight and Apgar scores were similar.
text: Infusing 5% glucose acetated Ringer’s solution during cesarean delivery significantly increases maternal blood glucose levels (252.5 ± 41.8 mg/dL) compared to 0% (103.3 ± 11.2 mg/dL) or 1% (74.6 ± 4.6 mg/dL) (PMC3622020).

memory: A clinical study compared extracorporeal shock wave therapy (ESWT) with trigger point injections (TPI) plus transcutaneous electrical nerve stimulation (TENS) for treating neck pain. Both interventions led to significant improvements in neck range of motion (ROM) over time, except for extension (p<0.05 for time effect), with no significant group differences in ROM (p>0.05). Pain threshold (lb/cm²) increased significantly in the ESWT group (6.86±1.35 to 12.57±0.72) compared to TPI+TENS (6.20±1.92 to 9.60±2.19), with a significant group difference (p=0.045). Pain assessment using the visual analog scale (VAS) showed greater improvement in the ESWT group (6.86±0.90 to 1.86±0.69) compared to TPI+TENS (7.20±1.30 to 2.80±0.84), with significant group differences (p=0.010). However, the McGill pain questionnaire (p=0.816) and pain rating scale (p=0.644) did not show significant differences between groups. The study suggests that both ESWT and TPI+TENS are effective for improving neck ROM, but ESWT is more effective in reducing pain as measured by VAS and increasing pain threshold. Source: PMC3503942.

memory: A 15-minute, five-times-per-week, four-week whole-body vibration (WBV) training program was evaluated against a control group and baseline measurements. memory: A clinical trial compared immediate vs. delayed treatment in metastatic colorectal cancer (mCRC) and found no significant differences in overall quality of life (QoL) across multiple scales (EORTC, LASA, GLQ-8, QL index) at baseline and follow-ups. Median overall survival was 13.0 months for the immediate treatment group and 11.0 months for the delayed group (HR 1.08; 95% CI 0.79–1.47; P=0.49), with one-year survival rates of 57% and 46%, respectively. Adjustment for risk factors slightly increased the HR to 1.15 (95% CI 0.77–1.72), but the result remained non-significant. Time to disease progression was similar between groups (median 10.2 vs. 10.8 months; HR 1.01; 95% CI 0.72–1.41), and progression-free survival also showed no significant difference (HR 1.08; 95% CI 0.71–1.64; P=0.73). Multivariate Cox analysis found no significant influence of factors such as age, sex, liver metastases, ECOG performance status, baseline QoL, weight, disease-free interval, stage, or prior adjuvant chemotherapy on progression or survival. Trial suspension due to low accrual limited the sample size. Early treatment of asymptomatic patients did not improve survival or QoL compared to delayed treatment. Source: PMC2361520.
text: A clinical trial found no significant difference in overall QoL between immediate and delayed treatment in mCRC patients. Survival and progression outcomes were also similar. Source: PMC2361520.

memory: In a study comparing liraglutide 1.8 mg to placebo, 31% (11/35) of liraglutide participants discontinued the study, compared to 18% (6/33) in the placebo group (P = 0.26). Among those who continued, liraglutide users (n = 24) experienced significantly greater weight loss (6.8 kg) than placebo users (n = 27; 3.3 kg; P < 0.001). Liraglutide also led to a significant improvement in steady-state plasma glucose (SSPG) concentration (−3.2 vs. 0.2 mmol/L; P < 0.001). Additionally, liraglutide resulted in significantly greater reductions in systolic blood pressure (−8.1 vs. −2.6 mmHg; P ≤ 0.04), fasting glucose (−0.5 vs. −0 mmol/L; P ≤ 0.04), and triglycerides (−0.4 vs. −0.1 mmol/L; P ≤ 0.04). Inflammatory markers showed no differences between groups, but pulse increased more in the liraglutide group (6.4 vs. −0.9 bpm; P = 0.001). These findings indicate liraglutide’s effectiveness in promoting weight loss and improving metabolic parameters, though its impact on pulse should be noted. Source: [PMC3781545]

memory: A study compared home-based cardiac rehabilitation with telemonitoring to centre-based training in 90 low-to-moderate cardiac risk patients. Both groups showed significant improvements in peakVO2 at discharge (+11% and +15%, p < 0.01) and at one-year follow-up (+16% and +17%, p < 0.01), with no between-group differences (p = 0.25 and p = 0.89). Physical fitness improved similarly in both groups (p < 0.01), and physical activity levels remained stable (p > 0.38). Health-related quality of life showed no differences between groups. Patient satisfaction was higher in the home-based group (p = 0.02). Healthcare costs were non-significantly lower in the home-based group (€437 per patient, 95% CI –562 to 1436, p = 0.39). From a societal perspective, a non-significant cost difference of €3160 per patient favored home-based training (95% CI –460 to 6780, p = 0.09). The probability of home-based training being more cost-effective ranged from 75% to 97% depending on willingness-to-pay thresholds. The study concluded that home-based training with telemonitoring is a viable alternative to centre-based training, with higher patient satisfaction and potential cost benefits.
text: Home-based training with telemonitoring had similar effects on peakVO2 as centre-based training, with no significant between-group differences (p = 0.25 and p = 0.89). Both groups showed significant improvements in peakVO2 at discharge and follow-up.

Borderline differences were observed in men's number of partners (p = 0.054) and women's condom use (p = 0.052). Source: PMC4569275.
text: The vaccine group had a higher estimated infection hazard ratio (2.46, 1.22–4.93, p = 0.01) compared to the placebo group for men. This effect was more significant when combining data (2.75, 1.49–5.06, p = 0.001). Source: PMC4569275.

Fasting plasma glucose (FPG) decreased by −8.88 mg/dL with linagliptin compared to an increase of +16.22 mg/dL with placebo (P = 0.0003). Urinary albumin-to-creatinine ratio (UACR) decreased by 32% (95% CI −42 to −21; P < 0.05) at 24 weeks with linagliptin versus 6% with placebo (between-group difference −28%; P = 0.0357). A significant albuminuria-lowering effect was observed as early as 12 weeks (−29%; P < 0.05; between-group difference −25%; P = 0.0750). Baseline UACR was similar between groups (73.8 vs. 80.5 mg/g Cr). The albuminuria-lowering effect was independent of race, baseline HbA1c, or systolic blood pressure (SBP).
text: Linagliptin significantly reduced urinary albumin-to-creatinine ratio (UACR) by 32% at 24 weeks compared to control (P < 0.05), with a between-group difference of −28% (P = 0.0357). This effect was independent of baseline factors and occurred as early as 12 weeks. Source: [PMC3816860].

memory: A study compared transurethral nephroscope via resectoscope outer sheath (Group 1) with conventional percutaneous cystolithotripsy (Group 2). Both groups had similar mean transurethral access numbers (1.2 [0.41] vs. 1.28 [0.58], P = 0.643) and operative times (32.73 [8.71] vs. 34.31 [7.00] minutes, P = 0.428). However, hospital stay duration was significantly longer in Group 2 (2.12 [0.35] days) compared to Group 1 (1.17 [0.47] days, P = 0.000). Patient age was 53.3 [11.4] years in Group 1 and 49.9 [12.8] years in Group 2, with comparable stone sizes (3.2 [0.8] vs. 3.2 [0.7] cm). All patients achieved 100% stone clearance. These results suggest that the transurethral approach may offer a shorter hospital stay without compromising operative time or stone clearance rates.
text: The transurethral nephroscope via resectoscope outer sheath significantly reduces hospital stay duration compared to conventional percutaneous cystolithotripsy (P = 0.000). Both techniques had similar operative times and stone clearance rates.
intervention: transurethral nephroscope via resectoscope outer sheath

memory: A clinical study investigated the effect of flush volume (3 mL vs. 10 mL of 0.9% sodium chloride) and flush frequency (every 24 hours vs. every 6 hours) on peripheral intravenous catheter (PIVC) failure rates. The average PIVC dwell time was 3.1 days. Failure rates were 4.84 vs. 7.44 per 1000 hours for 3 mL vs. 10 mL, with a non-significant difference (p = 0.06, log-rank). For frequency, failure rates were 5.06 vs. 7.34 per 1000 hours for 24-hour vs. 6-hour flushing, also non-significant (p = 0.05, log-rank). A Cox proportional hazards regression analysis showed no significant association between volume, frequency, or their interaction with PIVC failure (p = 0.21). Univariable Cox regression revealed large effect estimates for both interventions but without statistical significance. No significant interaction was found between volume and frequency, indicating their effects were independent. Primary endpoint analysis confirmed similar non-significant trends (p = 0.063 for volume, p = 0.054 for frequency, log-rank). The study did not identify a statistically significant benefit of higher flush volume or more frequent flushing in reducing PIVC failure rates. Source: PMC4960789.
text: A study found no statistically significant difference in PIVC failure rates between 3 mL and 10 mL 0.9% sodium chloride flushes (p = 0.06, log-rank). Source: PMC4960789.
outcome: Peripheral intravenous catheter failure rates per 1000 hours

memory: A study compared Aloe cream and Calendula ointment for treating diaper dermatitis (DD). Baseline characteristics, such as age, gender, and diaper care practices, were similar between the two groups (Table 1). No statistically significant differences were found in the prevalence of prior conditions that could influence DD, including diarrhea, immunodeficiency, renal deficiency, hypersensitivity, hematochezia, wheezing, eczema, oral thrush, or anemia (Table 2; P > 0.05). Both treatments resulted in significant improvements in DD severity (P < 0.001). However, the Calendula ointment group showed a significantly lower number of rash sites compared to the Aloe cream group (P = 0.001). No adverse effects were reported for either treatment. These findings suggest that both Aloe cream and Calendula ointment are effective for treating DD, with Calendula ointment potentially offering a slight advantage in reducing the number of rash sites.
text: The effect of Aloe cream compared with Calendula ointment on baseline characteristics showed no significant differences in age, gender, diaper care practices, or prevalence of prior conditions influencing DD (P > 0.05). Both groups were similar at baseline.

memory: A study compared the mobiletype program, which monitors mood, stress, and daily activities, to an attention-comparison group monitoring only daily activities. GPs found the mobiletype program significantly more helpful in several areas. It improved decision-making regarding medication (p = .013, d = 0.55) and referrals (p = .012, d = 0.56) compared to the attention-comparison group. The program also enhanced GPs' diagnosis (p = .002, d = 0.69) and communication with patients (p = .031, d = 0.47). Furthermore, it aided in identifying patients’ specific medical (p = .023, d = 0.52) and mental health problems (p = .011, d = 0.56) more effectively and provided a better understanding of patients' current functioning (p = .023, d = 0.48). However, the GP Confidence scale (α = 0.93), after adjusting for baseline scores, showed no statistically significant difference in confidence between the intervention and comparison groups (β = 1.05, p = .131). Three rapport-based scales—GPAQ Communication and Enablement subscales, and TPS—were analyzed using mixed model analysis, with results presented in Table 3.
text: The intervention group using the mobiletype program significantly improved GPs' diagnosis, communication, and identification of medical and mental health problems compared to the attention-comparison group (p < .05, d = 0.47–0.69). However, no significant difference in GP confidence was found (p = .131).
intervention: intervention group (where mood, stress and daily activities were monitored with program mobiletype)
comparator: attention-comparison group (where only daily activities were monitored)
outcome: helping to diagnosed and communication, specific medical and mental health problems

memory:
Source: [PMC5520118]  
Intervention: Meditation Awareness Training (MAT) vs. control group.  
Baseline: No significant differences between groups in BWAS, AJIGS, DASS, RBPS, Work Engagement, or Work Involvement (p > 0.05), as determined by independent sample t-tests.  
Study purpose: To evaluate MAT's effectiveness in reducing workaholism and improving related outcomes in a larger sample. Primary outcome: reduction in workaholism. Secondary outcomes: improved job satisfaction, job performance, reduced psychological distress, reduced work duration, and reduced work involvement.  
Results: MAT participants showed significant and sustained improvements compared to control groups in workaholism symptoms, job satisfaction, work engagement, work duration, and psychological distress. MAT participants also experienced a significant reduction in hours worked without a decline in job performance. These findings are supported by statistical data from the abstract and results sections of the study.
text: Meditation Awareness Training (MAT) significantly reduces workaholism symptomatology compared to a control group, as shown in [PMC5520118]. MAT also improved job satisfaction, work engagement, and reduced psychological distress without compromising job performance.

memory: A study compared neonatal bag and mask resuscitation with oral antibiotic therapy (intervention) to routine care (control) across multiple outcomes. Early fetal loss rates were similar between groups (61 vs 63 per 1000 pregnancies; RR 0.97, 95% CI 0.88–1.08; p=0.60). Facility births and skilled birth attendant deliveries were not significantly different (53% vs 54% and 54% vs 56%, respectively; p>0.5). Intervention clusters had significantly higher rates of home deliveries attended by lady health workers (LHWs) (14% vs 1%; p<0.0001) and greater use of clean delivery kits (p<0.0001). Stillbirth rates were not significantly different (RR 0.89, 95% CI 0.76–1.04; p=0.13), but neonatal mortality was significantly lower in the intervention group (42 vs 55 per 1000 livebirths; RR 0.80, 95% CI 0.68–0.93; p=0.005). Neonatal mortality was similar during the first surveillance round but remained consistently lower in intervention clusters thereafter. The study included 51,436 pregnancies, with 5% early fetal deaths, 10% migration, and 11% ongoing pregnancies at trial completion. Data were collected through quarterly surveillance rounds 1–11 and summarized in tables 4 and 5 of the source article [PMC5762815].
text: The effect of neonatal bag and mask resuscitation and oral antibiotic therapy on early fetal loss rates was similar to routine care (RR 0.97, 95% CI 0.88–1.08; p=0.60) [PMC5762815].
intervention: neonatal bag and mask resuscitation and oral antibiotic therapy
comparator: routine care through the existing national programme

Source: PMC3504298

Face-based attention bias modification (ABM) significantly reduced depressive (BDI) and anxiety (STAI) symptoms compared to placebo during follow-up, while word-based ABM showed no significant effects on symptoms. Face-based ABM also reduced cortisol awakening response, a marker of recurrence risk, which was not observed with word-based ABM. The effect of ABM on depressive symptoms was dependent on stimulus type, with face-based ABM showing significant benefits over placebo [F(2,112) = 3.7, p = .03], whereas word-based ABM did not [F(2,56) < 1, p = .4]. Face-based ABM showed a trend-level effect on observer-reported depressive symptoms (HRSD) [F(1,28) = 2.9, p = .09] and a significant reduction in anxiety symptoms during follow-up [t(15) = 2.4, p = .03]. Word-based ABM demonstrated a differential effect on attentional bias (visual-probe task) compared to placebo [F(2,112) = 3.1, p = .05], but no significant difference between face- and word-trained groups [F(2,112) < 1, p = .9]. This effect was maintained during the bias modification period [F(1,57) = 8.3, p = .006].
text: Face-based attentional bias modification significantly reduced anxious symptoms compared to placebo, as shown by significant reductions in STAI scores (t(15) = 2.4, p = .03). This effect was not observed with word-based ABM. Source: PMC3504298.

memory: In an experimental model of mild extrapulmonary acute lung injury (ALI) with intra-abdominal hypertension (IAH), pressure support ventilation (PSV) was compared to pressure-controlled ventilation (PCV). The study evaluated the effect of PSV versus PCV on mRNA expression of interleukin (IL)-6 in lung tissue. Regardless of IAH presence, PSV resulted in lower mean airway pressure and reduced mRNA expression of inflammatory (IL-6) and fibrogenic (type III procollagen) biomarkers compared to PCV. In the presence of IAH, PSV improved oxygenation, decreased alveolar collapse, interstitial edema, and diffuse alveolar damage (DAD), while increasing surfactant protein B expression compared to PCV. In non-IAH (nIAP) animals, no significant differences were observed between PCV and PSV regarding alveolar collapse, interstitial edema, septal thickening, or DAD score. However, in the IAH group, PSV was associated with less alveolar collapse, interstitial edema, and DAD compared to PCV. Six of the 30 rats were used for molecular biology analysis and were not mechanically ventilated. Statistical analysis was performed using two-way repeated-measures ANOVA followed by Bonferroni’s post-hoc test (p < 0.05). Values are given as mean ± standard deviation of 6 animals per group. Source: [PMC5444773]
text: In animals with IAH, PSV reduced alveolar collapse, interstitial edema, and DAD compared to PCV, while showing no significant differences in non-IAH animals. Source: [PMC5444773].
outcome: Alveolar collapse, interstitial edema, or DAD score in animals with IAH

memory: A clinical study [PMC3591547] compared Alfentanil (10 μg/kg initial dose, 1 μg/kg/min infusion) and Remifentanil (0.5 μg/kg initial dose, 0.1 μg/kg/min infusion) in 40 patients. Groups were comparable in baseline characteristics, including age, gender, blood pressure, heart rate, and anesthesia duration. The average time for respiration to return after drug discontinuation was shorter in the Alfentanil group (2 minutes) than in the Remifentanil group (3.3 minutes), though this difference was not statistically significant (P=0.08). No significant differences were found between groups in the time from drug discontinuation to eye opening, verbal response, or discharge from recovery. No respiratory complications were observed in the recovery phase. However, nausea and vomiting were more common in the Remifentanil group (n=6) compared to the Alfentanil group (n=1), with a statistically significant difference (P<0.05). Results are summarized in Table 2, which includes the average time from drug discontinuation to recovery milestones and the incidence of nausea and vomiting.
text: The effect of Alfentanil compared to Remifentanil on recovery milestones showed no significant differences in time to eye opening, verbal response, or discharge. Alfentanil had a shorter, though non-significant, time to respiratory recovery. Remifentanil was associated with more nausea and vomiting (PMC3591547).
intervention: 10 μg/kg of Alfentanil, infusion of Alfentanil 1 μg/kg/min
comparator: Remifentanil 0.5 μg/kg, infusion of Remifentanil 0.1 μg/kg/min
outcome: stopping the anesthesia drugs up to opening eyes, return to verbal response, and discharge from the recovery

memory: In a study [PMC5462369], adding primaquine to dihydroartemisinin-piperaquine (DHP) significantly improved gametocyte clearance. Among 12 gametocytemic participants, the median time to gametocyte clearance was 1 day with primaquine versus 12 days without, with a hazard ratio (HR) of 7.3 (95% CI 1.3–42), p=0.01. At baseline, 9% were gametocyte positive by microscopy, and 46% by Pfs25 RT-PCR. By day 2, 12% had microscopic gametocytemia. Post-primaquine treatment, 2.1% had patent gametocytes compared to 15% in the DHP-only group, with a prevalence ratio of 0.12 (95% CI 0.02–0.9), p=0.03. Only 1/4 of day 2 gametocytemic subjects in the primaquine group remained positive at day 7, with all cleared by day 14. Hemoglobin drops were greater in 6 primaquine-treated subjects with mild/moderate G6PD deficiency (median 24.8% reduction) compared to 2 not treated (7.1%), p=0.14. Five participants with severe G6PD deficiency were excluded. All hemoglobin values were >11.0 g/dL by day 14.
text: Adding primaquine to dihydroartemisinin-piperaquine significantly reduces gametocyte carriage (HR 7.3, p=0.01; prevalence ratio 0.12, p=0.03). However, it caused greater hemoglobin drops in those with mild/moderate G6PD deficiency (PMC5462369).

Source: [PMC5350209]

Health warning labels (text and image) significantly reduced alcohol acceptance compared to no warning (F(2, 42) = 7.01, p = .002, ηp² = .25). Pictorial warnings showed significantly lower acceptance than no warning (p = .002), while text warnings did not differ from no warning (p = .10). Health warning labels also significantly slowed alcohol consumption compared to no warning (F(2, 42) = 22.25, p < .001, ηp² = .514). The 'no health warning' condition resulted in significantly faster consumption than both text and pictorial warning conditions (p < .001). There was no significant difference in consumption speed between text and pictorial warning conditions (p = .76). The presence of a health warning label had a greater impact on consumption speed than the type of warning (text vs. image). Figure 1 illustrates the mean duration of drinking across the different conditions.
text: Visual warning (text) significantly slowed alcohol consumption compared to no warning (p < .001). However, text warnings did not differ from no warning in acceptance (p = .10). The presence of any warning had a greater impact on consumption speed than the type of warning. Source: [PMC5350209].

memory: In a study comparing raloxifene to vehicle in ZDSD rats, raloxifene treatment was associated with a lower incidence of type 2 diabetes and significantly lower blood glucose levels compared to both diabetic and non-diabetic vehicle-treated groups [Abstract]. Cumulative blood glucose area under the curve (AUC) was lower in raloxifene-treated rats than in vehicle-treated non-diabetic rats (p = 0.048), though endpoint blood glucose values were not significantly different [not located]. No significant group differences were found in DXA or μCT measures of L4 vertebrae [not located]. Raloxifene-treated rats exhibited greater femoral toughness, due to enhanced energy absorption in the post-yield region of the stress-strain curve, along with improved structural mechanical properties, including energy-to-failure, post-yield energy-to-failure, and post-yield displacement [Abstract]. No significant differences were observed in pQCT measures of the femoral midshaft. In the distal femur, vehicle-treated diabetic rats (VEH-D) had reduced bone volume normalized to tissue volume, trabecular thickness, and trabecular number, along with increased trabecular separation and structure model index (indicating a more rod-like structure), compared to raloxifene-treated rats [not located].
text: Raloxifene significantly increased femoral toughness compared to control, as shown by enhanced energy absorption and improved structural mechanical properties in the post-yield region of the stress-strain curve [Abstract].

memory: Source: PMC3381083. A study compared alcohol-assisted epithelial removal (n=658) with mechanical removal (n=592) in refractive surgery. Preoperative spherical equivalent was −4.37±2.3 D (alcohol) vs. −3.8±1.3 D (mechanical), with no significant difference (P=0.78). Postoperative pain was also not significantly different (P=0.22). Uncorrected visual acuity ≥ 20/20 was achieved in 90.9% (alcohol) vs. 93.4% (mechanical) (P=0.08), and ≥ 20/40 in 98.9% vs. 99.5% (P=0.36). Final refractive error within 1D of emmetropia was achieved in 90% (alcohol) vs. 92.2% (mechanical) (P=0.23). Alcohol-assisted debridement took significantly less time (96±18 vs. 118±26 seconds, P=0.035). Re-epithelialization time was 4.2±1.6 days (alcohol) vs. 3.8±1.3 days (mechanical), with no significant difference (P=0.75). Early and late postoperative complications were comparable. No significant differences were found in preoperative refractive error distribution (P=0.96). Both methods showed similar efficacy in achieving visual and refractive outcomes, but alcohol-assisted removal was faster.
text: The effect of alcohol-assisted epithelial removal compared with mechanical removal on mean spherical equivalent shows no significant difference (P=0.78). Both methods achieved similar refractive outcomes, though alcohol-assisted removal was faster. (Source: PMC3381083)

memory: A study compared ATP administration methods, focusing on their effects on uric acid levels and lithium absorption. Uric acid significantly increased (~50%) following proximal-release pellets (P = 0.003) and naso-duodenal tube (P = 0.001), but not with distal-release pellets. Blood ATP concentrations did not rise with enteric-coated pellets or naso-duodenal tube administration. To evaluate disintegration timing, plasma lithium concentrations were measured over 7 hours after coated pellet administration. Proximal-release pellets led to a significantly higher increase in plasma lithium compared to distal-release pellets (P = 0.001). Additionally, lithium AUC was significantly lower in ATP-containing proximal-release pellets compared to placebo (P = 0.001). These results suggest that pellet release profiles influence ATP metabolism and lithium absorption, with proximal-release pellets causing greater systemic effects than distal-release pellets. Source: [PMC3441280].
text: Administration via proximal-release pellets significantly increases plasma lithium compared to distal-release pellets (P = 0.001). This suggests that release profile affects lithium absorption. Source: [PMC3441280].

memory: A clinical study compared the effects of a Pap smear (intervention, n=41) versus no intervention (control, n=39) on cervicovaginal lavage (CVL) inflammatory markers. CVL samples were collected at baseline (+3 days post-menses) and follow-up (14 days later or +17 days post-menses). Total protein concentrations in CVLs showed no significant differences within or between groups. Inflammatory cytokines IL-8, IL-1β, and IL-6 levels remained unchanged in both groups following a Pap smear. However, the intervention group exhibited significant increases in Th1-associated cytokines TNF-α (p = 0.025) and IL-12 p70 (p = 0.0016), as well as the regulatory cytokine IL-10 (p = 0.0003). These findings suggest that a Pap smear may induce immune responses related to cell-mediated immunity and T cell regulation, without altering proinflammatory cytokine levels. Baseline characteristics were comparable between groups, with no significant differences in socio-demographic, reproductive, or sexual factors. No participants withdrew, though one control participant was lost to follow-up. Four women in each group had abnormal Pap smears during the study, with no significant difference (p = 0.95). The study highlights that Pap smear procedures may influence specific inflammatory markers in CVLs, indicating a potential immune response not previously recognized.
text: Performing a Pap smear at enrollment significantly increases IL-10 levels compared to no intervention (p = 0.0003). This suggests the procedure may induce regulatory immune responses. Source: Clinical study comparing Pap smear vs. no intervention on cervicovaginal inflammatory markers.

memory: A study compared SB4 (etanercept biosimilar) with etanercept (ETN) in 596 RA patients on methotrexate. At week 24, the ACR20 response rate was 78.1% for SB4 and 80.3% for ETN, with an adjusted treatment difference of -9.41% to 4.98% (95% CI), which fell within the predefined equivalence margin of -15% to 15%, confirming therapeutic equivalence. ACR50 and ACR70 response rates were also equivalent, with ACR50 at 46.6% vs 42.3% and ACR70 at 25.5% vs 22.6% in the per-protocol set. Subgroup analyses showed comparable results regardless of ADA status. Adverse events were similar (55.2% vs 58.2%), but the incidence of ADA development was significantly lower in SB4 (0.7%) compared to ETN (13.1%, p<0.001). ADAs in ETN appeared early (weeks 2–8) and mostly disappeared after week 12, with only one ETN sample showing neutralizing capacity. Other efficacy and pharmacokinetic endpoints were comparable between the two groups.
text: SB4 (etanercept biosimilar) is therapeutically equivalent to etanercept in RA patients on methotrexate, as shown by comparable ACR20, ACR50, and ACR70 response rates within predefined margins (N=596). Adverse events were similar, but SB4 had significantly lower anti-drug antibody development (0.7% vs 13.1%, p<0.001). (Source: Study cited in working notes)
outcome: therapeutic equivalence - Patients with moderate to severe rheumatoid arthritis (RA) despite methotrexate (MTX) treatment

Source: [PMC4535555]

A study compared robotic-assisted navigation (Hansen Sensei® X) with standard navigation, focusing on outcomes related to late gadolinium enhancement (LGE) and T2 signal encirclement. Early scans showed that robotic navigation achieved a greater mean circumferential extent from LGE&T2 overlay (94 ± 6%) compared to standard navigation (88 ± 10%; P = 0.03). Robotic navigation also demonstrated higher mean LGE encirclement (72 ± 8%) compared to standard (60 ± 17%; P = 0.002). T2-weighted (T2W) signals showed no significant difference between groups (80 ± 12% vs. 76 ± 15%; P = 0.45). On late imaging, T2W signals resolved to baseline, while LGE remained dominant, with robotic navigation showing higher LGE (56%) compared to standard (45%; P = 0.04). At 6-month follow-up, arrhythmia-free patients had similar LGE encirclement (64% vs. 60%; P = 0.45), but those with recurrences showed higher LGE in the robotic group (43% vs. 30%; P = 0.001). At 3-year follow-up, the robotic group required fewer procedures (1.3 vs. 1.9; P < 0.001) and had a higher success rate (80% vs. 75%).
text: At 6 months, robotic-assisted navigation (Hansen Sensei® X) showed higher mean LGE encirclement compared to standard navigation (64% vs. 60%; P = 0.45). However, in patients with arrhythmia recurrences, robotic navigation had significantly higher LGE encirclement (43% vs. 30%; P = 0.001). Source: [PMC4535555].
outcome: mean LGE encirclement at 6 months follow-up

memory: In a clinical study comparing paracetamol 250 mg to a control group, fewer systemic reactions were observed in the paracetamol group, particularly in infants, with significant differences noted for fever, rash, irritability, drowsiness, decreased appetite, persistent inconsolable crying, and decreased activity (all p < 0.05). After the toddler dose, systemic reactions occurred more frequently, but only "decreased activity" was significantly lower in the paracetamol group (p = 0.005). Fever ≥38°C was reduced in the intent-to-treat (ITT) population following the infant series, with an efficacy of 43.0% (95% CI: 17.4, 61.2), though this reduction was not significant after the toddler dose (efficacy 15.9%; 95% CI: −19.9, 41.3). Similar results were observed in the per protocol (PP) population. Fever >39°C was rare during the infant series, making assessment difficult. However, after the toddler dose, paracetamol significantly reduced fever >39°C in the PP population only, with an efficacy of 79% (95% CI: 3.9, 97.7). Paracetamol also reduced reactogenicity, though few significant differences were observed between groups after any dose. No vaccine-related serious adverse events were reported.
text: Paracetamol 250 mg significantly reduced decreased activity compared to control (p = 0.005). Fewer systemic reactions were observed in the paracetamol group, particularly in infants. However, efficacy in reducing fever was inconsistent across doses and populations.

memory:
A crossover study involving 24 infants compared Nutrilon Omneo (new formula; NF) to standard formula (SF). Defecation frequency was similar between groups, with means of 5.5/week for NF and 5.9/week for SF (p = 0.38). However, the frequency of soft stools was significantly higher during the NF period, with 17% (n = 4) of infants having soft stools on NF versus none on SF (p = 0.046). Painful defecation and presence of abdominal or rectal mass were not significantly different between the two periods. 

Pre- and post-treatment defecation frequency increased in both groups, from 3.5/week to 5.6/week with NF and from 3.6/week to 4.9/week with SF, but the difference was not statistically significant (p = 0.36). Improvement of hard stool consistency to soft stool consistency was more common with NF than SF (90% vs. 50%), though not statistically significant (p = 0.14). Painful defecation decreased in both groups, from 75% pre to 65% post with NF and from 89% pre to 67% post with SF. Presence of abdominal or rectal mass also decreased, from 35% pre to 10% post with NF and from 44% pre to 5.6% post with SF. 

In summary, while NF showed a trend toward improved stool consistency and soft stools, differences in defecation frequency and painful defecation were not statistically significant. The study involved 24 infants completing the crossover, with data from 35 infants in the abstract.
text: The new formula (NF) increased the frequency of soft stools compared to standard formula (SF), with 17% of infants having soft stools on NF versus none on SF (p = 0.046). Defecation frequency was similar between groups (p = 0.38).
