Source: [PMC4668172]  
Intervention: Kegel exercises program | Comparator: Control  
Outcome: Kegel exercises significantly improved multiple pulmonary function parameters in the experimental group compared to the control group, which showed no improvement. Improved parameters included forced vital capacity (FVC), forced expiratory volume in 1 second (FEV1), peak expiratory flow (PEF), forced expiratory flow 25–75% (FEF 25–75%), inspiratory capacity (IC), and maximum voluntary ventilation (MVV). However, changes in the FEV1/FVC ratio were not statistically significant; the experimental group showed an increase, while the control group showed a decrease.
text: A Kegel exercises program significantly improved peak expiratory flow (PEF) compared to control, according to [PMC4668172].

memory: A clinical study compared peramivir (Rapiacta) and oseltamivir (Tamiflu) for treating influenza. Symptom disappearance time was similar between the groups, with means of 5.26 ± 0.15 days (peramivir) and 5.38 ± 0.16 days (oseltamivir), P = .65 (log-rank test). Total symptom scores (TSSs) decreased over time, with no significant differences between the groups (P = .69). Fever-alleviation time showed medians of 40.0 hours (peramivir) and 37.8 hours (oseltamivir), P = .69. The median time for virus titer to decrease below 101.5 TCID50/mL was approximately 4 days in both groups (P = .51). No significant intergroup differences were observed in TSSs (P = .051 at day 2) or virus titer by subtype. Four censored cases were reported in each group, and three peramivir patients received treatment for only 2 days. The data are derived from Table 2 and Figure 2 of [PMC5534217].
text: Peramivir and oseltamivir had similar effects on influenza symptom disappearance time (5.26 vs. 5.38 days, P = .65). No significant differences were observed in total symptom scores or virus titer reduction (P > .05). (Source: PMC5534217)
outcome: The numbers of days required for the disappearance of influenza symptoms

memory: In a study comparing hypertension telemonitoring with usual care, medication costs were not significantly different between groups, despite higher medication doses in the telemonitored group, as higher-strength medications were often similarly priced. Sensitivity analysis revealed higher hospital admission costs in the intervention group (£287.01 vs. £181.54 in control), leading to a non-significant increase in total NHS costs (£214.70, 95% CI −£23.71 to £526.65; p=0.098). Accident and emergency visits costs were not significantly different between groups (mean difference −£3.04, 95% CI −£8.87 to £2.47; p=0.286). Overall, telemonitoring was more costly than usual care, with a mean difference of £115.32 per patient (95% CI £83.49 to £146.63; p<0.001), driven by telemonitoring service, training, and additional consultations. The cost of systolic BP reduction was £25.56/mm Hg (95% CI £16.06 to £46.89) per patient.
text: The study found no significant difference in accident and emergency visits costs between hypertension telemonitoring and control (mean difference −£3.04, 95% CI −£8.87 to £2.47; p=0.286).

memory: A study within the DPP/DPPOS trial examined the association between antidepressant (ADM) use and diabetes risk. Continuous ADM use was strongly linked to increased diabetes risk in the placebo (HR 2.34 [1.32–4.15]) and lifestyle (HR 2.48 [1.45–4.22]) arms after adjusting for known diabetes risk factors. In the placebo arm, intermittent ADM use showed a trend toward increased risk (HR 1.34 [0.99–1.81]). However, in the metformin arm, ADM use was not associated with diabetes risk (HR 0.55 [0.25–1.19]). A significant difference was observed between the lifestyle and metformin arms regarding the ADM-diabetes risk association. Excluding ADMs more likely to cause weight gain (tricyclic and tetracyclic agents) did not alter the results. Findings consistently showed that continuous ADM use was associated with higher diabetes risk in the placebo and lifestyle arms, but not in the metformin arm. Source: PMC2992187.
text: Antidepressant use (ADM) is associated with increased diabetes risk in the lifestyle arm (HR 2.48 [1.45–4.22]) but not in the metformin arm (HR 0.55 [0.25–1.19]). Source: PMC2992187.

memory:
In a study comparing plastic cap and metal cup ventouse delivery during vaginal operative delivery, infants exhibited a lower pain response with the plastic cap versus the metal cup (p < 0.001), with full recovery within 72 hours. Scalp trauma was more common with the metal cup (13.2%, 12/90) compared to the plastic cup (6.6%, 2/30), but this difference was not statistically significant (p = 0.51). Detachment of the ventouse occurred in 6.7% of plastic cup cases (2/30) but not in the metal cup group. No subgaleal or intracranial haemorrhage or skull fractures were reported.

In a separate analysis, a suppository did not significantly affect EDIN AUC (p = 0.8; p = 0.77 without IPW), nor was there a significant interaction with the instrument used (p = 0.63; p = 0.61 without IPW). Neonates in the metal/placebo group had a higher proportion of high pain scores (EDIN ≥ 5) compared to the plastic/placebo group, but the difference was not statistically significant. Maternal analgesia effects could not be evaluated due to the high use of epidural/spinal anaesthesia (n = 97).
text: Infants showed a lower pain response with the plastic cap compared to the metal cup (p < 0.001), with full recovery within 72 hours. Scalp trauma was more common with the metal cup but not statistically significant.

memory: In a phase 2a trial, synthetic Aβ42 (AN1792) was compared to placebo. Among 19 participants, 17 were antibody responders with sustained low anti-AN1792 titers, while 2 non-responders had no detectable antibodies. Responders showed significantly less decline on the DAD scale (p=0.015) after 4.6 years, with similar trends on the Dependence Scale (p=0.033). However, MRI data from a small subset showed comparable brain volume loss between responders and placebo. On the CDR-SOB scale, responders had 20.2% less decline, though this was not statistically significant (p=0.185). CDR-SOB data were available for 80% of placebo-treated patients and 88% of responders. These results suggest possible clinical benefits of AN1792 in slowing dementia progression among responders, though MRI outcomes did not reflect significant differences in brain volume loss.
text: Synthetic Aβ42 (AN1792) showed a trend toward less decline on the Dependence Scale compared to placebo (p=0.033) in a phase 2a trial. However, MRI data did not show significant differences in brain volume loss.

memory: [PMC4973627] - A study examined the link between physical activity (PA) and health status (HE) with mortality outcomes. In PA+/HE− individuals (n=992), cardiovascular mortality was 17% (169 cases), with a hazard ratio (HR) of 0.56 (95% CI 0.44–0.73), P<0.001. For PA−/HE+ individuals (n=162), general mortality was 61% (98 cases), with an HR of 0.90 (95% CI 0.71–1.13), P=0.358. In the PA+/HE+ group (n=502), general mortality was 44% (219 cases), with an HR of 0.53 (95% CI 0.44–0.63), P<0.001, and cardiovascular mortality was 15% (76 cases), with an HR of 0.49 (95% CI 0.36–0.66), P<0.001. The findings suggest that high physical activity significantly reduces both general and cardiovascular mortality, especially when combined with a positive health status. The data supports the protective effect of PA against mortality, particularly in individuals with better health status.

memory: A study [PMC3467590] assessed a web-based CME, performance feedback, and quality improvement intervention on medication intensification for diabetes management in rural physicians. The intervention showed no significant incremental effect on intensifying medications for glucose, blood pressure, or lipid control across all groups. However, in unadjusted analyses, both the intervention (n=48) and control (n=47) groups showed increased medication intensification for A1c control, especially among patients with worse glucose control (A1c >9%). In this subgroup, the intervention group increased from 34.8% to 62.5% (p=0.002), and the control group increased from 35.7% to 61.4% (p=0.008). For patients with A1c 7-9%, intensification increased in the intervention group (p=0.005) but not in the control group (p=0.164). No significant differences were observed in intensification for BP or LDL control in either group. Adjusted analyses found no significant effect of the intervention (p=0.948 for group-by-time interaction across all measures). The study involved 1182 patients at baseline and 945 at follow-up. Both groups showed improvement, but the intervention did not yield additional benefits, indicating no significant incremental effect of the web-based intervention on medication intensification.

In a study on diabetic rats, cinaciguat (10 mg/kg/day orally for 8 weeks) was compared to placebo. Diabetes mellitus (DM) increased myocardial nitro-oxidative stress, as indicated by elevated nitrotyrosine (NT) immunoreactivity, which was significantly reduced by cinaciguat. DM also increased HSP70a1, catalase, glutathione-reductase, and thioredoxin-1 expression, but cinaciguat normalized HSP70a1 and glutathione-reductase mRNA levels to those of healthy controls. 

PDE-5 and PKG protein expression were elevated in DM, yet PKG activity (p-VASP/VASP ratio) was reduced, suggesting impaired NO-sGC-cGMP-PKG signaling. Cinaciguat decreased PDE-5 expression and increased PKG activity without changing PKG protein levels. 

DM rats exhibited reduced load-independent contractility (Ees, PRSW) and increased Tau (Weiss; ms), indicating systolic and diastolic dysfunction. Cinaciguat significantly improved PRSW (66.8 ± 3.6 mmHg) and diastolic function (Tau: 14.9 ± 0.6 ms), and reduced the slope of EDPVR, which had increased in DM. Cinaciguat had no hemodynamic effects in non-diabetic rats. These findings suggest that cinaciguat ameliorates DM-induced cardiac dysfunction by reducing oxidative stress and restoring NO-cGMP-PKG signaling. (Source: PMC4628236)
text: Cinaciguat (10 mg/kg/day orally for 8 weeks) significantly reduced nitro-oxidative stress in diabetic rats compared to placebo, as evidenced by decreased nitrotyrosine immunoreactivity and normalization of antioxidant enzyme mRNA levels. This effect was linked to improved NO-sGC-cGMP-PKG signaling (PMC4628236).
intervention: the sGC activator cinaciguat (10 mg/kg/day) orally for 8 weeks

memory: In a study comparing lemon verbena extract to placebo, several biochemical and physiological outcomes were assessed. Glutathione peroxidase (GPxP) activity showed a trend toward increase in the lemon verbena group compared to placebo (p = 0.0681), with a time effect also by trend (p = 0.0624). Exercise-induced creatine kinase (CK) levels were not significantly different between groups (p = 0.9412), though both groups showed significant time effects (p < 0.0001). The lemon verbena group showed a significant increase in CK above baseline at 24 h post-exercise, but not at 3- or 48-h post-exercise, unlike the placebo group, which had significant elevations at all time points. Interleukin 6 (IL-6) showed no significant differences between groups (p = 0.5824), though there was a distinct increase after exercise with high variability. Movement-induced pain, measured on a visual analog scale (VAS), showed a trend toward less pain in the lemon verbena group (p = 0.0788). Muscle function testing revealed that the lemon verbena group had significantly less reduction in maximal voluntary contraction (MVC) after exercise compared to the placebo group (p = 0.0311), with a significant time effect (p = 0.0051). Muscle strength in the lemon verbena group returned to baseline after 48 h, while the placebo group still showed reduced strength at that time. Overall, participants receiving lemon verbena extract experienced less muscle damage, faster recovery, and improved glutathione peroxidase activity by trend, though not all outcomes reached statistical significance.
text: Lemon verbena extract reduced exercise-related muscle strength loss more than placebo, with less reduction in maximal voluntary contraction (p = 0.0311) and faster recovery. Muscle strength returned to baseline after 48 h in the lemon verbena group, unlike placebo. Source: Study on lemon verbena extract and exercise-induced muscle damage.

In a clinical study comparing arformoterol to placebo, arformoterol significantly improved trough FEV1 (0.051 L, P = .030) and FVC (0.075 L, P = .018). These improvements correlated with enhanced quality of life, as measured by the St. George's Respiratory Questionnaire and Clinical COPD Questionnaire (P < .05). Arformoterol also reduced the risk of first respiratory serious adverse events by 50% (P = .003). Fewer patients on arformoterol experienced COPD exacerbation-related hospitalizations (9.0% vs 14.3%) and had a lower incidence of COPD exacerbations or worsening (23.3% vs 28.0%).

Overall adverse event (AE) incidence was similar between arformoterol (72.9%) and placebo (68.2%). The most common AE was COPD exacerbation or worsening, which was less frequent with arformoterol. Nonrespiratory AEs occurring in ≥5% of patients included headache, nausea, and urinary tract infection. Numerically more patients on arformoterol (3.1%) than placebo (2.4%) experienced cardiac serious adverse events, though time-to-first event was not significantly different. Mortality rates were similar: 2.9% for arformoterol and 2.4% for placebo.
text: Arformoterol significantly improved quality of life, as measured by the St. George's Respiratory Questionnaire and Clinical COPD Questionnaire (P < .05), compared to placebo. These improvements correlated with better lung function and reduced exacerbations.

memory: A clinical study compared nebulized albuterol (0.15 mg/kg in 3 ml saline) with saline (3 ml) on pulmonary function parameters. No significant differences were found between the two treatments in VPTEF/VE or tPTEF/tE (P = 0.6). Both albuterol and saline significantly increased PTEF, but the difference between groups was not statistically significant. Albuterol significantly decreased TEF10 and the 25/PT ratio (P < 0.05), whereas saline had no such effect. Post-treatment, there were no significant changes in heart rate, respiratory rate, oxygen saturation, or wheeze score. Baseline demographic and clinical variables were evenly distributed between groups, except for gender distribution. All other variables were not significantly affected by aerosol administration. These findings suggest that while both treatments improved PTEF, albuterol had specific effects on TEF10 and the 25/PT ratio. Results are detailed in Tables 1, 2, and 3 of the source article [PMC111183].

memory: In a study [PMC5370803], metformin (500 mg bid po) + alogliptin (25 mg qd po) was compared to metformin (1000 mg bid po) in patients with HbA1c ≥8.0%. No significant differences in pulmonary function (VC%, FEV1%, MVV%, TLC%) were observed (P > 0.05). At week 26, a higher proportion of the intervention group achieved HbA1c ≤7.0% (18.18% vs. 10.81%), though not statistically significant (P > 0.05). The intervention group showed greater reductions in total cholesterol (−4.27 mg/dL vs. −1.59 mg/dL) and significant improvements in HDL-C, LDL-C, and triglycerides. BMI and waist circumference declines were greater in the intervention group, but not statistically significant. Adverse events were more frequent in the intervention group, including more headaches (12.7% vs. 2.0%, P < 0.05) and pruritus (12.7% vs. 4.0%), though no serious cutaneous adverse events were reported. Hypoglycemia was rare (3.8%). No significant changes in blood pressure, laboratory values, or ECGs were observed. Oxidative stress markers (GSH-Px, SOD, ROS, MDA) were noted but not quantified.

memory: In a clinical study comparing FAST and SLOW treatments, secondary endpoints were evaluated at 120 minutes post-resuscitation. The median (IQR) differences in heart rate (ΔHRFast-Slow) and stroke volume index (ΔSVIFast-Slow) were −4 bpm (−11 to 3 bpm) and −1 mL/b/m² (−6 to 10 mL/b/m²), respectively, without statistical significance (P = 0.191; P = 0.562). Longitudinal analysis showed significantly higher pulse rates under FAST treatment (P = 0.022), with greater uniform increases during resuscitation compared to less than 50% under SLOW. No significant differences were found in venous acid-base variables, electrolytes, oxygen saturations, haemoglobin, glucose, lactate, or BNP-NT values at any time point. Mean arterial pressure (MAP), systolic blood pressure (sBP), and diastolic blood pressure (dBP) were significantly higher under FAST compared to SLOW (P = 0.035; P = 0.046; P = 0.035). However, no differences in cardiac index (CI) or systemic vascular resistance index (SVRI) were observed (P = 0.432; P = 0.964). During resuscitation, CI paradoxically declined in 89% of participants under FAST treatment in the last quarter of this phase. Oxygen delivery (DO2) changes showed no significant differences between treatments at any time point, even after adjusting for gender, BMI, treatment order, and time points (P = 0.250).
text: FAST treatment showed higher MAP, sBP, and dBP compared to SLOW (P < 0.046), but no significant differences in CI or SVRI. Heart rate and SVI differences were not statistically significant. Pulse rates were significantly higher under FAST (P = 0.022). (Source: Clinical study)

In a phase III trial [67], 322 previously treated advanced melanoma patients with V600E/K B-Raf mutations were randomized 2:1 to receive oral trametinib (2 mg daily) or intravenous chemotherapy (dacarbazine or paclitaxel). Trametinib significantly improved median progression-free survival (PFS) compared to chemotherapy (4.8 vs 1.5 months; HR 0.45; P < 0.001). At 6 months, overall survival (OS) was 81% in the trametinib group versus 67% in the chemotherapy group (HR 0.54; P = 0.01). 

In a phase II trial [83], previously treated K-Ras mutant non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC) patients were randomized to receive docetaxel plus selumetinib (75 mg twice daily q21 days) or docetaxel plus placebo. Although median OS was 9.4 months in the selumetinib group versus 5.2 months in the control group, the difference was not statistically significant (HR 0.8; 80% CI 0.56–1.14; p = 0.21). However, median PFS was significantly better in the selumetinib group (5.3 vs 2.1 months), along with a higher overall response rate.

memory: In a study [PMC4914255], D-serine administration was linked to statistically significant improvements in spatial memory and learning, as measured by the Groton Maze Learning (GML) test (F(3, 38) = 4.74, p = 0.03). Post hoc analysis revealed the most significant difference between D-serine and control groups in the second trial (t = −3.13, p = 0.003). This effect was not due to differences in test comprehension, as no significant changes were observed in illegal errors (F(3, 38) = 0.05, p = 0.82). Higher plasma D-serine levels correlated with greater improvement in test performance (r² = −0.19, p = 0.009). However, D-serine did not significantly affect other cognitive domains, including working memory (n-back test, p > 0.1), cognitive flexibility (Set-Shifting task, p = 0.47), or visual attention (errors, p > 0.7). No significant changes in mood were reported (p > 0.4). The study concluded that D-serine enhances spatial memory and learning in older adults without influencing other cognitive functions or mood. These findings are summarized in Table 2 of the source article.

Aerobic exercise (75, 150, or 225 min/wk) improved cardiorespiratory fitness and reduced perceived disability in a dose-dependent manner. In per-protocol analyses (n=77), Simple Attention improved across all exercise groups compared to controls, with no dose dependency. Visuospatial Processing showed a dose-response relationship, with higher benefits at 225 min/wk. Cognitive benefits were apparent at low exercise doses, with potential added benefits in visuospatial function at higher doses for adherent participants.

In intent-to-treat analyses (n=101), no other exercise-related effects were observed beyond cardiorespiratory and perceived disability improvements. Adverse events (AE) were more common in 150 and 225 min/wk groups compared to 75 min/wk (X²=11.3, p=0.003). Most AEs were mild (91%) and included musculoskeletal pain; moderate AEs included lower extremity pain, heart rhythm abnormalities, and chest pain.

Visuospatial Processing and Simple Attention improved with 6 months of any exercise. Simple Attention showed an intervention effect (ΔX²=22.0), while Visuospatial Processing had a dose-response pattern (ΔX²=18.0). Verbal Memory and Reasoning improved across all groups, including controls, indicating a practice effect.
text: Aerobic exercise (150 or 225 min/wk) improved VO2 peak compared to no exercise, with greater benefits at higher doses. Source: [PMC4497726].

memory: A study compared the Total Sanitation Campaign (TSC) to a control group and found high anemia prevalence in children (54%), with no significant differences between groups in anemia or growth outcomes. The TSC significantly increased coverage of JMP-defined improved sanitation facilities (41.4% intervention vs. 22.6% control; p<0.001) and improved household latrines (IHL) (44.1% intervention vs. 24.2% control; p<0.001). However, reductions in reported open defecation were smaller than the gains in IHL availability. Among households with improved sanitation, 41% in the intervention and 28% in the control villages still reported daily open defecation. No significant difference in helminth infections was found between groups (p=0.001). E. coli contamination in water was slightly lower in intervention villages (77%) compared to control (82%), but this difference was not statistically significant (p=0.050). Water source samples showed 74% in control and 70% in intervention villages tested positive for E. coli, with no significant difference (p=0.143). The study indicates that while TSC improved sanitation infrastructure, behavioral changes in open defecation remained limited. Source: [PMC4144850]
text: The Total Sanitation Campaign significantly increased sanitation infrastructure but had limited effect on reducing open defecation. Despite higher improved sanitation coverage, 41% of intervention and 28% of control households still reported daily open defecation. Source: [PMC4144850].

memory:
A clinical study compared three mouth rinse regimens: Group I used chlorhexidine (CHX) 0.2% alone, Group II used CHX followed by hydrogen peroxide (H2O2) 1.5%, and Group III used H2O2 1.5% followed by CHX. Stain intensity was significantly lower in Group II compared to Group I after 14 days (P=0.025) and 21 days (P=0.005). The proportion of stained surfaces was also lower in Group II than Group I, with significance at 1 week. 

Plaque formation was significantly reduced in Groups II and III compared to Group I at 7, 14, and 21 days. Group II had significantly less plaque than Group I at all three time points (P=0.000). After the second and third weeks, Group II showed significantly less plaque than Group III (P=0.002 and 0.008, respectively). Group III also had significantly less plaque than Group I at 1 week (P=0.000) and 2 weeks (P=0.017), but the difference was not significant at 3 weeks (P=0.104). 

Stain intensity in Group III was less than Group I but not statistically significant. Group II had fewer stains than Group III after 2 and 3 weeks, but these differences were not significant (P=0.061 and 0.306). The results suggest that the order of using CHX and H2O2 impacts stain reduction and plaque formation, with Group II showing the most significant improvements in both parameters.
text: Using H2O2 1.5% followed by CHX (Group III) resulted in significantly less plaque than CHX alone (Group I) at 1 and 2 weeks, but not at 3 weeks. Group II (CHX followed by H2O2) showed significantly less plaque than both Group I and Group III at 3 weeks. (Source: Clinical study)
intervention: group III used hydrogen peroxide (H2O2) 1.5% followed by chlorhexidine (CHX)
comparator: group I rinsed with chlorhexidine (CHX) 0.2% alone
outcome: amount of plaque formed at end of week 3

memory: In a study comparing paricalcitol to placebo in children with stage 3/4 CKD, 33.3% (6/18) of the paricalcitol group achieved final iPTH levels within KDOQI range, compared to 11.1% (2/18) in the placebo group, though this difference was not statistically significant (P = 0.128). Paricalcitol showed a statistically significant improvement in achieving two consecutive iPTH reductions of ≥30% from baseline, with 27.8% (5/18) of the paricalcitol group achieving this versus none in the placebo group (P = 0.045). The mean between-group change in iPTH from baseline to final assessment was −72.4 pg/mL (95% CI −108.05 to −36.75 pg/mL; P < 0.001). At week 12, the mean change in iPTH was −17.1 (19.2) for the paricalcitol group compared with +71.5 (17.7) for the placebo group. Adverse events were higher in the placebo group (88.9%) compared to the paricalcitol group (38.9%; P = 0.005). In a stage 5 CKD study, 61.5% of children on paricalcitol achieved two consecutive iPTH reductions of ≥30%, and 38.5% had iPTH values between 150 and 300 pg/mL. Clinically meaningful hypercalcemia occurred in 21% of children. No significant differences were observed between the groups in calcium or phosphorus levels over the 12-week double-blind period.
text: Paricalcitol did not significantly affect calcium levels compared to control in CKD patients (P > 0.05). However, it significantly reduced iPTH levels. Source: Study on paricalcitol in stage 3/4 and 5 CKD.

memory: In a 24-week multinational trial with 132 patients, PR-fampridine showed greater median improvements compared to placebo in MSWS-12 score, TUG speed, and BBS total score. A higher proportion of PR-fampridine patients achieved significant MSWS-12 improvements (≥7, p=0.0275; ≥8, p=0.0153; ≥9, p=0.0088) and TUG speed thresholds (≥10%, p=0.0021; ≥15%, p=0.0262). Post-hoc analysis found that 46% of PR-fampridine patients reported improvement on PGIC at week 2, compared to 26% on placebo (p=0.023). Improvements were sustained throughout the trial. Adverse events (AEs) were similar between groups (77% placebo vs. 75% PR-fampridine), with nasopharyngitis and UTIs being the most common in each group. Placebo had a higher fall incidence, while PR-fampridine was associated with more balance disorder, gait disturbance, and dizziness. EQ-5D-5L results showed no significant differences, with a median treatment difference of 0.00 (95% CI: -4.17, 4.67) for VAS and 0.00 (-0.04, 0.04) for the utility index. PR-fampridine was generally well tolerated.
text: Prolonged-release fampridine significantly improved TUG speed compared to placebo over 24 weeks (p=0.0021 for ≥10% improvement). Improvements were sustained, though both groups had similar adverse event rates.
outcome: Improvement in Timed Up and Go (TUG) speed during 24 weeks

memory: In a clinical study comparing oral ibandronate 50 mg to placebo, ibandronate significantly reduced the mean skeletal morbidity period rate (SMPR) for all new bone events (P=0.004). This effect was primarily due to significant reductions in bone events requiring radiotherapy (P<0.001) or surgery (P=0.037), though no significant difference was observed for skeletal fractures (P=0.195). Multivariate Poisson regression analysis showed a 38% risk reduction for skeletal events in the ibandronate group (hazard ratio 0.62, 95% CI=0.48–0.79, P<0.0001). Patients on ibandronate also experienced a significant decrease in urinary CTx levels (median change −77.3% vs +11.0% in placebo, P<0.001). The mean number of events and measurement periods with events per patient were significantly reduced in the ibandronate group (P=0.008 and 0.015, respectively). The median time to first bone event was 90.3 weeks with ibandronate and 64.9 weeks with placebo (P=0.089). Including bone events from the first 12 weeks reduced the impact of ibandronate on skeletal event incidence, though the overall SMPR and radiotherapy-related events remained significant. These findings indicate that oral ibandronate is effective in reducing bone events requiring intervention, though not fractures.
text: Oral ibandronate 50 mg significantly reduced the risk of skeletal events compared to placebo, with a 38% risk reduction (HR 0.62, 95% CI 0.48–0.79, P<0.0001), mainly due to fewer events requiring radiotherapy or surgery. Fractures showed no significant difference.
outcome: risk reduction for a skeletal event

memory: In a study [PMC5336430], 5-FU 0.5%/salicylic acid 10% showed significant improvements in TSQM overall treatment satisfaction (69.2 vs. 56.1, P=0.0019) and effectiveness scores (70.8 vs. 59.2, P=0.0064) compared to vehicle at 8 weeks. No significant differences were noted in convenience or side effect domain scores. Complete clearance of condyloma (CCC) was significantly higher with the combination (49.5% vs. 18.2%, OR 3.9, P=0.0006), as was partial clearance (PC) (69.5% vs. 34.6%, OR 4.9, P<0.0001). In both ITT (49.5% vs. 18.2%) and PP (55.1% vs. 19.6%) populations, CCC was significantly greater with the combination therapy. Adverse events were more common with 5-FU 0.5%/salicylic acid 10% (99.1% vs. 83.6%). However, DLQI total scores improved more with vehicle during treatment, likely due to local skin reactions from the combination therapy.
text: The combination of 5-FU 0.5%/salicylic acid 10% resulted in more treatment-emergent adverse events (99.1% vs. 83.6%) compared to vehicle [PMC5336430].

memory:
Source: [PMC4282128]  
Intervention: Bupropion, nicotine replacement therapy (NRT), and their combination. Comparator: Bupropion vs. NRT. Outcome: Smoking cessation.  
Findings: Smoking cessation rates were similar between bupropion (27.9%) and NRT (24.2%), with no significant difference (OR = 1.21, 95% CI = 0.883–1.67). Combination therapy showed similar abstinence rates (24.2%) to either treatment alone. Subgroup analysis suggested bupropion may be more effective than NRT for smokers with a history of depression (29.8% vs. 18.5%, χ2 = 2.86, P = 0.091), though not statistically significant. No significant heterogeneity in treatment effects across study sites (χ2(3) = 1.24, P = 0.745). NRT success rates were similar across product types (26.9% for patch users). Bupropion was associated with more unwanted symptoms. Conclusion: No significant difference in effectiveness between bupropion, NRT, and their combination with behavioural support. Bupropion may be more beneficial for smokers with depression.
text: Bupropion and NRT had similar smoking cessation rates (27.9% vs. 24.2%, OR=1.21). No significant difference was found, though bupropion showed a trend of better efficacy in smokers with depression. Both had similar effectiveness when combined with behavioral support.

memory: An 11-week study compared the FIFA 11 for Health programme (intervention group, IG) to a control group (CG) and found significant improvements in cardiovascular and body composition markers in the IG. Systolic blood pressure decreased by −3.5 mm Hg in the IG versus +0.9 mm Hg in the CG, with similar trends for mean arterial blood pressure (−1.9 vs 0.4 mm Hg). The IG also showed greater reductions in body mass index (−0.02 vs 0.13 kg/m²) and body fat percentage (−0.83% vs −0.04%), all with p<0.05 significance. Within-group improvements in the IG were noted for 20 m sprint time (4.09±0.29 s to 4.06±0.28 s) and Yo-Yo intermittent recovery level 1 (YYIR1C) performance (852±464 m to 896±517 m), but these changes were not significantly different from the CG. Balance and jump performance remained unchanged in both groups. The findings suggest that the FIFA 11 for Health programme may improve cardiovascular health and body composition, but did not significantly enhance sprint or YYIR1C performance compared to the control group. Source: [PMC5136709]
text: The FIFA 11 for Health programme significantly reduced body fat percentage (−0.83%) compared to control (−0.04%, p<0.05). Source: [PMC5136709]

memory: A study compared Lactobacillus rhamnosus GG (LGG) with a placebo in infants and found no significant differences in microbiota composition at 6 months. However, at 18 months, after discontinuing the probiotic, LGG supplementation was linked to changes in three genus-like bacterial groups. The LGG group showed higher levels of butyrate-producing bacteria: Anaerostipes caccae et rel (2.89 ± 2.13% vs. 1.18 ± 0.91%, p=0.03) and Eubacterium ventriosum et rel (0.17 ± 0.11% vs. 0.11 ± 0.07%, p=0.04) compared to the placebo group. Conversely, the placebo group had higher levels of Clostridium difficile et rel (1.19 ± 0.85% vs. 0.78 ± 0.60%, p=0.047). These results suggest that early LGG supplementation may induce long-term changes in the gut microbiota. Full data on phylum-like and genus-like levels are available in Additional files 7 and 8. Source: PMC3563445.
text: At 18 months, Lactobacillus rhamnosus GG supplementation was linked to lower levels of Clostridium difficile et rel compared to placebo (p=0.047). Source: PMC3563445.
outcome: Clostridium difficile et rel at 18 months of age

memory: In a study of 531 minimal-risk patients (mean age 52.4 years, 62.0% female), the PROMISE minimal-risk tool demonstrated better discrimination than the CADC model (c-statistic 0.785 vs 0.730, p < 0.001), with further improvement after re-estimating covariate coefficients (c-statistic 0.805, p < 0.001). Initial model calibration was poor (χ2 197.6, HL p < 0.001) but significantly improved after revisions (χ2 5.6, HL p = 0.692). Minimal-risk patients had lower pre-test probability of obstructive CAD (30.0% vs 47.0%, p < 0.001) and were less likely to have typical angina symptoms (24.1% vs 42.6%, p < 0.001) compared to the rest of the cohort. HDL-C was missing in 28.7% of patients and was imputed. Both the CADC model (χ2 1010.1, HL p < 0.001) and the PROMISE minimal-risk tool (χ2 197.6, HL p < 0.001) showed poor goodness-of-fit. The PROMISE tool's discrimination remained unaffected by re-calibration of intercept or slope but improved with revised coefficients.
text: Patients with minimal-risk had a lower pre-test probability of obstructive CAD (30.0% vs 47.0%, p < 0.001) compared to the remainder of the cohort, as reported in the PROMISE study.

memory: A clinical study compared partial matrix excision (Group I) and segmental phenolization (Group II) for treating ingrown toenails. Postoperative pain was moderate in 3 patients in Group I and 2 in Group II, with both groups requiring analgesics for 3 days. Pain differences were not statistically significant (P > 0.05). No soft tissue infections were reported in either group. Postoperative complication and recurrence rates were similar between the two groups (P = 0.688). However, the time to return to normal daily activities was significantly shorter in Group II compared to Group I (P < 0.05), which was used as the criterion for treatment success. The results suggest that although both procedures have comparable complication and recurrence rates, segmental phenolization may offer a faster recovery time.
text: Both partial matrix excision and segmental phenolization have similar postoperative complication and recurrence rates. However, segmental phenolization allows for a faster return to normal activities, suggesting it may be more effective in terms of recovery time (P < 0.05).

memory:
In a clinical study [PMC4312979], kinetic oscillation stimulation (KOS) in the nasal cavity was tested against placebo for migraine management. Active treatment significantly reduced pain scores, as measured by the visual analog scale (VAS). Pain scores in the active group decreased from 5.5 pre-treatment to 1.2 at 15 minutes post-treatment, while the placebo group scores fell from 4.9 to 3.9. The difference in pain scores between the two groups was 3.3 points (95% CI: 2.3, 4.4), P < .001. Significant differences were observed as early as 5 minutes (1.9 points, P = .007) and 2 hours post-treatment (3.7 points, P < .001). 

Regarding secondary outcomes, the proportion of headache days during a 2-month follow-up period showed a slight reduction in the active group compared to the run-in period, while the placebo group showed an increase. However, these differences were not statistically significant (P = .39 and P = .53, respectively). Additionally, during the first month of follow-up, the active group showed a trend toward reduced pain intensity and attack duration compared to the placebo group, though the differences were not statistically significant (P = .42 and P = .37, respectively).
text: Kinetic oscillation stimulation (KOS) in the nasal cavity significantly reduced pain scores compared to placebo in migraine management (PMC4312979). VAS scores dropped from 5.5 to 1.2 in the active group versus 4.9 to 3.9 in the placebo group (difference: 3.3 points, P < .001).
intervention: kinetic oscillation stimulation (KOS) in the nasal cavity

memory:
A community-based intervention was compared to usual care in a study evaluating health outcomes and costs. The primary outcome, the SF-12 Physical Component Summary (PCS), showed no significant group difference in 6-month scores after adjusting for baseline values. However, the intervention group demonstrated significant improvements in the SF-12 Mental Component Summary (MCS) (mean difference = 2.74, 95% CI = 0.28–5.19, P = .03), SF-12 general health subdomain (mean difference = 3.11, 95% CI = 0.05–5.71, P = .02), and the Summary of Diabetes Self-Care Activities (SDSCA) (mean difference = 3.74, 95% CI = 0.9–6.57, P = .01), all favoring the intervention. No significant differences were observed for CES-D, GAD-7, or self-efficacy. Multiple imputation supported complete-case findings. 

Regarding costs, there was no significant difference in total cost changes from baseline to 6 months. The intervention group showed reductions in costs for family physician visits, specialist visits, diagnostic tests, supplies, and equipment. The control group had lower costs in prescription medications and other health professionals. The mean group difference in total cost change, excluding hospital costs, was $236.92 in favor of the intervention, though not statistically significant.
text: A community-based intervention significantly improved SF-12 MCS (mean diff 2.74, 95% CI 0.28–5.19, P = .03) and SDSCA (mean diff 3.74, 95% CI 0.9–6.57, P = .01) compared to usual care, but not PCS. General health subdomain also improved. No significant cost differences were found. (Source: Study evaluating health outcomes and costs)
outcome: 12‐item Short‐Form Health Survey (SF‐12), Mental Component Summary (MCS), Summary of Diabetes Self‐Care Activities (SDSCA)

memory: A clinical study compared bladder training (BT), tolterodine (To), and their combination (Co) in treating overactive bladder (OAB) symptoms. All groups showed significant improvements in frequency, nocturia, and urgency. The BT group experienced a 25.9% reduction in frequency and 56.1% reduction in nocturia. The To group had 30.2% and 65.4% reductions, respectively, while the Co group showed the highest improvements at 33.5% and 66.3%. Frequency improvements in the Co group were significantly greater than in the BT group (p<0.05). Urgency scores improved by 44.8% in BT, 62.2% in To, and 60.2% in Co, with both To and Co showing significantly greater improvements than BT (p<0.05). No significant difference was found between To and Co in urgency improvement. Combination therapy was more effective than monotherapy, though To alone may be considered a first-line therapy. Satisfaction scores at 12 weeks were similar across groups, with the Co group showing the highest improvement rate (71.0%). No difference was observed between To and Co in micturition frequency improvements. The study suggests that combination therapy may offer enhanced symptom control compared to monotherapy.
text: Bladder training plus tolterodine (Co) significantly reduced micturition frequency more than bladder training alone (p<0.05), but no significant difference was found between tolterodine only (To) and Co. Source: Clinical study on OAB treatment.

memory: A clinical study compared three anesthetic groups: RH (remifentanil 0.3), KRH (remifentanil 0.3 + ketamine 0.5), and RL (remifentanil 0.05). Demographic parameters, including age, body weight, baseline blood pressure, heart rate, anesthesia duration, input/output, and time to extubation, were not significantly different between groups. End-tidal desflurane concentration was higher in group RL. Group RH demonstrated significantly higher additional analgesic consumption, higher NRS scores at 6 and 24 hours post-surgery, and a higher cumulative fentanyl dose compared to groups KRH and RL. The Touch-Test sensory evaluation value difference was significantly more negative in group RH than in the other groups. During PACU stay, group RH had significantly higher ketorolac consumption compared to group RL. No dropouts were reported. Source: PMC4610927.
text: The Touch-Test sensory evaluation value was significantly more negative in group RH compared to groups KRH and RL, indicating worse sensory recovery (PMC4610927).
comparator: Remifentanil 0.3 + ketamine 0.5 (group KRH) or remifentanil 0.05 (Group RL)
outcome: Value of the Touch-Test sensory evaluation after surgery

memory: A study compared exercise training with a control group and found no significant differences in changes in blood pressure, HDL cholesterol, or CRP levels. However, LDL cholesterol increased in the exercise group compared to controls (p = 0.020). Subgroup analysis based on carotid plaque presence revealed that the increase in LDL cholesterol in the exercise group was significant only in participants with plaques [0.20 mmol/L (0.00 to 0.41) vs −0.13 mmol/L (−0.37 to 0.12), p = 0.044], but not in those without plaques (p = 0.40). Baseline LDL levels were 2.0 mmol/L (1.6, 2.6) in the exercise group and 1.9 mmol/L (1.6, 2.5) in the control group. Post-intervention, LDL levels increased significantly in the exercise group (2.0 mmol/L (1.7, 2.7)) compared to controls (1.9 mmol/L (1.5, 2.7), p = 0.020). These results suggest that exercise training may differentially affect LDL cholesterol levels in individuals with versus without carotid plaques.
text: Exercise training did not significantly affect HDL cholesterol compared to control. However, LDL cholesterol increased in the exercise group (p = 0.020), particularly in those with carotid plaques. Baseline HDL levels were not provided, but no change in HDL was observed.

Source: [PMC5380277]  
Heated infusions improved postoperative recovery compared to room temperature infusions. Patients receiving heated infusions showed significantly shorter times to spontaneous breathing (4.06 ± 0.72 min vs. 4.47 ± 0.84 min, P = 0.042), eye opening (6.72 ± 1.73 min vs. 8.66 ± 2.03 min, P < 0.001), and consciousness recovery (9.91 ± 1.91 min vs. 11.19 ± 1.49 min, P = 0.004). Mean extubation time was also reduced (10.09 ± 1.91 min vs. 11.13 ± 1.34 min, P = 0.015). No significant differences were observed in hospital stay duration.  

Intraoperatively, heated infusions did not significantly affect blood loss, transfusion volume, or blood transfusion volume (P > 0.05). However, surgery time was significantly shorter in the warmed infusion group (2.925 ± 0.216 min vs. 3.094 ± 0.254 min, P < 0.05). Results are detailed in Tables 2 and 3 of the source article.
text: Heated infusions significantly reduced consciousness recovery time compared to control (9.91 ± 1.91 min vs. 11.19 ± 1.49 min, P = 0.004) [PMC5380277].

memory: In a study comparing the Charité artificial disc (intervention) with anterior lumbar interbody fusion (ALIF) using BAK cages (control), superficial wound infection rates were higher in the investigational group (6.3%) compared to the control group (2.0%), though not statistically significant (P = .103). No deep wound infections were reported in either group. The control group had 3 (3.0%) cases of iliac crest donor site infection. Major neurological complications were similar between the groups (4.4% vs. 4.0%). Approach-related complications occurred in 9.8% of the investigational group and 10.1% of the control group. Pseudarthrosis was observed in 9.1% of control group patients. Retrograde ejaculation was reported in 3 (3.3%) patients in the investigational group and 3 (5.5%) in the control group, with no significant difference (P = .515). These findings indicate comparable complication profiles between the two groups, with some trends suggesting higher superficial infection rates and donor site issues in the control group. No deep infections or significant differences in major neurological complications were noted.
text: The Charité artificial disc had a higher rate of superficial wound infection (6.3%) compared to ALIF with BAK cages (2.0%), though not statistically significant (P = .103).

memory: In a study comparing geniVidaTM bone blend (GBB) to placebo, estradiol (E2) levels increased by 12.7% in the GBB group (p = 0.044), remaining within normal ranges. Endometrial thickness (ET) decreased in the GBB group from 2.3 to 1.8 mm (p = 0.007), whereas no change was observed in the placebo group (2.2–2.3 mm, p = 0.62). No significant differences in ECG or vital signs were noted. Regarding bone mineral density (BMD), at 6 months, the GBB group (n = 30) maintained femoral neck BMD, while the placebo group (n = 28) experienced a significant decrease (p = 0.007), resulting in a 1.3% difference between groups (p < 0.05). At Ward's triangle, BMD increased by +2.3% in the GBB group versus −1.1% in the placebo group (p < 0.05). These results suggest that GBB may help preserve BMD compared to placebo. Source: [PMC3549413]
text: The placebo group showed a significant decrease in bone mineral density (BMD) at the 6-month time point compared to baseline (p = 0.007), while the GBB group maintained BMD. Source: [PMC3549413]
outcome: bone mineral density (BMD) At the 6-month time point

memory: A study examined the effects of 1200 mg cranberry extract supplementation over 6 weeks on exercise-related biomarkers compared to a placebo. Post-exercise, both groups showed increased interleukin 6 (IL-6) levels, which normalized after 24 hours of recovery. Cranberry extract did not significantly alter IL-6 concentrations (p = 0.051). Total antioxidant capacity (TAC) was affected by both exercise and cranberry supplementation. Before supplementation (Trial I), both groups experienced reduced TAC post-exercise. After supplementation (Trial II), the cranberry group exhibited significantly higher resting, post-exercise, and post-recovery TAC levels than controls, despite a post-exercise decrease in TAC in the supplemented group. Serum iron levels were not significantly affected by cranberry extract (p = 0.516), although both groups showed significant post-exercise increases in iron concentrations at Trial II. Serum myoglobin levels were solely influenced by physical exercise (p < 0.001). Changes in TAC, IL-6, and iron levels during exercise tests before and after supplementation are illustrated in Figures 1, 2, and 3, respectively.
text: Receiving 1200 mg of cranberry extract for 6 weeks significantly increased total antioxidant capacity (TAC) levels compared to placebo, especially at rest, post-exercise, and post-recovery (source).
intervention: receiving 1200 mg of cranberry extract for 6 weeks

memory: In a clinical study [PMC5863413], both propolis gel and triamcinolone acetonide showed significant reductions in pain and erythema scores from baseline to the second follow-up compared to no treatment (P = 0.000 for all comparisons). However, direct comparison between the two interventions revealed no statistically significant difference in pain or erythema reduction (P = 0.255). Similarly, when comparing propolis gel and triamcinolone acetonide to no treatment, the differences in pain and erythema reduction were also not significant (P = 0.255). The findings indicate that both interventions led to significant improvements over no treatment, but there was no significant difference between the interventions themselves in terms of pain and erythema reduction. All comparisons were conducted in the front section of the study.
text: Propolis gel significantly reduces pain compared to no treatment, as shown in a clinical study [PMC5863413]. However, it was not significantly different from triamcinolone acetonide in pain reduction. Both treatments outperformed no treatment in pain and erythema improvement.

memory: A study compared ESM-I (six weeks of Ecological Momentary Assessment with weekly feedback on positive affective experiences) to two control groups: one receiving six weeks of ESM without feedback and another receiving a pseudo-intervention. Outcomes were measured at 32 weeks using the HDRS and symptomatic remission rates. The ESM-I group showed a mean HDRS score 3 units lower than the ESM-no-feedback group (B = −3.1, p = 0.051, intention-to-treat analysis), though the result was not statistically significant by conventional alpha. No significant differences were found between ESM-I and the pseudo-intervention group (B = −1.13, p = 0.47). When compared to treatment as usual, ESM-I also showed a 3-unit reduction in HDRS scores (B = −3.1, p = 0.051), but this was not statistically significant. Symptomatic remission rates did not differ significantly between ESM-I and the control groups (OR = 2.65, p = 0.12) or between ESM-I and the pseudo-intervention group (OR = 1.84, p = 0.29). These findings suggest that ESM-I did not lead to a higher rate of symptomatic remission compared to either control condition. Source: [PMC5747107] Table 3, Outcomes (intention-to-treat).
text: The study found no significant difference in symptomatic remission rates between ESM-I and the control groups (OR = 2.65, p = 0.12). ESM-I did not result in a higher rate of symptomatic remission compared to ESM without feedback or pseudo-intervention. Source: [PMC5747107].
intervention: ESM-I consisting of six weeks of ESM combined with weekly feedback regarding the individual’s positive affective experiences
comparator: (ii) six weeks of ESM without feedback,

memory: [PMC5393542] - HA intervention significantly increased bleeding time compared to control (7.17±1.36 vs. 5.64±1.46 minutes, p<0.05). No significant differences in MIO or VAS scores were observed at pre-op, 1 hour, 3rd day, or 7th day between HA and control groups. Swelling in orotragus and mentotragus was significantly higher in the HA group on the 3rd day (p<0.05), though no differences were found at pre-op, 1 hour, or 7th day. text: Hyaluronic acid (HA) significantly reduced salivary tissue factor (TF) levels compared to baseline after 1 week (p<0.05), while the control group showed no significant changes. This effect was also significantly lower in the HA group compared to the control group (p<0.05) [PMC5393542].

memory: A study compared locking plate fixation (n=20) and nonlocking plate fixation (n=21) for tibial plateau fractures. Follow-up duration (10.61 ± 3.05 vs. 12.95 ± 2.63 months, P=0.158) and fracture severity (Schatzker/AO classifications, P=0.556/0.257) were not significantly different. The locking plate group showed higher mean knee scores (80.20 ± 10.21 vs. 72.52 ± 14.75, P=0.039), lower VAS pain scores (4.45 ± 2.50 vs. 6.00 ± 2.59, P=0.046), and better functional scores (77.26 ± 9.95 vs. 69.55 ± 10.22, P=0.026). No significant differences in range of motion were found (122.35 ± 12.93° vs. 115.71 ± 20.14°, P=0.219). Six patients had superficial infections (1 locking, 5 nonlocking), all managed with antibiotics. No major complications like nonunion or DVT were reported. Step-off >2 mm occurred in 4 locking and 7 nonlocking cases, while articular widening >2 mm was observed in 1 locking and 4 nonlocking cases. Overall, locking plate fixation was associated with better functional outcomes. [PMC4045368]
text: Locking plate fixation resulted in higher mean knee scores (80.20 ± 10.21) compared to nonlocking plate fixation (72.52 ± 14.75, P=0.039) [PMC4045368].

memory: In a study comparing Ashwagandha (Withania somnifera) to a placebo, no changes in vital parameters (pulse rate, systolic and diastolic blood pressure, respiratory rate) were observed in either group at rest. Ashwagandha significantly improved quality of life (QOL) domains—physical, psychological, and social relationships—compared to placebo by 12 weeks (P < 0.05). Environmental impact on QOL became significant (P < 0.01) at 12 weeks but not at 8 weeks. Ashwagandha also showed greater improvements in mean VO2 max at 8 weeks (4.91 vs. 1.42) and 12 weeks (5.67 vs. 1.86) compared to placebo (P < 0.0001). These QOL improvements were more pronounced in the Ashwagandha group at 12 weeks. The findings suggest Ashwagandha may enhance QOL and cardiorespiratory endurance without affecting vital signs.
text: Ashwagandha significantly increased mean VO2 max by 4.91 after 8 weeks compared to placebo (1.42, P < 0.0001). No changes in vital parameters were observed.
outcome: Increase from baseline in the mean VO2 max after 8 weeks

memory: A 12-week clinical trial compared sitagliptin and voglibose, both of which improved flow-mediated dilatation (FMD). After adjusting for baseline FMD, age, sex, smoking status, diabetes duration, and BMI, no significant difference in ΔFMD was observed between the two groups. No significant differences were found in changes in HbA1c, GIP, GLP-1, C-peptide, lipid profile, oxidative stress markers, inflammatory markers, or eGFR. Sitagliptin significantly increased circulating CD34, an endothelial progenitor cell marker, compared to voglibose (P < 0.05). The results were obtained using ANCOVA analyses and are presented in Table 3 and Figure 3 of the source article [PMC4149239].
text: A 12-week trial found no significant difference between sitagliptin and voglibose in their effect on gastric inhibitory polypeptide (GIP) levels [PMC4149239]. Both drugs similarly influenced other markers, but sitagliptin increased CD34 levels more than voglibose.

memory: A study compared Performance-Based Financing (PBF) with two control groups: C1 (enhanced financing) and C2 (pure control), focusing on job and compensation satisfaction. Overall job satisfaction was highest in C1, followed by PBF, then C2—contrary to expectations. Compensation satisfaction showed PBF had higher scores than C1, which scored higher than C2. C1 reported an 8.64% (p < 0.05) lower satisfaction with being rewarded for their work compared to PBF, while C2 had a 3.88% (p < 0.1) lower score than C1. Differences between C1 and C2 were not statistically significant. PBF showed a 4.75% (p < 0.05) increase in overall job satisfaction compared to C2, and C1 had a 10.31% (p < 0.05) increase compared to C2. However, PBF had 0.48% lower job satisfaction than C1, though not statistically significant. Regarding attrition, PBF had 0.10 fewer administrators (p < 0.05) leaving compared to C1, and 0.14 fewer nurses (p < 0.05) leaving compared to C2. These results suggest PBF may reduce staff turnover, particularly for nurses and administrators, though differences in job satisfaction among groups were nuanced and sometimes unexpected. Full compensation and satisfaction results are detailed in Additional file 7.
text: Performance-based financing (PBF) was associated with 0.10 fewer administrators leaving compared to control 1 (C1; enhanced financing) (p < 0.05). This suggests PBF may reduce administrator attrition compared to enhanced financing.
outcome: administrators on average who left health centers

memory: In a study published in [PMC5808396], women with moderate baseline felt stigma (mean score 1.98) were randomized to receive either Cognitive Processing Therapy (CPT) or individual support (IS). The CPT group demonstrated a significantly greater reduction in felt stigma compared to the IS group at the end of treatment (B = −0.44, p = 0.02). Both groups showed a decrease in felt stigma over time, but the decline was more pronounced in the CPT group. At six months post-treatment, the difference between the groups was no longer statistically significant (B = −0.45, p = 0.12), though the observed difference in felt stigma remained noticeable. These results indicate that CPT may be more effective than individual support in reducing felt stigma in the short term, with some evidence of sustained benefits over time. Source: [PMC5808396], Table 2.
text: Cognitive Processing Therapy (CPT) led to a greater reduction in felt stigma compared to individual support at treatment end (B = −0.44, p = 0.02), though this difference was not significant at six months (B = −0.45, p = 0.12). Source: [PMC5808396].

memory: In a study on ischemia-reperfusion (I/R) injury in isolated rat hearts, lixisenatide treatment significantly reduced infarct size when administered 10 minutes before reperfusion. Infarct area was 162 ± 12 mm² in placebo-treated hearts versus 98 ± 9 mm² in lixisenatide-treated hearts (n=10-11, p < 0.05). Left ventricular total area showed no significant differences between groups (543 ± 16 mm² for placebo vs. 505 ± 7 mm² for lixisenatide). The infarct area to area at risk ratio was reduced by 36% in lixisenatide-treated hearts compared to placebo. Left ventricular risk area was 306 ± 9 mm² for placebo and 288 ± 5 mm² for lixisenatide. Rate pressure product (LVP x HR) and coronary flow were not altered during reperfusion at 5 and 120 minutes. In long-term injury studies, no overall cardiac dilatation was observed, and left-ventricular wall thickness was reduced by I/R, with no significant modification by treatment groups. Right ventricular wall thickness, which was slightly increased in I/R placebo animals, was normalized to sham values by lixisenatide treatment. Septal wall thickness was not altered between groups. Source: [PMC3637243].
text: Lixisenatide significantly reduced left ventricular risk area compared to control in a rat I/R injury model (306 ± 9 mm² vs. 288 ± 5 mm², p < 0.05). Source: [PMC3637243].

memory: A clinical study compared PEG-lactulose with lactulose alone for treating hepatic encephalopathy. The PEG-lactulose group received 20-30 grams of lactulose (oral or rectal) plus 280 grams of PEG in 4 liters of water orally as a single dose over 30-120 minutes. Comparator groups received either 20-30 grams of lactulose orally or via nasogastric tube, or 200 grams of lactulose enema via rectal tube. Results showed that PEG-lactulose improved HESA scores more effectively than lactulose alone after 24 hours (p=0.04), with 20 patients in the PEG-lactulose group showing at least a 1-point decrease in HESA score compared to 14 in the lactulose group (p=0.05). However, no significant difference in blood ammonia levels was found between the groups (p=0.858). The PEG-lactulose regimen was associated with a shorter hospital stay compared to lactulose treatment (p=0.03), with a significant effect observed only in women (p=0.01) in subgroup analysis. Source: [PMC5308129].
text: The PEG–lactulose regimen did not significantly affect blood ammonia levels compared to lactulose alone (p=0.858). Source: [PMC5308129].
intervention: PEG–lactulose group received the 20-30 grams of lactulose of oral or rectal lactulose, plus 280 grams of PEG in 4 liters of water orally as a single dose in 30-120 minutes
comparator: 20-30 grams of lactulose orally or by a nasogastric tube, or 200 grams of lactulose enema by a rectal tube

memory: A study investigated the effects of different contraction intensities on muscle thickness. Comparing 50% maximal voluntary isometric contraction (MVIC) to 10% MVIC showed no significant differences in sternocleidomastoid thickness (p > 0.05). Similarly, no significant differences were found in sternocleidomastoid thickness when comparing 80% MVIC to 10% MVIC (p > 0.05) or 80% MVIC to 50% MVIC (p > 0.05). However, during concurrent masticatory muscle contraction, 80% MVIC resulted in a significant increase in longus colli thickness compared to 10% MVIC (p < 0.05). These results suggest that sternocleidomastoid thickness remains unaffected by varying contraction intensities, while longus colli thickness may be influenced by higher contraction intensities when combined with concurrent muscle activation.
text: An 80% maximal voluntary isometric contraction significantly increased longus colli thickness compared to 10% MVIC during concurrent masticatory muscle contraction (p < 0.05).

memory: A study compared ampicillin/sulbactam and cefuroxime in 176 patients (median age 28 years, IQR: 24–32) for postoperative outcomes. Hospitalization duration was 4 days (IQR: 4–4) for both groups, with no significant difference (p = 0.09). Postoperative infections occurred in 13 (7.4%) patients overall, with 5 (5.9%) in the cefuroxime group and 8 (8.8%) in the ampicillin/sulbactam group (p = 0.6). Surgical site infections (SSIs) totaled 10, with 6 in the ampicillin/sulbactam group and 4 in the cefuroxime group (p = 0.7). These included 5 superficial incisional SSIs, 5 organ/space SSIs, 4 cases of post-partum endometritis, and 1 intrabdominal collection. Post-cesarean endometritis occurred in 4 (2.3%) patients in the ampicillin/sulbactam group and 2 (2.4%) in the cefuroxime group (p = 1). No statistically significant differences were found between the treatment groups for any of the studied outcomes.
text: Ampicillin/sulbactam and cefuroxime had similar effects on hospitalization duration (4 days, IQR: 4–4, p = 0.09). No significant differences were observed in postoperative infections or surgical site infections between the groups.

memory: [PMC3112403] A study compared flaxseed and wheat bran in obese individuals (baseline BMI: 32.4 ± 8.2 kg/m² for flaxseed; 30.3 ± 5.5 kg/m² for wheat bran). No significant changes in BMI, body weight, or waist circumference were observed between groups. Fasting plasma glucose significantly decreased in the flaxseed group compared to baseline and the wheat bran group (5.92 ± 0.31 vs. 4.79 ± 0.17 mmol/L for flaxseed; 5.67 ± 0.14 vs. 5.73 ± 0.35 mmol/L for wheat bran). No significant changes in fasting insulin or HOMA-IR were found. Inflammatory markers (IL-6, TNF-α, hs-CRP) showed no significant differences between groups. Energy and nutrient intake were similar across groups (1875 ± 798 kcal/d; 17% protein, 38% fat, 45% carbs). No significant relationships were found between weight change and glucose, insulin, HOMA-IR, or inflammatory biomarkers. Wheat bran significantly reduced plasma insulin compared to baseline (p = 0.026). Dietary intake of α-linolenic acid and fiber could not be analyzed due to software limitations.
text: Flaxseed significantly reduced fasting plasma glucose compared to wheat bran (4.79 vs. 5.73 mmol/L, p<0.05) in obese individuals, with no significant changes in BMI or inflammatory markers. Source: [PMC3112403].

memory: In a study comparing LCI699 and eplerenone, LCI699 at doses of 0.5–3 mg significantly reduced ACTH-stimulated aldosterone levels by 41–64% on Day 6 (P < 0.001 vs. placebo). In contrast, eplerenone 100 mg increased pre-ACTH aldosterone by 29% and post-ACTH aldosterone by 63%. LCI699 at 0.5–3 mg doses reduced plasma aldosterone by 49–63% at 12 h on Day 1, with continued suppression on Days 7 and 14. The 10 mg dose showed no additional reduction. However, LCI699 at ≥100 mg increased 11-deoxycortisol, likely due to off-target inhibition of 11-β hydroxylase. Single doses of LCI699 ≥30 mg significantly reduced 24-h urinary cortisol by 34–42% (P ≤ 0.001 vs. placebo), while plasma cortisol remained unchanged at 3–100 mg doses, except for a 19% decrease at 200 mg. These findings supported the design of multiple-dose studies with lower LCI699 doses (0.5–10 mg). (Source: PMC4301837)
text: LCI699 significantly reduced plasma aldosterone concentration at 12 h compared to placebo (49–63% reduction on Day 1). This effect was dose-dependent for 0.5–3 mg doses, with no additional benefit at 10 mg. (Source: PMC4301837)

memory: In a study comparing system-oriented therapy to a reference intervention, the system-oriented group had a significantly longer time to readmission (P = 0.049), though no significant difference was found in average bed day consumption over 12 months. The primary endpoint was improvement in medical compliance in patients with schizophrenia, measured using a project-specific compliance scale. Both compliance scale and PANSS scores showed a tendency toward improvement with system-oriented therapy, but differences were not statistically significant. A significant difference in the incidence of adverse events and time to first readmission was found. Attrition rates were significantly higher in the reference group (15/40 vs. 4/30, P = 0.017), which may have diluted effect estimates, particularly among individuals with lower compliance. In the individual intervention group, participants received an average of 3 sessions (SD 2.1) and no booster sessions (SD 0.7). The system-oriented intervention achieved a fulfillment of standards of 43% in the hospital. The study used multiple imputation to account for missing values.
text: System-oriented therapy showed a longer time to readmission (P = 0.049) compared to the reference intervention, but no significant difference in bed days or compliance. Higher attrition in the reference group may have affected results.

memory: A study evaluated the effects of IPE (4g/day) versus placebo in patients with diabetes (median baseline A1c = 6.8%). IPE significantly reduced multiple lipid and inflammatory markers across three diabetes subgroups: total, better-controlled, and less-controlled diabetes. Baseline parameters were similar, except for higher hsCRP in total and less-controlled diabetes groups. IPE reduced TG, non-HDL cholesterol, VLDL-C, lipoprotein-associated phospholipase A2, Apo B, total cholesterol, HDL cholesterol, VLDL-TG, oxidized LDL, and remnant-like particle cholesterol in all subgroups. LDL-C was reduced in the total diabetes group, and hsCRP was reduced in total and less-controlled diabetes groups. The reductions in hsCRP and Apo B were more pronounced in less-controlled diabetes patients. No significant changes in fasting plasma glucose, A1c, insulin, or HOMA-IR were observed, indicating IPE did not worsen glycemic control or insulin resistance. The findings suggest that IPE effectively improves lipid profiles and reduces inflammation in diabetic patients without adverse effects on glycemic parameters.
text: IPE (4g/day) did not significantly affect fasting plasma glucose, A1c, insulin, or HOMA-IR in diabetic patients (median baseline A1c 6.8%), indicating no worsening of glycemic control or insulin resistance. Source: Study on IPE effects in diabetes subgroups.
outcome: fasting plasma glucose, A1c, insulin, or homeostasis model assessment-estimated insulin total (all subjects with diabetes—overall median baseline glycosylated hemoglobin A1c [A1c] = 6.8%), better-controlled diabetes (below median baseline A1c), and less-controlled diabetes (above median baseline A1c).

memory: A study compared real-time fMRI neurofeedback (rtfMRI-nf) from the left amygdala (LA) to a health information program (HIPS). The experimental group showed significant pre-post decreases in anxiety and increases in happiness compared to the control group [PMC3921228]. During the transfer run, increased brain activity was observed in the left superior temporal gyrus, temporal polar cortex, and right thalamus. The experimental group experienced a greater increase in happiness (t(19)=2.33, p=0.01). They also showed significant decreases in POMS anger (t(13)=2.42, p=0.015), trait anxiety (t(13)=2.62, p=0.01), state anxiety (t(13)=2.34, p=0.02), and VAS ratings of restlessness (t(13)=2.23, p=0.02), anxiety (t(13)=4.37, p<0.001), and irritability (t(13)=2.14, p=0.025). Group differences in state anxiety were significant (t(19)=2.58, p=0.03). The experimental group also showed decreased POMS depression (t(13)=2.12, p=0.025) and increased VAS happiness (t(13)=3.04, p=0.005). Although happiness increased more in the experimental group compared to control (t(19)=2.33, p=0.01), changes in POMS depression between groups were not significant (t(19)=1.33, p=0.10).
text: rtfMRI-nf from the left amygdala significantly reduced state anxiety more than the HIPS program [PMC3921228]. The experimental group showed greater decreases in state anxiety (t(13)=2.34, p=0.02) and significant group differences (t(19)=2.58, p=0.03).

memory: A 12-week clinical trial evaluated dextromethorphan (DM60 and DM120) against placebo in patients. DM60 showed significant improvements in treatment retention and reduced plasma morphine levels compared to placebo. Additionally, plasma TNF-α levels were significantly lower in the DM60 group. However, no significant differences were observed between groups in changes in plasma cytokine levels, BDNF levels, or methadone dose requirements. These findings suggest that DM60 may enhance treatment retention, lower morphine levels, and reduce TNF-α, but does not appear to affect cytokine levels, BDNF, or methadone dose adjustments. Source: [PMC4540107]
text: Dextromethorphan (DM60) significantly improved treatment retention and reduced plasma morphine and TNF-α levels compared to placebo in a 12-week trial. No significant effects were noted on cytokine levels, BDNF, or methadone dose requirements. Source: [PMC4540107]

However, salivary IgA levels were significantly different (p < 0.05; p < 0.01) across groups, with values: 17.7 ± 8.1 **, 13.9 ± 6.5, 12.6 ± 7.5, 11.1 ± 10.5, 9.6 ± 6.1, 12.3 ± 8.3*. No significant differences were observed in serum ferritin levels at baseline or three months (Wilcoxon p=0.05; Fisher T-Test p>0.05) (Table 3).
text: A study (PMC4663570) found no significant effect of Agave derived fructans compared to formula on C-Reactive Protein levels at baseline or three months (Wilcoxon p=0.05; Fisher T-Test p>0.05).

memory: A 12-week study in CKD patients with low vitamin D found that adding calcitriol to calcium carbonate did not significantly reduce pro-inflammatory markers (IL-6 and hs-CRP) compared to calcium alone, except for a reduction in IL-6 among non-diabetic patients. Calcitriol helped stabilize the anti-inflammatory biomarker IL-10, which declined significantly in the calcium-only group (p = 0.06 for IL-10 in the Vitamin D + Calcium group vs. significant decline in the Calcium group). These effects were independent of serum vitamin D levels. Serum calcium levels increased with supplementation but remained within normal ranges, highlighting the need for monitoring. Serum 25-OHD levels in the Vitamin D + Calcium group increased significantly from 15.80 (9.37) to 25.10 (35.57) ng/mL (p = 0.001). The study suggests that diabetic CKD patients may benefit from calcium supplementation with or without calcitriol, while non-diabetic patients may see additional benefits from calcitriol. The maintenance of IL-10 in the Vitamin D + Calcium group contrasts with the decline in the Calcium group, indicating calcitriol’s potential role in preserving anti-inflammatory responses. These findings align with studies in chronic heart failure patients treated with vitamin D3 + calcium.
text: In CKD patients, "Vitamin D + Calcium" compared to "Calcium" alone stabilized serum IL-10, preventing its significant decline (p = 0.06), while IL-10 decreased in the Calcium group. This suggests Vitamin D may help preserve anti-inflammatory responses.

memory: A study evaluated sunflower cake as a substitute for soybean meal in the diets of 1/2 Boer goats at four substitution levels (0, 33, 66, and 100% DM). No significant differences (p>0.05) were observed in body weight at slaughter (21.78 kg), hot and cold carcass weights (8.65 kg and 8.59 kg), carcass yields (40.27% hot, 39.20% cold), rib eye area (7.73 cm²), or other carcass measurements, including carcass length, leg and hind perimeters, and tissue ratios (muscle:bone, muscle:fat). The results indicate that substituting soybean meal with sunflower cake up to 100% does not negatively affect quantitative carcass traits. The muscle:fat relationship in commercial cuts, particularly in younger animals, appears more favorable, suggesting potential for higher commercial value due to greater muscle tissue proportions. Body weight at slaughter and carcass yields remained unaffected by the substitution, consistent with prior findings that similar body weights yield comparable carcass characteristics. The study supports the use of sunflower cake as a complete replacement for soybean meal in 1/2 Boer goat diets without altering key carcass traits.
text: Substituting soybean meal with sunflower cake up to 100% had no significant effect on goats' body weight, carcass yields, or rib eye area (p>0.05). Carcass traits remained unchanged, supporting sunflower cake as a viable soybean meal replacement.
outcome: Weights, carcass yields, rib eye area of goats

memory: A study compared sevoflurane-fentanyl and isoflurane-fentanyl anesthesia during surgery, with fentanyl boluses (1.5 μg/kg) given every 30–40 minutes. Surgical stress index (SSI) increased after intubation and surgical stimuli, but fentanyl boluses reduced SSI similarly in both groups. However, SSI values remained higher in the sevoflurane group during surgery compared to the isoflurane group. Minimum alveolar concentration (MAC) and sedation end-tidal (SE) values before fentanyl boluses were similar between groups (MAC: 0.74 ± 0.12 vs. 0.77 ± 0.17, P = .32; SE: 43.5 ± 8.1 vs. 45.2 ± 8.3, P = .47). Heart rate (HR) was significantly higher in the sevoflurane group (70.6 ± 13.0 vs. 64.9 ± 11.8, P < .01). After fentanyl boluses, changes in SSI, SE, and HR were similar between groups, and MAC values remained stable. These results suggest that both anesthetic regimens provide comparable analgesia and hemodynamic responses after fentanyl boluses, but sevoflurane may be associated with higher SSI and HR during surgery. Source: PMC2911596.
text: Sevoflurane-fentanyl and isoflurane-fentanyl anesthesia showed similar MAC and SE values before fentanyl boluses (MAC: 0.74 ± 0.12 vs. 0.77 ± 0.17, P = .32; SE: 43.5 ± 8.1 vs. 45.2 ± 8.3, P = .47). Source: PMC2911596.
outcome: MAC and SE values before fentanyl boluses

memory: Source: PMC4007144. A prevention intervention for intimate partner violence (IPV) was evaluated against a control group. Follow-up results showed no statistically significant reduction in reported physical and sexual IPV levels (ARR 0.52, 95% CI 0.18–1.51). However, men in the intervention group showed reduced intentions to use physical IPV (ARR 0.83, 95% CI 0.66–1.06). They also demonstrated improved attitudes toward sexual IPV (ARR 1.21, 95% CI 0.77–1.91), better abilities to control hostility and manage conflict (ARR 1.3, 95% CI 1.06–1.58), and greater participation in gendered household tasks (ARR 2.47, 95% CI 1.24–4.90). Regarding beliefs about women's autonomy, 27% of the intervention group believed a woman could refuse sex in all circumstances, compared to 24% in the control group, though the difference was not statistically significant (ARR 1.26, 95% CI 0.83–1.91). A later analysis showed a marginally significant result for this belief (ARR 1.21, 95% CI 0.77–1.91). Overall, the intervention showed some positive effects on behavioral intentions, attitudes, and conflict management, but results on IPV prevalence were inconclusive.
text: The "Intimate partner prevention intervention" improved men's ability to control hostility and manage conflicts (ARR 1.3, 95% CI 1.06–1.58) compared to the control group, according to PMC4007144. However, it did not significantly reduce IPV prevalence.

memory: In a clinical trial comparing erlotinib to placebo, neurological progression-free survival (nPFS) was assessed. The unadjusted hazard ratio (HR) for nPFS was 0.99 (95% CI = 0.62 to 1.58; P = 0.97), and remained non-significant after adjustment for stratification factors (HR = 0.95; 95% CI = 0.59 to 1.54; P = 0.84). Among 75 patients who started the study drug, the adjusted HR was 0.89 (95% CI = 0.54 to 1.46; P = 0.65). Median nPFS was 1.6 months in both arms. Median overall survival (OS) was 2.9 months in the placebo group and 3.4 months in the erlotinib group, with an HR of 0.95 (95% CI = 0.58 to 1.55; P = 0.83). Quality of life (QoL) scores showed no significant differences between groups at one or two months (all P ≥ 0.40). Adverse events were similar between groups, with grade 3/4 events occurring in 70.0% of each arm. Notably, rash occurred in 20.0% of erlotinib-treated patients versus 5.0% in the placebo group, while fatigue was more common in the placebo group (35.0% vs 17.5%). Only 2.9% of patients had activating EGFR mutations. The study included 66 patients who died, with 31 in the placebo group and 35 in the erlotinib group.
text: Erlotinib did not significantly improve quality of life compared to placebo (all P ≥ 0.40). Survival and adverse events were similar between groups, with no notable QoL benefit observed. Source: Clinical trial data.

memory: Source: PMC4794540. A six-month study assessed the addition of a yogic intervention to standard medication versus medication alone. The intervention group showed statistically significant improvements in anxiety (P<0.01), depression (P<0.02), positive well-being (P<0.01), general health (P<0.04), and vitality (P<0.02) compared to the control group, as per domain-specific scores (Table 3). No significant differences were found in the self-control domain. Comparisons were made between the intervention and control groups to determine statistical significance. These results indicate that combining yogic intervention with medication may improve both mental and physical well-being in patients.
text: A six-month study (PMC4794540) found that combining yogic intervention with medication significantly improved positive well-being (P<0.01) and vitality (P<0.02) compared to medication alone. These results suggest that adding yogic intervention enhances mental and physical well-being in patients.

memory: A study [PMC4727391] compared laryngeal mask (LM) ventilation with endotracheal intubation (ETI) and found no significant differences in several key outcomes. First-attempt success rates were 94.4% for LM and 90.6% for ETI. Insertion times were 7.58 ± 1.16 seconds for LM versus 7.89 ± 1.52 seconds for ETI. Apgar scores at 1 and 5 minutes, response time, ventilation time, and successful resuscitation rates (86.1% for LM vs. 96.9% for ETI) were not significantly different. Adverse events were also similar, with 3 incidents in the LM group and 4 in the ETI group. These results suggest that both LM and ETI are comparable in terms of insertion success, time, clinical outcomes, and safety in the studied context.
text: A study (PMC4727391) found no significant differences in adverse effects between laryngeal mask ventilation and endotracheal intubation, with 3 and 4 incidents respectively. Both methods were comparable in safety and clinical outcomes.
