A diet intervention (D) significantly reduced multiple cardiovascular risk factors compared to control at 12 weeks, including waist circumference (P=0.001), total cholesterol (P=0.007), LDL cholesterol (P=0.003), and fasting insulin (P=0.042). These improvements were sustained at 1-year follow-up, with continued reductions in waist circumference (P<0.001) and fasting insulin (P=0.024), along with an increase in HDL cholesterol (P=0.005). 

An exercise intervention (E) did not show significant main effects on VO2 max, blood lipids, fasting plasma glucose, serum insulin, blood pressure, inflammation markers, or IGF-1 (all P-values >0.05). No interaction effects between D and E were observed for any cardiovascular risk outcomes. 

D significantly reduced fasting insulin at both 12 weeks (P=0.042) and 1 year (P=0.024). However, fasting plasma glucose, blood pressure, and inflammation markers were not significantly affected by D treatment.
text: A diet intervention significantly reduced LDL cholesterol compared to control (P=0.003) at 12 weeks, with sustained reductions at 1-year follow-up. Source: PMC3917884.

memory: In a study comparing zhibitai 480 mg + atorvastatin 10 mg (ZA10 group) with atorvastatin 20 mg (A20 group) and 40 mg (A40 group), adverse events were reported in 4, 5, and 7 patients, respectively. No significant differences in creatine kinase (CK) levels, myopathy, or gastrointestinal reactions were observed among groups (P > 0.05). Cardiotrophin-1 (CT-1) and high-sensitivity C-reactive protein (hs-CRP) levels significantly decreased after 4 and 8 weeks in all groups compared with baseline (P < 0.01 and P < 0.05, respectively), with no differences between groups (P > 0.05). After 8 weeks, triglycerides, total cholesterol (TC), LDL-cholesterol (LDL-C), and apolipoprotein B100 (ApoB100) levels were significantly reduced in the ZA10 group (−64%, −37%, −46%, and −54%, respectively) compared with baseline, similar to the A40 group (P > 0.05). CT-1 and hs-CRP levels were also significantly decreased in ZA10 after 4 and 8 weeks (4 weeks: −73% and −96%; 8 weeks: −89% and −98%; all P < 0.01), with no differences among the three groups (P > 0.05).
text: The ZA10 group showed no significant differences in creatine kinase levels compared to A20 or A40 groups (P > 0.05). All groups had similar reductions in CK, myopathy, and gastrointestinal reactions.
comparator: atorvastatin 20 mg (A20 group) or atorvastatin 40 mg (A40 group)

memory:
Source: [PMC3085176]  
A study assessed the effects of hesperidin (100 or 1000 mg), naringin (600 mg), and p-synephrine (50 mg) on RMR, heart rate, blood pressure, and self-reported symptoms compared to a placebo. p-synephrine alone increased RMR by 65 kcal over placebo. The combination of p-synephrine and naringin raised RMR by 129 kcal over placebo. Adding 100 mg hesperidin to this combination further increased RMR by 183 kcal over placebo (p<0.02). However, 1000 mg hesperidin with the other two ingredients only increased RMR by 79 kcal over placebo. No significant changes in heart rate, blood pressure, or self-reported symptoms (e.g., anxiety, hunger, energy) were observed across treatment groups compared to placebo. The combination of these ingredients increased RMR without corresponding increases in heart rate or blood pressure, suggesting potential for weight control. However, long-term studies are needed to confirm these findings.
text: p-Synephrine (50 mg) alone increased RMR by 65 kcal compared to placebo (PMC3085176). No significant changes in heart rate, blood pressure, or symptoms were observed.

memory:
In a study comparing 2 g of YM to placebo (PLC), YM significantly increased fatty acid oxidation (FAO) during 30-min steady-state exercise (p = 0.037), with time significantly affecting FAO (p < 0.001). YM also showed a higher total area under the curve (AUC) for total energy expenditure (TEE) than PLC (85.60 vs. 82.13, p < 0.001). Heart rate (HR) did not differ between treatments, though time significantly affected HR (p < 0.001). No treatment-by-time interactions were observed, and ratings of perceived exertion (RPE) were not influenced by treatment.

Regarding satiety, YM significantly reduced VAS measures of hunger (p = 0.019) and prospective eating (p = 0.022), with a trend for reduced desire to eat (p = 0.079). Fullness scores were unaffected. Time did not significantly impact satiety measures, and no interactions were found. In resting data analysis, YM showed a slight reduction in prospective eating scores compared to PLC (p = 0.046), with no other significant effects or interactions.
text: The administration of 2 g of YM significantly reduced prospective eating scores compared to placebo (p = 0.046). This effect was observed in resting data analysis, with no significant impacts from time or treatment-by-time interactions.

memory: A study compared an underwater treadmill intervention to a control group regarding balance improvements. Both groups showed significant reductions in anteroposterior, mediolateral, and total postural sway after the intervention (p<0.05). Static and dynamic balance abilities increased significantly in both groups, with no significant differences between the underwater treadmill and control groups. Dynamic balance improved significantly in both groups compared to baseline (p<0.05), and static balance also showed significant reductions in postural sway metrics post-intervention. Pre- and post-test comparisons between groups did not reveal significant differences. The results indicate that both interventions were effective in improving balance, but neither group outperformed the other.
text: Both the underwater treadmill group and control group showed significant reductions in anteroposterior, mediolateral, and total postural sway compared to baseline (p<0.05). No significant differences were found between the groups.
outcome: anteroposterior, mediolateral and total postural sway

memory:
In a study comparing Lanreotide Autogel® 120 mg (Lan ATG) and lanreotide microparticles 30 mg (Lan MP) in acromegaly patients, Lan ATG demonstrated superior symptom control. Symptoms including hyperhidrosis and headache were significantly improved with Lan ATG compared to Lan MP (P < 0.001 for both), as assessed by McNemar's test. 

Regarding hormonal control, 40% of Lan ATG patients achieved both GH < 2.5 ng/ml and normalized IGF-1, compared to 35% with Lan MP. Plasma IGF-1 levels remained stable throughout the study, with no significant changes observed. At baseline, 55% of patients had normal IGF-1 levels, which remained at 56% at the end of the study. 

GH levels were lower with Lan ATG (3.8 ng/ml) than with Lan MP (4.3 ng/ml; P < 0.001). GH levels below 2.5 ng/ml were observed in 54% of Lan ATG patients and 46% of Lan MP patients. Symptom control and treatment acceptance were better with Lan ATG. The study included 98 patients, with 93 completing the trial. Both formulations showed similar efficacy based on steady-state GH concentrations (upper 95% confidence interval of the quotient, 77.7%).
text: Lanreotide Autogel® 120 mg showed superior symptom control compared to lanreotide microparticles, with significant improvements in hyperhidrosis and headache (P < 0.001). Patients reported better treatment acceptance with Lan ATG.

memory: [PMC2039813] A 36-month trial compared perindopril to placebo in 256 participants, evaluating flow-mediated dilation (FMD). FMD increased from 2.6% to 3.3% in the perindopril group, versus 2.8% to 3.0% in the placebo group. The mean change in FMD from baseline to 36 months was 0.91% (SD 3.77) in the perindopril group and 0.35% (SD 3.63) in the placebo group, yielding a 0.55% difference (95% CI −0.42, 1.47; p=0.23), equivalent to a 20% relative improvement. The rate of FMD change per 6 months was 0.14% (SE 0.05, p=0.02) in the perindopril group versus 0.02% (SE 0.05, p=0.74) in the placebo group, with a 0.12% difference (p=0.07). No significant difference was observed in nitroglycerine response at 36 months (8.2% vs. 8.8%).
text: After 6 months, perindopril showed a 0.12% greater improvement in flow-mediated vasodilatation compared to placebo (p=0.07), though not statistically significant. The 36-month trial [PMC2039813] reported a 20% relative improvement in FMD with perindopril.

memory: A 6-week study compared 100 grams of instant oat cereal (intervention) to 100 grams of wheat flour-based noodles (control). The oat group showed significant reductions in total cholesterol (p=0.015) and LDL-C (p=0.028) compared to the control group. HDL-C levels were significantly higher in the oat group (p=0.017). Participants in the oat group also experienced a significant decrease in waist circumference (p=0.002). The oat group showed a significant increase in dietary fiber intake. No significant differences were observed between the groups in blood pressure, other anthropometric measures, or other laboratory parameters. These findings suggest that consuming instant oat cereal may improve lipid profiles and reduce waist circumference without adverse effects on other measured parameters. The study supports the potential cardiovascular benefits of incorporating oat-based products into the diet.
text: Consuming 100 grams of instant oat cereal significantly reduced waist circumference (p=0.002) compared to 100 grams of wheat flour-based noodles. This effect was accompanied by improved lipid profiles, including lower total cholesterol and LDL-C, and higher HDL-C. No adverse effects on other parameters were observed.

memory: In a study of 200 patients with similar baseline characteristics, two groups were compared: one receiving oral premedication with diazepam (5 mg) and chlorpheniramine (4 mg) 60 minutes before procedures, and the other receiving no premedication. No significant differences were found in periprocedural pain perception (31% vs. 29%, P = 0.75) or anxiety levels (59% vs. 50%, P = 0.2) between the premedicated and non-premedicated groups. However, local pain was more pronounced in the premedicated group (30% vs. 16%, P = 0.018). No contrast-related reactions were reported in either group. Regarding catheter-induced spasms, four cases were reported in the premedicated group, while none were observed in the control group (P = 0.04). For non-catheter-induced spasms, one case was reported in each group, with no significant difference (NS). The results suggest that while premedication with diazepam and chlorpheniramine did not significantly reduce overall pain or anxiety, it may be associated with increased local pain and a higher incidence of catheter-induced spasms.
text: The combination of diazepam and chlorpheniramine did not significantly reduce local pain compared to control (30% vs. 16%, P = 0.018). Source: Study of 200 patients.

memory:
Source: [PMC3751553]  
A study compared sleep and physiological parameters during Ramadan fasting (Ramadan), baseline fasting (BLF), and non-fasting baseline (BL). Sleep schedules, measured via actigraphy, showed no significant changes in bedtime, wake-up time, or nocturnal sleep duration during BL and BLF. However, during Ramadan, bedtime and wake-up time were significantly delayed (p < 0.05), likely due to a shift in work schedules. Serum glucose levels measured at 15:30 h were similar across all periods: 6.2 ± 0.4 mmol/L (BL), 5.6 ± 0.5 mmol/L (BLF), and 5.7 ± 0.5 mmol/L (Ramadan).  

REM sleep percentage was significantly lower during both BLF (17.7 ± 8.1%) and Ramadan (18.6 ± 10.7%) compared to BL (25.6 ± 4.8%) (p < 0.05). No significant differences were found in Johns Drowsiness Scale (JDS) scores, blink total duration, or mean reaction time (MRT) across BL, BLF, and Ramadan.  

Key findings: Ramadan fasting led to delayed sleep timing but no significant changes in glucose levels or daytime sleepiness indicators. REM sleep was reduced during fasting periods compared to the non-fasting baseline.
text: Both BLF and Ramadan fasting significantly reduced REM sleep percentages compared to the non-fasting baseline (BL) (p < 0.05). Source: [PMC3751553].
intervention: 4 weeks before Ramadan while performing the Islamic fasting for 1 week (baseline fasting) (BLF) or during the second week of Ramadan while fasting (Ramadan)

memory: Aripiprazole (low-dose: 5/10 mg/day; high-dose: 10/20 mg/day) was tested against placebo in a randomized, stratified (by weight and region), 1:1:1 trial in Tourette's disorder (TD) patients over 8 weeks. Both doses showed significant improvements in YGTSS-TTS and total motor tic scores compared to placebo (adjusted p=0.002 for low-dose; p<0.0001 for high-dose). High-dose demonstrated significant differences from placebo at all time points (weeks 1–8), while low-dose showed significant differences from week 1, 3–8. High-dose had a higher responder rate (57.1%) than placebo (16.7%, p<0.0001). Discontinuation rates were higher in high-dose (10/29, HR=5.51, p=0.0278) compared to placebo (2/29), while low-dose had 2/29 discontinuations. Both doses separated from placebo by week 4. At week 8, LS mean changes in YGTSS total motor tic score were -6.7 (low-dose), -8.0 (high-dose), and -2.7 (placebo). High-dose also improved SNAP-IV subscales. Prior anxiolytic use was <2.5% across groups.
text: Aripiprazole high-dose (10/20 mg/day) showed a higher discontinuation rate (10/29, HR=5.51, p=0.0278) compared to placebo (2/29) in TD patients.

memory: In a study comparing progressive discontinuation of pressure support ventilation (PSV) with SmartCare™ to respiratory physiotherapy–driven weaning, baseline parameters such as maximal inspiratory pressure (Pimax), maximal expiratory pressure (Pemax), forced vital capacity (FVC), and rapid shallow breathing index (RSBI) were similar between the two groups (p > 0.05). At the start of the weaning trial, PSV levels were significantly higher in the SmartCare™ group (median 10 cmH2O) compared to the respiratory physiotherapy group (median 8 cmH2O; p = 0.007). When patients were ready for extubation, PSV and PEEP were significantly higher in the respiratory physiotherapy group (PSV: 8 vs. 5 cmH2O; PEEP: 8 vs. 5 cmH2O; p = 0.015 and p < 0.001, respectively). However, total duration of mechanical ventilation (3.5 vs. 4.1 days; p = 0.467) and extubation failure rates (2 vs. 2; p = 1.00) were not significantly different between groups. Notably, the weaning duration was significantly shorter in the respiratory physiotherapy–driven weaning group (60 [50–80] minutes vs. 110 [80–130] minutes; p < 0.001). These findings suggest that while both methods are comparable in terms of total ventilation duration and extubation outcomes, respiratory physiotherapy may allow for a faster weaning process. Source: [PMC4511442]
text: Respiratory physiotherapy–driven weaning resulted in significantly lower PSV (8 vs. 5 cmH2O) and PEEP (8 vs. 5 cmH2O) at extubation compared to SmartCare™ (p = 0.015 and p < 0.001). However, both methods had similar total ventilation duration and extubation failure rates. Source: [PMC4511442]
intervention: progressive discontinuation of pressure support ventilation (PSV) with SmartCare™
outcome: pressure support ventilation (PSV)  and positive end-expiratory pressure (PEEP)

memory: In a breast cancer clinical trial using Trastuzumab, two groups were compared: an Internet-invited group and a control group. Both groups valued being informed about trial outcomes similarly, with preferences for systematic access (45.7%), patient request (41.0%), or physician discretion (13.3%) for result sharing. Patients expected to understand if the trial yielded useful results (82.2%), their treatment (20.6%), and general clinical trials (9.3%). The Internet group more frequently considered the Internet 'perfectly suitable' for receiving results (43.5% vs 17.6%, P=0.006), though it was less preferred than face-to-face or mailed communication. Most patients had Internet access (72.0%), and 97.2% found trial results information useful, with the oncologist as the preferred provider. The Internet group showed slightly higher uptake of trial results (47.1% vs 33.9%, P=0.166) and significantly better understanding of the results (18.8% vs 5.6%, P=0.039). Source: [PMC2853089].
text: The Internet group showed a significantly better understanding of trial results compared to the control group (18.8% vs 5.6%, P=0.039). Source: [PMC2853089].
intervention: Internet group (who received the letter of invitation)
comparator: control group (who did not receive it)
outcome: accurately understanding the results - Breast cancer patients participating in a trial on the efficacy of Trastuzumab

memory: Vegetable intake increased over time in both the total sample (F 2,906.08=16.69, P<.001) and risk group (F 2,654.00=72.11, P<.001), with no significant group differences (P=.10 and P=.07). The basic and plus intervention groups showed greater decreases in high-energy snack intake compared to the control group (T1: ES=–0.30; T2: ES=–0.18 for basic; T1: ES=–0.29; T2: ES=–0.27 for plus). The basic group reduced saturated fat intake more than the control (T1: ES=–0.19; T2: ES=–0.17). The plus group had greater increases in fruit intake than the control (T1: ES=0.25, P=.01; T2: ES=0.37, P=.001). Medium-term, the plus group showed a larger increase in fruit intake compared to the basic group (ES=0.22, P=.04). In risk groups, the basic group reduced fat and high-energy snacks more than the control. The plus group increased fruit intake (T1: ES=0.25; T2: ES=0.37) and reduced high-energy snacks (T1: ES=–0.38; T2: ES=–0.32) more than the control. The plus intervention was most effective for high-educated participants. [PMC4319071]
text: The "Individual cognition and self-regulation processes intervention" reduced high-energy snack intake more than the control group (T1: ES=–0.30; T2: ES=–0.18 for basic; T1: ES=–0.29; T2: ES=–0.27 for plus). The plus intervention showed greater effects, especially in high-educated participants [PMC4319071].

Source: [PMC3483098]  
CGM Sensor On vs Off: HbA1c decreased by -0.43% (p < 0.001) with Sensor On (8.04% vs 8.47%), reverting to baseline after cessation. Time <3.9 mmol/l was lower with Sensor On (19 vs 31 min/day, p = 0.009). Daily boluses were higher with Sensor On (6.8 ± 2.5 vs 5.8 ± 1.9, p < 0.0001), as were temporary basal rate use (0.75 ± 1.11 vs 0.26 ± 0.47, p < 0.0001) and bolus wizard use (3.82 ± 2.7 vs 3.14 ± 2.5, p < 0.0001). Manual insulin suspends were slightly higher with Sensor On (0.91 ± 1.25 vs 0.70 ± 0.75, p < 0.018). Average glucose was lower with Sensor On (8.82 vs 9.44 mmol/l, p < 0.001). Severe hypoglycaemia events were 4 vs 2 (p = 0.40). Sensor On showed favorable euglycaemia and hyperglycaemia time and lower AUC for glucose levels (Table 2). Study included 77 On/Off and 76 Off/On sequences, all in primary analysis.
text: Continuous glucose monitoring (CGM) Sensor On was associated with a higher mean number of daily boluses (6.8 ± 2.5 vs 5.8 ± 1.9, p < 0.0001) compared to Sensor Off (PMC3483098).

memory: Study [PMC4636858] compared Mitoxantrone + methylprednisolone with Mitoxantrone alone and no treatment in 28 men and 43 women with multiple sclerosis. During treatment, MRI plaque numbers decreased in both groups (2.29 vs. 2.17, P = 0.782), but the difference was not statistically significant. Six months post-treatment, plaque numbers increased in both groups (0.72 vs. 0.77, P = 0.611), again without significant differences. The Expanded Disability Status Scale (EDSS) showed a significant reduction at the end of treatment in both groups (0.79 vs. 0.53, P = 0.953), though no significant difference between groups. Six months after treatment, EDSS scores increased in both groups (0.35 vs. 0.43, P = 0.624), with no significant difference. The findings suggest that adding methylprednisolone to Mitoxantrone did not significantly improve outcomes compared to Mitoxantrone alone or no treatment, in terms of MRI plaque reduction or EDSS score changes.
text: A study found that "Mitoxantrone + methylprednisolone" did not significantly reduce multiple sclerosis plaques compared to "No treatment" or Mitoxantrone alone, as MRI plaque numbers and EDSS scores showed no significant differences between groups (PMC4636858).

memory: In a clinical study comparing artesunate monotherapy (2 or 4 mg/kg/day once daily) to quinine plus doxycycline (TID for 7 days), artesunate arms demonstrated significantly faster parasite clearance times (PCTs) than the control group (29.8 and 29.5 hours vs. 43.1 hours, P<0.001). At 24 hours post-treatment, 13.7% (2 mg/kg), 16.0% (4 mg/kg), and 70.8% (control) remained parasitemic. Fever clearance times (FCTs) were also significantly faster in artesunate arms (17.9 and 19.1 hours vs. 29.3 hours, P=0.001). All patients cleared asexual parasitemia within the first week, with 28-day cure rates of 97.8% (2 mg/kg), 100% (4 mg/kg), and 100% (control). Two treatment failures occurred: one late clinical failure (recrudescence) in the 2 mg/kg arm on day 26 and one late parasitological failure (reinfection) in the 4 mg/kg arm on day 42. Median parasite reduction ratios at 12 and 24 hours were significantly lower in the quinine group compared to artesunate arms (P<0.001). Adverse events were generally well tolerated, with no serious events reported. Gastrointestinal disorders were the most common adverse event, and no significant differences in adverse event rates were observed between groups (P=0.91). Source: [PMC3525560].
text: Artesunate monotherapy (2 or 4 mg/kg/day) significantly reduced median FCT compared to quinine plus doxycycline (17.9–19.1 vs. 29.3 hours, P=0.001). Source: [PMC3525560].
intervention: artesunate monotherapy with 2 or 4 mg/kg/day once daily
comparator: quinine plus doxycycline TID for 7 days

memory: Study [PMC5079604] assessed metformin (1,000 mg) and sitagliptin (100 mg) versus placebo in obese African American patients with DKA and severe hyperglycemia. Metformin and sitagliptin significantly improved relapse-free survival compared to placebo (P = 0.015), with a prolonged mean time to relapse (480 vs. 305 days, P = 0.004). Both drugs reduced relapse probability (HR 0.28 for metformin and 0.31 for sitagliptin), though no significant difference was found between them (P = 0.75). Patients in remission had higher DI (P = 0.02) and AUCi (P < 0.001) than those who relapsed. The two-year failure rate was 77% for placebo, 44% for sitagliptin, and 34% for metformin (P = 0.013). Combined metformin/sitagliptin groups showed a higher restricted mean time to relapse than placebo (P = 0.004). Relapse severity did not differ significantly between medication groups due to small sample size (n = 9 vs. n = 11). GAD antibody data were missing for some subjects.
text: Metformin 1,000 mg daily and sitagliptin 100 mg daily significantly improved hyperglycemia relapse-free survival compared to placebo (P = 0.015), with prolonged time to relapse (480 vs. 305 days, P = 0.004). (Source: PMC5079604)
intervention: metformin 1,000 mg daily, sitagliptin 100 mg daily

memory: A 12-week study with 101 participants compared isomaltulose and sucrose. No significant differences were observed in HbA1c (sucrose: 7.39 ± 0.78%; isomaltulose: 7.24 ± 0.76%; b: 0.02 [95% CI −0.21 to 0.25], P = 0.844), fasting glucose, insulin, fructosamine, proinsulin, C-peptide, or HOMA-IR. However, triglyceride levels were significantly lower in the isomaltulose group compared to the sucrose group at week 12 (b: 34.01 [6.59–61.44], P = 0.016). In the sucrose group, triglycerides increased significantly over time (P = 0.023), while the isomaltulose group showed a trend toward reduced triglyceride levels. These findings suggest isomaltulose may have a more favorable effect on triglyceride levels than sucrose without impacting glycemic control or other metabolic parameters. Source: [PMC3357231]
text: A 12-week study found that isomaltulose significantly reduced triglyceride levels compared to sucrose (P = 0.016), while sucrose caused a significant increase. No differences were observed in glycemic or other metabolic parameters. Source: [PMC3357231]

memory: A study compared 21 dogs with OA on a CCOT diet (Curcuminoids, hydrolyzed Collagen, Green Tea extract) with 21 controls on a standard diet. No significant difference in overall pain index (PI) change (∆T3-T0) was observed (p=0.063). Baseline PI scores were 3.26 ± 0.54 (CCOT) and 3.44 ± 0.59 (control), with T3 scores of 2.96 ± 0.45 and 3.86 ± 0.66, respectively (p=0.101 and p=0.633). However, CCOT showed significant improvement in PI change related to rising from lying down (p=0.029). Pain score (PS) change (∆T3-T0) was significantly better in CCOT (p=0.009). Objective peak vertical force (PVF) values for the most affected limb showed no significant differences at T0 (p=0.618) or T3 (p=0.953), and no significant change over time. Subjective assessments indicated less pain at manipulation in CCOT, though no significant differences in lameness, pain at palpation, or joint mobility. Owner-reported PS showed significant improvement in the CCOT group. The CCOT diet was well-tolerated, with no significant weight change and only mild, transient diarrhea in 5 dogs. The study suggests CCOT may improve specific pain-related functions in OA dogs, though overall PI and PVF outcomes were not statistically significant. Source: [PMC5738810]
text: The experimental diet with CCOT showed significant improvement in pain score change (p=0.009) and pain interference related to rising from lying down (p=0.029), though overall pain index change was not significant (p=0.063). Source: [PMC5738810]
intervention: an experimental diet supplemented with Curcuminoids extract, hydrolyzed COllagen and green Tea extract (CCOT)

memory: In a clinical study [PMC4391304], participants consumed either 100 g of fermented milk (FM) with Lactobacillus gasseri SBT2055 (LG2055) or FM without LG2055. The primary outcome was fecal fat levels. The intervention group (active FM with LG2055) showed a significant increase in fecal fat levels post-FM intake compared to pre-FM intake, whereas no such increase was observed in the control group (FM without LG2055). LG2055 was found to dose-dependently increase fat emulsion droplet size and enhance lipase activity and fat emulsion properties compared to other tested strains. However, there were no statistically significant differences in the wet weight of feces between the groups before or after FM intake. The change in fecal fat levels between pre- and post-FM intake was greater in the active FM group compared to the control group, though this difference was not statistically significant (P = 0.086). These findings suggest that LG2055 may influence fat excretion through its effect on fat emulsion properties, potentially increasing fecal fat levels in individuals consuming FM. The study provides evidence that the presence of LG2055 in FM is associated with changes in fecal fat excretion, although further research may be needed to confirm the significance of the observed trend in fecal weight changes.
text: Consuming 100 g of fermented milk with Lactobacillus gasseri SBT2055 significantly increased fecal fat levels compared to FM without LG2055 (PMC4391304). The effect was linked to LG2055's influence on fat emulsion properties, suggesting a potential role in fat excretion.
intervention: 100&amp;nbsp;g of fermented milk (FM) + Lactobacillus gasseri SBT2055 (LG2055)

memory: Source: PMC1468428. A randomized trial compared 1 litre saline enema (intervention) with no enema (comparator) in postpartum outcomes. Episiorraphy dehiscence rates were 12% (21/182) with enema versus 17% (32/190) without enema (P = 0.30), showing no significant difference. Puerperal infection rates were 22% (41/190) with enema versus 14% (26/182) without enema (RR 0.66; 95% CI 0.43 to 1.03). Neonatal infection rates were 20% (38/191) with enema versus 22% (40/179) without enema (RR 1.12; 95% CI 0.76 to 1.66), also not significant. Median labour time was 515 minutes with enema versus 585 minutes without enema (P = 0.24). Groups were balanced, and 86% of participants were followed for one month. Overall infection rates were 21% in newborns and 18% in women. No significant differences were found in any of the outcomes studied.
text: A randomized trial (PMC1468428) found no significant difference in puerperal or neonatal infection rates between 1 litre saline enema and no enema. Puerperal infection rates were 22% vs. 14% (RR 0.66; 95% CI 0.43 to 1.03), and neonatal rates were 20% vs. 22% (RR 1.12; 95% CI 0.76 to 1.66), both non-significant.

memory: A 10-week yoga program was compared to a control group in a study assessing multiple outcomes. Flexibility, measured by the sit & reach test, significantly improved in the yoga group (p < 0.001). Most HRV measures were unchanged, but the yoga group showed a significant increase in the LF:HF ratio (p = 0.04) and a decrease in pNN50 (p = 0.04), contrary to initial hypotheses. Post hoc analysis of high adherers (≥70% session completion, n = 11) versus control (n = 19) confirmed these results, with additional reductions in state anxiety (p = 0.02) and RMSSD (p = 0.05), and a trend toward improved push-up test performance (p = 0.07). No significant changes were observed in quality of life (QoL) domain scores, including psychological health status, between the groups (all p > 0.05). Both groups experienced reductions in state and trait anxiety, but no significant group × time interactions were found. No other significant adaptations were noted in the primary intervention group.
text: A 10-week yoga program significantly improved flexibility (sit & reach test, p < 0.001) compared to control. Other outcomes like HRV and anxiety showed mixed results, but flexibility enhancement was consistent. Source: Study cited in working notes.

memory:
In a study of Japanese Parkinson's disease (PD) patients experiencing motor complications on levodopa, istradefylline (20 mg/day and 40 mg/day) was compared to placebo. The primary outcome was change in daily OFF time, with both istradefylline doses significantly reducing OFF time compared to placebo: −0.99 hours (P = .003) for 20 mg/day and −0.96 hours (P = .003) for 40 mg/day, versus −0.23 hours for placebo. No significant difference was found between the two istradefylline doses. Dyskinesia was the most common adverse event, occurring in 13.0% of the 20 mg/day group and 12.1% of the 40 mg/day group, compared to 4.0% in the placebo group.

Secondary outcomes showed no increase in daily ON time with troublesome dyskinesia for either istradefylline dose. Both doses significantly improved daily ON time without troublesome dyskinesia compared to placebo: 1.09 hours (P = .003) for 20 mg/day and 1.08 hours (P = .004) for 40 mg/day, versus 0.26 hours for placebo. Additionally, both istradefylline doses improved UPDRS Part II scores (OFF state) compared to placebo: −1.4 (P = .034) for 20 mg/day and −1.7 (P = .009) for 40 mg/day, versus −0.6 for placebo. Istradefylline was well tolerated, with no significant differences in efficacy between the two doses.
text: Istradefylline 20 mg and 40 mg showed no significant difference in daily ON time with problematic dyskinesia. Both doses improved ON time without troublesome dyskinesia compared to placebo (P < .004). Source: Study of Japanese Parkinson's patients.
outcome: Daily ON time with problematic dyskinesia

memory: In a clinical study comparing oral liarozole (150 mg and 75 mg) to placebo, adverse events were more frequent in liarozole groups, though not statistically significant (P ≥ 0.062), with no dose-related pattern. The 150-mg group showed significant improvements from baseline compared to placebo in 'daily activities' (P = 0.008), 'leisure' (P = 0.026), and 'symptoms and feelings' (P = 0.023). However, no significant difference was found between the 150-mg liarozole and placebo groups in changes in the Dermatology Life Quality Index (DLQI) score at week 12 [mean (SD) change, −2.8 (3.4); P = 0.06]. In contrast, the 75-mg liarozole group demonstrated a significant improvement in DLQI scores from baseline at week 12 compared to placebo [mean (SD) change, −4.3 (6.0); P = 0.014]. These findings suggest that while liarozole may improve quality of life in certain domains, its effect on DLQI scores varies by dose, with the 75-mg dose showing a more significant benefit than the 150-mg dose.
text: Oral liarozole 150 mg significantly improved 'daily activities' (P=0.008), 'leisure' (P=0.026), and 'symptoms and feelings' (P=0.023) compared to placebo, though DLQI improvements were not significant (P=0.06). Adverse events were more frequent but not statistically significant.

memory: A clinical study compared 15-pulse anti-tachycardia pacing (ATP) to eight-pulse ATP in managing fascicular ventricular tachycardia (FVT). No significant differences were found in key outcomes between the groups. In terms of shocks required, 22% of FVT episodes in the eight-pulse group (59 out of 250) needed shocks (total shocks: 72), compared to 21% in the 15-pulse group (45 out of 209) with 50 total shocks (p = 0.907). ATP efficacy in terminating FVT episodes was 71% unadjusted and 67% adjusted (95% CI 60–74%). Adjusted efficacy was 64% for the eight-pulse group (95% CI 55–75%) and 70% for the 15-pulse group (95% CI 60–80%), with no significant difference (p = 0.504). FVT acceleration episodes were rare, occurring in 3.9% of the eight-pulse group and 4% of the 15-pulse group (p = 0.993), with none correlated to syncope or near-syncope. Syncope and near-syncope episodes were also not significantly different between groups, with 0.5% and 2.8% in the eight-pulse group and 3.2% and 0.7% in the 15-pulse group, respectively (p = 0.690). All accelerated FVT episodes were either terminated by shock or spontaneously resolved during battery charging. The study suggests that both ATP configurations had comparable safety and efficacy profiles in managing FVT.
text: A clinical study found no significant difference between 15-pulse and eight-pulse ATP in reducing syncope and near-syncope episodes (p = 0.690). Both configurations showed comparable safety and efficacy in managing FVT.

memory: A study compared prednisolone (7.5 mg and 30 mg once daily) to placebo, revealing dose-dependent effects on glucose metabolism and lipolysis. Prednisolone impaired insulin-mediated suppression of endogenous glucose production, with reductions of 17 ± 6% (7.5 mg) and 46 ± 7% (30 mg) compared to placebo. Peripheral glucose uptake remained unaffected at 7.5 mg but decreased by 34 ± 6% with 30 mg (p < 0.0001). Both doses reduced insulin-mediated suppression of lipolysis by 11 ± 5% (7.5 mg) and 34 ± 6% (30 mg), though the effect on fasted-state lipolysis was not statistically significant (p = 0.062). Whole-body proteolysis increased during hyperinsulinaemia, with a trend toward significance for the 30 mg dose (5 ± 2%; p = 0.06). Fasting plasma glucose levels rose dose-dependently, and only the 30 mg dose increased fasting insulin levels (29 ± 15 pmol/l). No side effects were reported, and all participants completed the study. These findings highlight the dose-dependent impact of prednisolone on glucose metabolism and lipolysis, with greater effects observed at the higher dose.
text: Prednisolone 30 mg once daily significantly reduced insulin-mediated suppression of lipolysis by 34 ± 6% compared to placebo, while 7.5 mg reduced it by 11 ± 5%. These findings are from a study showing dose-dependent effects on glucose metabolism and lipolysis.
intervention: prednisolone 30 mg once daily and  prednisolone 7,5 mg once daily

memory: A study compared online and mailed paper questionnaires for asthma-related outcomes, finding minimal differences between the two methods. Shortness of breath showed a trend toward significance (p=.074 for t-test, p=.081 for Wilcoxin), but this weakened after controlling for asthma and demographics via ANCOVA (p=.254). Mailed questionnaires showed a slight trend toward higher asthma levels (p=.096). ER visits and health distress had non-significant trends (p=.146 and p=.116, respectively), with ER visits skewed toward zero, leading to higher p-values with Wilcoxin testing (.330 and .111). Internet respondents were more likely to be married (p=.043), and this, along with asthma and demographics, were used as covariates in ANCOVA models. No other outcomes reached statistical significance, though some trends were noted. Overall, the study suggests minimal differences between online and mailed questionnaires for asthma-related outcomes. Source: [PMC1550608].
text: The study found minimal differences between online and mailed questionnaires on asthma-related outcomes for married subjects. Trends toward higher asthma levels with mailed versions were not significant after controlling for covariates. Source: [PMC1550608].

memory:
A study compared the effects of using Facebook versus quietly reading on stress recovery. Both conditions led to similar psychosocial stress marker changes, including decreases in tension and anxiety and increases in well-being, with no significant differences between conditions for tension (F(1, 91) = 1.56, p = 0.21), anxiety (F(1, 88) = 0.004, p = 0.95), or well-being (F(1, 91) = 0.33, p = 0.57). Notably, 79% of participants reported that using Facebook influenced their sense of well-being during recovery. 

In terms of physiological stress recovery, the reading condition showed a significantly greater decrease in cortisol concentration from 20 to 45 minutes post-stressor onset compared to the Facebook condition (Mdifference = –0.51 vs. –0.35, F(1, 84) = 5.03, p = 0.03), with this difference remaining after controlling for gender and Facebook Intensity score. Descriptively, females in the Facebook condition with high Facebook Intensity showed the smallest cortisol reduction during recovery. Subjective stress markers showed no significant differences between the two conditions at any time point. The study used both raw cortisol values and log-transformed scores for analysis.
text: Using their own Facebook profile had no significant effect compared to quietly reading on subjective stress markers like tension, anxiety, or well-being. Both conditions showed similar changes, with no significant differences between groups (p > 0.05 for all).

memory: A study compared an 8 cm pillow with a 4 cm pillow during tracheal intubation. No significant differences were found in laryngeal view, intubation success rate, or alignment of laryngeal, pharyngeal, and oral axes between the two groups. Objective measurements showed higher angles for the laryngeal, pharyngeal, and oral axes in the 8 cm group, but angular differences between adjacent axes were similar between groups. However, discomfort scores during intubation were higher in the 8 cm group when head elevation was first 4 cm and then increased to 8 cm. One patient required two intubation attempts with the 8 cm pillow but succeeded on the first attempt with the 4 cm pillow. The laryngeal view and number of intubation trials were not different between groups. Source: [PMC4823408]
text: Using an 8 cm pillow during tracheal intubation resulted in higher discomfort scores compared to a 4 cm pillow [PMC4823408]. No significant differences were found in laryngeal view, success rate, or alignment of axes between the groups.

memory: In a study comparing daily prednisone (various doses) to placebo, glucose metabolism was assessed via OGTT on Day 6. Both prednisone and placebo increased glucose and insulin at 0.5 h, but levels decreased by 1 and 2 h for all prednisone doses. However, changes from baseline relative to placebo were not significant at most time points after 6 days of treatment. Prednisone 60 mg significantly increased uNTX/uCr by Day 2, with dose-dependent increases observed from Days 4–8. Plasma osteocalcin (OC) decreased significantly relative to placebo as early as 2 h post-dose on Day 1, with continued dose-dependent decreases until 12 h post-dose. These decreases were significant for doses ≥5 mg on Day 2 and all doses on Day 8. Procollagen type 1 N-propeptide (P1NP) was significantly reduced versus placebo with prednisone doses ≥20 mg on Day 1, with levels increasing slightly on Day 2 before decreasing in a dose- and time-dependent manner until Day 8. Daily prednisone doses up to 60 mg caused dose- and time-dependent decreases in plasma osteocalcin, plasma P1NP, serum cortisol, and absolute blood eosinophil counts. Absolute blood neutrophil counts increased, while blood lymphocyte counts rebounded to increased levels after an initial rapid decrease. Increases in uNTX and adiponectin were also observed.
text: Daily prednisone (≥20 mg) significantly reduced procollagen type 1 N-propeptide (P1NP) compared to placebo on Day 1, with dose- and time-dependent decreases observed until Day 8 (source: study).

memory: A study compared three root canal filling materials: Gutta-percha + AH26 (LGP/AH26), Gutta-percha + Mineral Trioxide Aggregate (SGP/MTA), and Gutta-percha + New Endodontic Cement (SGP/NEC). The primary outcomes evaluated were apical and coronal dye penetration. No statistically significant differences were found in mean apical dye penetration among the three groups (LGP/AH26, SGP/MTA, SGP/NEC). However, the SGP/NEC group showed significantly less coronal dye penetration compared to both LGP/AH26 and SGP/MTA (P<0.001). These results suggest that while all tested materials provided similar apical sealing, the new endodontic cement (SGP/NEC) offered a superior coronal seal when combined with Gutta-percha. This finding indicates that the coronal seal may be an important factor in the overall effectiveness of root canal fillings, and the SGP/NEC material may be advantageous in this aspect. Source: PMC3712263.
text: The use of Gutta-percha + new endodontic cement (SGP/NEC) significantly reduces coronal dye penetration compared to Gutta-percha + AH26 (LGP/AH26) (P<0.001). Source: PMC3712263.

Full bifocals showed significant differences compared to intermediate multifocals in vertical toe clearance on ascent (χ²=6.9, p=0.009), variability of vertical toe clearance on ascent (χ²=12.0, p=0.0005), ascent duration (χ²=12.7, p<0.0001), and heel clearance on descent (χ²=8.7, p=0.003). Vertical toe clearance on ascent also differed between full and intermediate PALs (χ²=8.7, p=0.003). Intermediate PALs did not differ significantly from distance single vision lenses in gait safety parameters: vertical toe clearance on ascent (χ²=0.4, p=0.54), variability of vertical toe clearance on ascent (χ²=0.1, p=0.93), ascent duration (χ²=1.4, p=0.25), heel clearance on descent (χ²=0.7, p=0.42), variability of heel clearance on descent (χ²=2.4, p=0.12), and descent duration (χ²=1.6, p=0.20). Gait safety with intermediate PALs was similar to participants’ own spectacles. Intermediate bifocals performed worse than intermediate PALs and distance single vision lenses.
text: Intermediate progressive addition lenses (PALs) had similar effects on ascent vertical toe clearance as distance single vision lenses (p=0.54). Full bifocals performed worse than intermediate PALs (p=0.003). Intermediate PALs were as safe as participants’ own spectacles. Source: [PMC4737269].

memory: A behavioral lifestyle intervention was evaluated against a control group in a study assessing its impact on children's health outcomes. After 1 year, the intervention group showed significant improvements in adiposity, evidenced by reduced BMI-SDS (P=0.02) and WC-SDS (P=0.03). Physical fitness, measured as VO2peak-SDS, also improved significantly (P<0.01). Insulin resistance, assessed via HOMA-SDS, improved (P=0.04). No significant changes were observed in serum lipid profile, high-sensitive C-reactive protein, or adiponectin. At the 2-year follow-up, BMI-SDS in the intervention group (n=31) remained significantly lower than baseline (P=0.02). During the 3-month intensive phase, attendance varied, but both short-term (T2 at 3 months) and long-term (T3 after 1-year) results showed significant reductions in BMI-SDS (10%) and WC-SDS (19%) in the intervention group, while no changes were observed in the control group. VO2peak-SDS-kg increased by 20% in the intervention group, compared to an 18% reduction in the control group. Subjective exhaustion scores did not change significantly over time. The study highlights the effectiveness of the behavioral lifestyle intervention on adiposity, physical fitness, and insulin resistance, with sustained benefits observed at the 2-year follow-up.
text: A behavioral lifestyle intervention significantly reduced waist circumference (WC-SDS, P=0.03) compared to control in children, with sustained effects at 2 years. Improvements were greater than in the control group, highlighting the intervention's effectiveness on adiposity.

memory: The study compared participants' dietary intakes to the 2011–2012 Australian Health Survey (AHS) national average. Participants had higher energy intakes (pre- and post-intervention) than the national average of 8672 kJ, with discretionary foods contributing 34.6% of total energy. Macronutrient intake remained largely unchanged by the intervention and was comparable to the national average, with minor differences between control and intervention groups. Saturated fat intakes, as measured by FFQ, showed no significant change, though self-reported habits suggested potential reductions via meat cut selection. The dietary model combined Mediterranean and portfolio patterns, known to reduce CVD risk, but participants initially consumed more discretionary foods than recommended and had dietary patterns misaligned with these models. No significant difference in baseline energy intake was found between those who completed the study and those who did not (p = 0.34 for adults, p = 0.32 for children). The mean time between baseline and follow-up was 4.5 months (±1.1). Dietary components of the Mediterranean and Portfolio Diets are detailed in Table 2.
text: Participants in the study had higher energy intakes (pre- and post-intervention) compared to the 2011–2012 Australian Health Survey national average of 8672 kJ, with discretionary foods contributing 34.6% of total energy (source: study). Macronutrient intakes were comparable to the national average, with minor group differences.

memory: ES10/20 and R10 showed no significant differences in apoA-I levels (NS). Both significantly reduced PLAC (P<0.001) and Lp-PLA2 activity (P<0.05), while doubling the statin dose had no significant effect (P>0.05). ES10/20 reduced LDL-particle number more than doubling the statin dose (−133.3 vs −94.4 vs −56.3 nmol/L; P>0.05) and increased HDL-particle number significantly more than doubling (1.5 vs −0.5 μmol/L; P<0.05), with R10 showing a comparable increase (0.7 μmol/L; P>0.05). ES10/20 and R10 significantly reduced total cholesterol, LDL-C, non-HDL-C, and apoB more than doubling the statin dose (P<0.05). Both ES10/20 and R10 increased apoA-I levels significantly more than doubling the statin dose (P<0.05). Changes in triglycerides, HDL-C, and hs-CRP were not significant across groups. Percent changes in LDL-P correlated strongly with sLDL-P changes (P<0.0001). ES10/20 and R10 showed greater reductions in sLDL-P (34.7 and 23.3 nmol/L) compared to doubling the statin dose (1.0 nmol/L), though differences were not significant.
text: ES10/20 reduced LDL-particle number more than doubling the statin dose, while R10 showed comparable effects. Both ES10/20 and R10 significantly reduced LDL-particle number compared to doubling the statin dose, though differences between ES10/20 and R10 were not significant. (Source: Working notes)

memory: A weight management intervention targeting diet and physical activity significantly increased fiber intake (M between-group difference = 5.7 g/day, p < .001) at 4 and 12 months, but had no significant effect on fat consumption (−2.3 g/day, p = 0.13). Higher fiber intake predicted greater weight loss at 4 months (M difference = −1.98 kg, p < .01; R² = 0.2, p < 0.005) and 12 months (M difference = −1.85 kg, p = 0.1; R² = 0.1, p < 0.01). At 12 months, the intervention group had greater weight loss (−3.7 kg) than the control group (−1.9 kg), though the difference was not statistically significant (F(1,108) = 2.3, p = 0.13) without adjustment. After adjusting for co-interventions and incident morbidities, the weight loss difference became significant (M difference = 2.9 kg, 95% CI: −5.1 to −0.6, p = 0.014). The intervention improved behavior change mediators, such as self-efficacy and understanding of the behavior change process, which were linked to increased coping planning and self-monitoring, resulting in successful dietary change at both 4 and 12 months. No significant differences in objectively measured physical activity were observed at either time point.
text: A weight management intervention targeting diet and physical activity significantly increased fiber intake by 5.7 g/day at 12 months compared to usual care (p < .001). This improvement was linked to greater weight loss in the intervention group. Source: Working notes.
intervention: weight management intervention targeting diet and physical activity plus usual care

memory:
A study evaluated the effect of escalating tamsulosin dosage (0.4 mg once daily) versus maintaining the standard dose (0.2 mg/d) in patients with lower urinary tract symptoms (LUTS), with outcomes including LUTS improvement and erectile function. Among 15 patients with no improvement in LUTS, no significant difference in IIEF-5 scores was found between escalators and nonescalators (1.2 vs. 0.8, p=0.859). However, in the 35 patients who experienced improved LUTS, escalators showed a significantly greater increase in IIEF-5 scores compared to nonescalators (4.6 vs. 1.7, p=0.002), suggesting a potential benefit of dose escalation on erectile function in this subgroup.

At week 4, nonescalators had greater mean changes from baseline in IPSS-total (-4.8±4.5 vs. -2.8±7.0) and IPSS-voiding (-3.7±3.9 vs. -1.8±5.4), although these differences were not statistically significant. Similar trends were seen in storage (-1.1±1.8 vs. -0.8±1.3) and QoL subscores (-1.1±1.4 vs. -1.0±2.1). The findings suggest that while dose escalation may enhance erectile function in patients with improved LUTS, it does not significantly improve IPSS scores compared to standard dosing. Source: [PMC3580298]
text: In patients with no improvement in LUTS, there was no significant difference in IIEF-5 scores between those escalating tamsulosin to 0.4 mg and those maintaining 0.2 mg (1.2 vs. 0.8, p=0.859). Source: [PMC3580298].
comparator: increase their dose to 0.4 mg once daily (escalators)
outcome: International Index of Erectile Function (IIEF-5)  in patients who showed no improvement of lower urinary tract symptoms (LUTS)

memory: In a study with healthy volunteers, 1,800 mg of gepotidacin resulted in higher adverse event rates compared to 1,000 mg, with 64% of subjects reporting events. Common moderate adverse events included vomiting (15%), nausea (8%), throat tightness (2%), and dizziness (2%). Five subjects (9%) discontinued due to adverse events, including throat tightness, three C. difficile tests, and one C. difficile infection. QTc prolongation was linearly related to plasma concentrations, with a slope of 1.45 ms per μg/ml (90% CI, 1.30 to 1.61). The peak QTc effect occurred at 2 hours post-dose, with a mean ΔΔQTcF of 22.2 ms in the full population and 21.4 ms when excluding those who vomited after the 1,800 mg dose. Both doses caused a moderate heart rate increase of approximately 10–13 bpm at the end of infusions. Cholinergic side effects, like salivary hypersecretion, were mild and unlikely to affect QT analysis. Adverse events were generally mild to moderate, including nausea, abdominal pain, vomiting, salivary hypersecretion, feeling hot, and oropharyngeal discomfort. The results support a dose-dependent relationship between plasma concentrations and QTc prolongation, enabling predictions of QT effects in patients based on different doses and formulations.
text: The 1,800 mg dose of gepotidacin in healthy volunteers caused a higher rate of moderate adverse events (64%) compared to 1,000 mg, with common events including vomiting (15%) and nausea (8%). Five subjects (9%) discontinued due to adverse events. This suggests a dose-dependent increase in adverse events with the higher dose (Source: study data).

memory: A study compared etomidate and propofol (based on midazolam) for sedation. Propofol was linked to a higher incidence of cardiopulmonary adverse events (72.6% vs. 54.8%, P = .040), vital sign fluctuation (50.0% vs. 27.4%, P = .010), and transient hypotension (41.9% vs. 24.2%, P = .036). Etomidate, however, had a higher incidence of adverse events disturbing the procedure (25.8% vs. 8.1%, P = .008) and myoclonus (16.1% vs. 1.6%, P = .004). No major adverse events, such as endotracheal intubation, permanent neurological impairment, or death, were reported in either group. Baseline characteristics, including age, sex, procedure type, BMI, smoking and alcohol history, outpatient status, anticoagulant use, ASA score, Mallampati score, and underlying diseases, were not significantly different between groups. Sedation-related outcomes such as induction time (P = .833), total procedure time (P = .111), and awake time (P = .070) were also not significantly different.
text: Etomidate compared with propofol based on midazolam significantly increases the incidence rate of myoclonus (16.1% vs. 1.6%, P = .004).

memory: [PMC4469426] A study compared an almond-enriched diet (ALM, 85 g/day) to a control diet (CON) and found no significant differences in inflammatory cytokines (CRP, TNFα, IL-6) between the two groups. ALM significantly increased vitamin E intake by 103% compared to CON. Plasma α-tocopherol levels increased by 10.2% (P=0.0065) post-intervention, while γ-tocopherol decreased by 16.5% (P=0.047) in the ALM group. Lipid profiles, including total cholesterol (TC), high-density lipoprotein cholesterol (HDL-C), low-density lipoprotein cholesterol (LDL-C), triglycerides (TG), small dense LDL-C, apolipoprotein B100 (Apo-B100), and apolipoprotein A-I (Apo-AI), remained unchanged between the ALM and CON diets. Endothelial function markers such as E-selectin, vascular cell adhesion molecule-1 (VCAM-1), and nitric oxide (NO) were not evaluated for significant changes in this study.
text: The CON diet with almonds (85 g/day) significantly increased plasma α-tocopherol by 10.2% (P=0.0065) compared to the CON diet, according to [PMC4469426].

memory: A study compared an area-wide, computerised diabetes register with structured recall and individualised patient management to a standard structured recall system. Economic analysis found no significant difference in average cost per patient between groups, though the intervention incurred one-off costs of £27,885 for guideline development, software, and education. Patients in the intervention group had higher odds (OR 1.87–2.77) of having recorded diabetes-related actions, including appointments, foot checks, dietary advice, and blood pressure recordings. However, mean HbA1c and BP levels were not significantly different. The intervention group had significantly lower mean cholesterol levels by -0.15 mmol/l (95% CI -0.25, -0.06). No significant differences were found in patient-reported outcomes, drug use, or health service uptake. The SF36 health status and diabetes symptom scores showed no statistically significant differences, with low reliability (ICCs 0.02–0.03). While the intervention improved documentation of diabetes care and showed a modest cholesterol benefit, it had no significant impact on patient-reported outcomes or overall costs. Additional administrative costs were incurred with the system.
text: The computerised diabetes register increased the odds of recorded diabetes-related actions (appointments, foot checks, dietary advice, blood pressure recording) compared to standard systems (OR 1.87–2.77). However, it did not significantly affect HbA1c, BP, or patient-reported outcomes.
intervention: area-wide, computerised diabetes register incorporating a full structured recall and individualised patient management system
comparator: standard structured and recall management system
outcome: Frequency of at least one diabetes appointment, a foot check, receiving dietary advice, recording of blood pressure

memory: In a study [PMC4215531], participants received facial affect training (FAT) over 20 daily 1-hour sessions. The primary outcome was alpha power during a far criterion task, assessed using magnetoencephalography (MEG). Results demonstrated a significant main effect of Time in the FAT group, F(1,18) = 5.61, p = .03 (p = .02), indicating increased alpha power from prestimulus baseline during the pre-recognition period of the FAR criterion task post-training compared to pre-training. This effect was visualized in Figure 4 (left panel). No significant effects involving Emotion were observed. The comparison was between the FAT group pre- and post-training. The findings suggest FAT may influence neural activity related to emotion processing, as reflected in changes in alpha power during specific task phases. The study did not report on other potential outcomes or long-term effects. Source: PMC4215531.
text: Facial affect training (FAT) over 20 daily 1-hour sessions significantly increased alpha power during the pre-recognition period of the FAR criterion task compared to baseline (F(1,18) = 5.61, p = .03). This suggests FAT enhances neural activity related to emotion processing. Source: PMC4215531.
intervention: facial affect training (FAT) in 20 daily 1-hour sessions

memory: In a clinical study comparing Ropivacaine-fentanyl-clonidine (RCF) with Ropivacaine-fentanyl (RF) and Ropivacaine-clonidine (RC), patient demographics and block characteristics were comparable across groups. The addition of clonidine to the ropivacaine-fentanyl combination (RCF group) did not significantly affect analgesic outcomes or hemodynamic parameters compared to RF and RC groups (P>0.05). However, the RCF group experienced a significant reduction in the incidence of side effects (P<0.05), leading to enhanced patient comfort. These findings suggest that while clonidine does not improve analgesia or hemodynamic stability, it may contribute to a safer profile and better patient experience. Source: [PMC4173331]
text: The addition of clonidine to ropivacaine-fentanyl (RCF) did not significantly affect hemodynamic parameters compared to ropivacaine-fentanyl (RF) or ropivacaine-clonidine (RC) groups (P>0.05). Source: [PMC4173331].

memory: A study compared high glycemic index (GI) and low GI diets and found that the low GI diet significantly reduced glycemic response (GR) after breakfast (p = 0.02), lunch (p = 0.02), and dinner (p = 0.05) compared to the high GI diet. Additionally, the low GI diet significantly reduced daily area under the curve (AUC) (p = 0.03), indicating lower overall glycemic exposure. A significant decrease in incremental AUC (IAUC) was also observed after a low GI breakfast compared to a high GI breakfast (p = 0.03). These results suggest that low GI diets are effective in lowering postprandial glycemic responses and overall glycemic exposure throughout the day. Source: PMC5684963.
text: A low glycemic index intervention significantly reduces glycemic response after lunch compared to a high glycemic index intervention (p = 0.02). Source: PMC5684963.

memory: A clinical study compared the effects of caudal sufentanil alone (Group CSu), caudal sufentanil with neostigmine (Group CSuNeo), and combinations with adrenalin (Group CSuAdr and Group CSuNeoAdr). The study evaluated the need for postoperative dipyrone, administered at the discretion of a trained nurse. Results showed that groups receiving caudal sufentanil alone (Group CSu, Group CSuAdr, and Group IVSu) had similar dipyrone requirements over 24 hours (P > 0.05). In contrast, groups receiving caudal sufentanil combined with neostigmine (Group CSuNeo and Group CSuNeoAdr) required significantly fewer dipyrone doses (P < 0.005). Facial pain, measured using the Visual Analog Scale (VAS) at the time of analgesic administration, was similar across all groups (5-6 cm, P > 0.05). No significant differences were observed in the incidence of postoperative nausea or vomiting among the groups. These findings suggest that adding neostigmine to caudal sufentanil may reduce the need for supplemental analgesia without affecting other aspects of postoperative recovery such as nausea and vomiting. Source: [PMC4141382].
text: Adding neostigmine to caudal sufentanil significantly reduces the need for dipyrone compared to caudal sufentanil alone (P < 0.005). Source: [PMC4141382].

memory: A study compared the transillumination-assisted technique (T group) with the midline approach technique (R group) in intubation. First, second, and third attempt success rates, as well as average intubation times, were not significantly different between the groups (P > 0.05). However, among patients who required a second attempt, the T group had significantly longer intubation times (P = 0.0006). The overall success rate of intubation was similar between the two groups (P > 0.05). Notably, the T group experienced higher rates of dry throat, sore throat, and hoarseness compared to the R group (all P < 0.05). These findings suggest that while both techniques are comparable in terms of success rates and time, the T group may be associated with increased post-intubation discomfort. Source: [PMC5320759]
text: The intubation success rates at first, second, and third attempts were not significantly different between the T group and R group (P > 0.05). Source: [PMC5320759]
outcome: The intubation success rates at the first, second, and third attempt

memory: Source article [PMC3525032] compares the effects of laryngeal mask airway (PLMA) and endotracheal intubation (ETT) on cortisol levels during CO2 insufflation. Serum cortisol levels were significantly lower in the PLMA group than in the ETT group 20 minutes after CO2 insufflation (p = 0.024). Within-group analysis showed that cortisol levels 20 minutes post-insufflation were significantly higher than immediately after anesthesia induction in both groups (p = 0.001). No significant differences were found between or within groups for adrenaline, noradrenaline, or dopamine. The study includes demographic data, respiratory parameters, and hemodynamic measurements in Tables 1, 2, and 3, respectively. These results suggest that PLMA may produce a lower cortisol response compared to ETT during CO2 insufflation.
text: Compared to baseline, both PLMA and ETT increased cortisol levels 20 minutes after CO2 insufflation (p=0.001). However, PLMA resulted in significantly lower cortisol levels than ETT (p=0.024). Source: [PMC3525032].
outcome: cortisol levels 20 minutes after CO2 insufflation

Source: [PMC4776564]  
Intervention: Hope-promoting interventions based on religious beliefs. Comparator: No intervention. Baseline characteristics (age, gender, marital status, employment, education, duration of heart disease, hospitalizations, and chronic illnesses) were comparable between groups (Tables 1 and 2). Pre-intervention independent t-tests showed no significant differences in mean quality of life (QOL) scores across performance and health, socioeconomic, psychological, spiritual, and familial dimensions, as well as satisfaction and importance areas. However, significant differences in mean QOL scores were found immediately after and 1 month post-intervention across the four dimensions, satisfaction, importance areas, and overall QOL scores (P < 0.05) [Tables 3 and 4]. Repeated measures ANOVA also showed significant differences in the control group across three time points in mean QOL scores for the four dimensions and two areas of satisfaction and importance.

intervention: Hope-promoting interventions based on religious beliefs

memory: A clinical study compared butoconazole nitrate 2% vaginal cream (Gynazole-1) with oral fluconazole 150 mg tablets (Diflucan) for treating vaginal infections. Butoconazole provided significantly faster symptom relief, with a median time to first symptom relief of 17.5 hours, compared to 22.9 hours for fluconazole (p < 0.001). The time at which 75% of patients experienced first relief was 24.5 hours for butoconazole versus 46.3 hours for fluconazole (p < 0.001). These findings suggest that butoconazole is more effective than fluconazole in achieving rapid symptom relief. Secondary outcomes, including overall symptom relief and reinfection rates within 30 days post-treatment, were evaluated, but specific data on these measures were not provided in the excerpt. Safety assessments were conducted via adverse event reporting for both treatments. Overall, the study suggests that butoconazole may be superior to fluconazole in terms of rapid symptom relief for vaginal infections. Source: PMC1784583.
text: Butoconazole nitrate 2% vaginal cream provides faster symptom relief than oral fluconazole 150 mg tablets. The median time to first relief was 17.5 hours for butoconazole versus 22.9 hours for fluconazole (p < 0.001). Source: PMC1784583.
intervention: butoconazole nitrate 2% Site Release vaginal cream (Gynazole-1)
outcome: The median time to first relief of symptoms

memory: In a study comparing vitamin D (50,000 IU/week) to placebo, proteinuria levels were measured at baseline and the end of the study. At baseline, the vitamin D group had a mean proteinuria level of 962.62±885.99 mg/day, while the placebo group had 755.71±640.94 mg/day (P=0.70). By the end of the study, these levels were 892.24±879.40 mg/day and 971.60±940.24 mg/day, respectively (P=0.48). However, the change in proteinuria levels from baseline to the end of the study showed a significant difference between the groups, with the vitamin D group showing a change of 70.38±553.71 and the placebo group showing a change of 215.89±451.44 (P=0.028). No significant differences were found between the groups in terms of fasting blood sugar (FBS), glycosylated hemoglobin (HbA1C), erythrocyte sedimentation rate (ESR), or C-Reactive Protein (CRP) levels (P>0.05). The results suggest that while vitamin D may not significantly affect FBS, HbA1C, ESR, or CRP, it may have a differential impact on proteinuria levels compared to placebo. Source: [PMC5106877]
text: The study found no significant effect of "Vit D as 50,000 IU/week" compared to placebo on fasting blood sugar (FBS), HbA1C, ESR, or CRP levels (P>0.05). Source: [PMC5106877].
outcome: fasting blood sugar (FBS), glycosylated hemoglobin (HbA1C), erythrocyte sedimentation rate (ESR) and C-Reactive Protein (CRP) levels

memory: A study compared lifestyle physical activity (LPA) with a fibromyalgia education (FME) control group. The LPA group engaged in 30 minutes of self-selected moderate-intensity activity five to seven days per week. At baseline, no significant differences were observed between groups in Fibromyalgia Impact Questionnaire (FIQ) scores, pain levels, fatigue, depression, number of tender points, BMI, or six-minute walk distance. Post-intervention results showed significant reductions in FIQ scores (P = .032; Cohen's d = .53) and pain levels (P = .006; Cohen's d = .67) in the LPA group compared to FME. The six-minute walk test difference approached significance (P = .067; Cohen's d = .53). No significant changes were observed in BMI, fatigue, depression, or tender points. The findings suggest that LPA may reduce pain and functional impairment in fibromyalgia patients, indicating potential benefits of increased physical activity for symptom management. Source: [PMC2888205].
text: The LPA group showed significant reductions in pain (P = .006) and FIQ scores (P = .032) compared to the FME group. Source: [PMC2888205].
intervention: lifestyle physical activity (LPA) - 30 minutes of self-selected moderate-intensity LPA, five to seven days per week
comparator: fibromyalgia (FM) education control (FME) group - received information and support

memory: In Experiment 1, cursor color (red or blue) was uniquely associated with one of two opposing curl field directions, with directions counterbalanced across participants. Performance was assessed using maximum perpendicular error (MPE) per trial and force compensation on clamp trials. Over the exposure period, MPE significantly decreased (F1,5 = 58.220; P = 0.001), indicating improved performance. However, no significant increase in force compensation was observed (F1,5 = 0.223; P = 0.657) between initial and final trials of the exposure period. During the postexposure period, when the force field was removed, no trajectory deviations from a straight line were observed, suggesting that participants had not learned specific compensation strategies for the opposing force fields. Source: [PMC3653044]
text: Over the exposure period, MPE significantly decreased (F1,5 = 58.220; P = 0.001) from initial to final trials, indicating improved performance. However, no significant change in force compensation was observed. Source: [PMC3653044].
outcome: over the course of the exposure period maximum perpendicular error (MPE) decrease - cursor color (red or blue)

memory: In clinical trials SMART-1, SMART-2, and SMART-5 (PMC3743641), breast pain/tenderness was evaluated for BZA/CE regimens (BZA 20 mg/CE 0.45 mg and BZA 20 mg/CE 0.625 mg) compared to placebo, raloxifene 60 mg, and BZA 20 mg alone. No significant differences in breast pain/tenderness were observed between BZA/CE groups and these comparators. In SMART-5, BZA/CE showed significantly lower breast tenderness than CE 0.45 mg/MPA 1.5 mg (P < 0.001). These findings are consistent with adverse event reports and discontinuation rates due to breast pain/tenderness from the SMART trials. Regarding breast density, BZA/CE treatment groups demonstrated non-inferiority to placebo in terms of mammographic breast density. In contrast, CE 0.45 mg/MPA 1.5 mg showed a significant increase in breast density compared to placebo. BZA/CE did not impact age-related changes in breast density, maintaining natural reductions seen during menopause.
text: BZA/CE did not significantly increase breast tenderness compared to placebo in SMART trials (PMC3743641). It showed lower breast tenderness than CE/MPA. Adverse event reports and discontinuation rates support these findings.
intervention: BZA/CE combines bazedoxifene (BZA), a selective estrogen receptor modulator, with conjugated estrogens (CE),

memory: In a study [PMC5126873], the UPBEAT intervention (diet and physical activity) was compared to a control group. At 28 weeks gestation, the intervention group showed significant reductions in Processed (−0.14; 95% CI −0.19, −0.08, P <0.0001) and Snacks (−0.24; 95% CI −0.31, −0.17, P <0.0001) dietary pattern scores. These improvements were sustained at 36 weeks gestation. No significant changes were observed in Fruit and vegetables or African/Caribbean dietary pattern scores between the groups at 28 or 36 weeks gestation. The data are presented in Table 2, which includes dietary pattern scores at baseline (15+0-18+6 weeks' gestation), after the UPBEAT intervention (27+0-28+6 weeks' gestation), and in late gestation (34+0 to 36+0 weeks' gestation). The intervention group showed consistent improvements in reducing processed and snack dietary patterns, but no significant effect on fruit and vegetable or African/Caribbean dietary patterns.
text: A study [PMC5126873] found that "Diet and physical activity" interventions did not significantly affect African/Caribbean food intake compared to control. No changes were observed in African/Caribbean dietary pattern scores at 28 or 36 weeks gestation.

memory: A clinical study compared resveratrol to a placebo in evaluating the need for ibuprofen. The resveratrol group (n=5) had a mean ibuprofen dose of 1200 mg (SD 848 mg), while the placebo group (n=5) had a mean dose of 5640 mg (SD 328 mg). The difference between the groups was statistically significant with a p-value of 0.09, suggesting a potential trend toward reduced ibuprofen use in the resveratrol group. However, the p-value does not reach conventional levels of statistical significance (p < 0.05). The small sample size of each group (n=5) may have limited the study's power to detect a significant difference. These results hint at a possible role of resveratrol in pain management or inflammation, but further investigation with larger sample sizes is needed. Source: [PMC5686687].
text: A study found a potential trend toward reduced need for ibuprofen with resveratrol (mean dose 1200 mg) compared to placebo (mean dose 5640 mg), though the difference was not statistically significant (p=0.09). The small sample size (n=5 per group) may have limited the study's power. Source: [PMC5686687].

memory: A study compared regular activity breaks (RAB) with prolonged sitting (SIT) on appetite and food intake over two days. Linear mixed models were used to evaluate the area under the appetite response curve (AUC) and ad libitum meal intake. On Day 1, RAB had a standardized effect on appetite AUC of 0.11 (95% CI: −0.28, 0.06; p = 0.212), and on Day 2, the effect was 0.04 (95% CI: −0.15, 0.24; p = 0.648). No significant differences in appetite AUC were found between RAB and SIT on either day. Additionally, energy consumed during the ad libitum lunch on Day 2 did not differ significantly between the groups. The findings suggest that interrupting prolonged sitting with regular activity breaks does not acutely affect appetite or food consumption, even though RAB may increase energy expenditure. Source: [PMC5852701].
text: Regular activity breaks (RAB) did not significantly affect appetite area under the curve (AUC) on Day 1 compared to prolonged sitting (SIT) (effect size 0.11, 95% CI: −0.28, 0.06; p = 0.212). No significant differences were observed between RAB and SIT on either day. Source: [PMC5852701].
outcome: Appetite area under the curve at day 1

memory: In a clinical study comparing artemether-lumefantrine (ALN) and mefloquine-artesunate (MAS3) for malaria treatment, 452 patients were monitored for P. vivax parasitaemia. A total of 119 patients (26.3%) developed P. vivax during follow-up. The MAS3 group had significantly fewer cases (29 out of 227 patients) compared to the ALN group (90 out of 225 patients), with a statistically significant difference (P < 0.001). The median time to P. vivax detection was longer in the MAS3 group (40 days, range 13–43 days) than in the ALN group (28 days, range 14–43 days), also with P < 0.001. These findings suggest that MAS3 may offer better protection against P. vivax recurrence compared to ALN. Source: PMC1261533, Results > Other Parasitological Findings.
text: Mefloquine-artesunate (MAS3) significantly reduces P. vivax parasitaemia during follow-up compared to artemether-lumefantrine (ALN), with fewer cases (29/227 vs. 90/225, P < 0.001) and a longer time to detection (40 vs. 28 days, P < 0.001). Source: PMC1261533.
outcome: P. vivax parasitaemia diagnosed during follow up

Source: [PMC5022334]  
Intervention: Robotic-assisted thyroidectomy (BABA) vs conventional open thyroidectomy.  
Outcome: Visual analogue scale (VAS) and neck dissection score (NSS).  
Key findings: Subclinical central lymph node metastasis rate was 35%. Robotic group had longer operative time (118.8 ± 16.5 min) compared to conventional (90.7 ± 10.3 min, P < 0.05). VAS scores were significantly lower in the robotic group (2.1 ± 1.0) versus conventional (3.8 ± 1.2, P < 0.05), indicating less postoperative pain. NSS scores were also significantly lower in the robotic group (8.9 ± 0.8) compared to conventional (4.8 ± 1.7, P < 0.05), suggesting better functional outcomes. No significant differences were found in intraoperative blood loss, postoperative hospital stay, number of lymph nodes removed, postoperative thyroglobulin levels, or complications (all P > 0.05). No iatrogenic implantation or metastasis was observed in the punctured porous channel or chest wall in either group.
text: Thyroidectomy via BABA resulted in significantly lower Visual Analogue Scale (VAS) scores (2.1 ± 1.0) compared to conventional open thyroidectomy (3.8 ± 1.2, P < 0.05), indicating less postoperative pain [PMC5022334].

memory: In a study comparing intubation techniques, the WEI JET group had significantly longer intubation times (110.8±18.3 s) compared to the Lightwand (LW) group (63.3±27.5 s) and Direct Laryngoscopy (DL) group (66.7±29.4 s), p = 0.000.
