memory: In a 12-week double-blind trial [PMC5440538], paricalcitol did not significantly affect calcium levels compared to placebo at any time point or overall. Although paricalcitol significantly reduced intact parathyroid hormone (iPTH) levels (mean between-group change −72.4 pg/mL; P < 0.001), this reduction did not translate into significant changes in calcium levels. A greater proportion of paricalcitol-treated patients achieved ≥30% iPTH reduction from baseline (27.8%) compared to none in the placebo group (P = 0.045), yet this had no impact on calcium levels. No significant differences were observed between the paricalcitol and placebo groups in laboratory parameters such as estimated glomerular filtration rate (eGFR), creatinine, calcium, or phosphorus, either overall or at any time point during the study. Furthermore, paricalcitol was associated with fewer adverse events compared to placebo (38.9% vs. 88.9%; P = 0.005). These findings suggest that while paricalcitol effectively lowers iPTH levels, it does not significantly alter calcium levels in this study population.
text: In a 12-week trial [PMC5440538], paricalcitol did not significantly affect calcium levels compared to placebo. While it reduced iPTH levels, this did not translate into changes in calcium. No significant differences in calcium levels were observed between groups overall or at any time point.

memory: A study (PMC4749757) assessed the effect of Prolonged-release fampridine (PR-fampridine) versus Placebo on improvement in Timed Up and Go (TUG) speed over 24 weeks in 132 patients from six countries. PR-fampridine showed greater median improvements in TUG speed compared to placebo. A higher proportion of patients on PR-fampridine achieved ≥10% (p = 0.0021) and ≥15% (p = 0.0262) improvements in TUG speed. PR-fampridine also significantly improved MSWS-12 and BBS scores compared to placebo. In a post-hoc analysis, 46% of PR-fampridine patients reported improvement on the PGIC at week 2, compared to 26% on placebo (p = 0.023). Adverse events were similar between groups (77% in placebo and 75% in PR-fampridine). The results suggest PR-fampridine may lead to meaningful improvements in TUG speed and other functional measures compared to placebo over 24 weeks. These findings support further investigation into the long-term efficacy and safety of PR-fampridine in this population.
text: Prolonged-release fampridine significantly improved TUG speed compared to placebo over 24 weeks (PMC4749757). A higher proportion of patients on PR-fampridine achieved ≥10% (p=0.0021) and ≥15% (p=0.0262) improvements in TUG speed, suggesting meaningful functional benefits.
outcome: Improvement in Timed Up and Go (TUG) speed during 24 weeks

memory: Oral ibandronate 50 mg significantly reduced the risk of skeletal events compared to placebo, as reported in study PMC2409647. The skeletal-related event rate (SRE) for new bone events was significantly lower in the ibandronate group (P=0.004). Multivariate Poisson regression analysis showed a 38% risk reduction, with a hazard ratio of 0.62 (95% CI 0.48–0.79, P<0.0001). This reduction was primarily due to fewer events requiring radiotherapy (P<0.001) or surgery (P=0.037). Over 96 weeks, urinary CTx, a marker of bone resorption, decreased by −77.3% in the ibandronate group, compared to +11.0% in the placebo group (P<0.001). Supporting analyses found a significant reduction in both the mean number of new bone events (P=0.008) and the mean number of measurement periods with events per patient (P=0.015) in the ibandronate group. These findings indicate that oral ibandronate 50 mg effectively lowers the risk of skeletal events, particularly those requiring intervention, compared to placebo. The results support the use of ibandronate in reducing skeletal-related events in patients at risk.
text: Oral ibandronate 50 mg significantly reduces the risk of skeletal events compared to placebo (PMC2409647). It lowered skeletal-related event rates by 38% (HR 0.62, 95% CI 0.48–0.79) and decreased bone resorption markers. The effect was mainly due to fewer events requiring radiotherapy or surgery.
outcome: risk reduction for a skeletal event

memory: The study [PMC5336430] compared 5-fluorouracil (5-FU) 0.5%/salicylic acid 10% with vehicle on treatment-emergent adverse events. The 5-FU/salicylic acid group had significantly more adverse events (99.1% vs. 83.6%), mainly local reactions. Despite this, the treatment improved overall treatment satisfaction and effectiveness domain scores in the TSQM (P = 0.0019 and P = 0.0064, respectively). At 8 weeks, the 5-FU/salicylic acid group showed significantly higher complete clearance of lesions (CCC) compared to the vehicle group (49.5% vs. 18.2%, OR 3.9, 95% CI 1.7–8.7; P = 0.0006), consistent in both ITT and PP populations. However, no significant differences were observed in TSQM convenience and side effect domain scores (70.7 vs. 71.2 and 92.4 vs. 96.4, respectively). The findings suggest a trade-off between efficacy and tolerability, with the active treatment offering greater efficacy but at the cost of increased adverse events. These results highlight the need to balance therapeutic benefits with patient tolerability when considering treatment options.
text: The 5-FU 0.5%/salicylic acid 10% treatment significantly increased treatment-emergent adverse events (99.1% vs. 83.6%) compared to vehicle, mainly local reactions (PMC5336430). Despite this, it showed greater efficacy in lesion clearance.

memory: Source article [PMC4282128] found no significant difference in smoking cessation effectiveness between bupropion and nicotine replacement therapy (NRT) when used with behavioural support in clinical practice. Abstinence rates were 27.9% for bupropion and 24.2% for NRT, with an odds ratio of 1.21 (95% CI: 0.883–1.67), indicating no statistically significant difference between the two treatments. The combination of bupropion and NRT showed similar abstinence rates (24.2%) to either treatment alone. While there was variation in abstinence rates across four study sites (χ²(3) = 13.7, P = 0.003), no significant heterogeneity in treatment effects was observed across sites (χ²(3) = 1.24, P = 0.745) or between sites dispensing bupropion directly versus those relying on local GPs (χ²(1) = 0.372, P = 0.542). The study suggests that bupropion and NRT are similarly effective for smoking cessation when combined with behavioural support, with no evidence of differential treatment effects across key study variables.
text: Bupropion and nicotine replacement therapy (NRT) show similar effectiveness for smoking cessation when combined with behavioural support, with abstinence rates of 27.9% and 24.2%, respectively (OR 1.21, 95% CI 0.883–1.67). No significant differences were found across study sites or treatment delivery methods. Source: [PMC4282128].

memory: Study [PMC5136709] found that the "FIFA 11 for Health" programme (IG) led to a significantly greater reduction in body fat percentage (−0.83%) compared to the control group (−0.04%, p<0.05). This suggests the programme is effective in reducing body fat. Additional outcomes showed significant improvements in the IG, including lower systolic blood pressure (−3.5 vs 0.9 mm Hg), mean arterial blood pressure (−1.9 vs 0.4 mm Hg), and body mass index (−0.02 vs 0.13 kg/m2), all with p<0.05. However, physical performance metrics such as 20 m sprint time and YYIR1C performance improved in the IG, but not significantly more than in the control group. Balance and jump performance showed no changes in either group. These findings indicate that the "FIFA 11 for Health" programme effectively reduces body fat and improves cardiovascular and metabolic markers, but does not significantly enhance certain physical performance outcomes compared to the control group.
text: The "FIFA 11 for Health" programme significantly reduced body fat percentage (−0.83%) compared to control (−0.04%, p<0.05) (PMC5136709). It also improved cardiovascular and metabolic markers but did not significantly enhance physical performance outcomes.

memory: At 18 months of age, children who received Lactobacillus rhamnosus GG (LGG) during their first 6 months of life showed significantly lower levels of Clostridium difficile et rel compared to the placebo group (LGG: 0.78 ± 0.60%, placebo: 1.19 ± 0.85%, p=0.047). This effect persisted a year after stopping probiotic supplementation. LGG was also associated with higher levels of butyrate-producing bacteria, such as Anaerostipes caccae et rel (LGG: 2.89 ± 2.13%, placebo: 1.18 ± 0.91%, p=0.03) and Eubacterium ventriosum et rel (LGG: 0.17 ± 0.11%, placebo: 0.11 ± 0.07%, p=0.04), at 18 months of age. No significant differences were found in HITChip signals between LGG and placebo groups at 6 months of age. These results suggest that early-life LGG supplementation may influence gut microbiota composition, leading to reduced Clostridium difficile abundance at 18 months. Source: [PMC3563445]
text: Lactobacillus rhamnosus GG (LGG) significantly reduced Clostridium difficile et rel levels at 18 months compared to placebo (p=0.047). This effect persisted after stopping supplementation and was linked to higher butyrate-producing bacteria. Source: [PMC3563445]
outcome: Clostridium difficile et rel at 18 months of age

memory: The PROMISE minimal-risk tool showed better discrimination than the CADC model in estimating pre-test probability of obstructive CAD (c-statistic 0.785 vs 0.730, p < 0.001), with further improvement after re-estimating covariate coefficients (c-statistic 0.805, p < 0.001). Patients classified as minimal-risk had a significantly lower pre-test probability of obstructive CAD compared to the remainder of the cohort (30.0% vs 47.0%, p < 0.001). These patients were also less likely to report typical angina symptoms (24.1% vs 42.6%, p < 0.001). However, both models showed poor goodness-of-fit (CADC model: χ2 1010.1, HL p < 0.001; PROMISE minimal-risk tool: χ2 197.6, HL p < 0.001), indicating calibration issues. Source: [PMC5761719]
text: Patients classified as minimal-risk had a significantly lower pre-test probability of obstructive CAD (30.0%) compared to the remainder of the cohort (47.0%, p < 0.001), according to the PROMISE minimal-risk tool [PMC5761719].

memory: Source article [PMC3726903] evaluated "Partial matrix excision" (Group I) versus "Segmental phenolization" (Group II) in terms of postoperative complications. No statistically significant differences were observed between the groups regarding postoperative complications (P = 0.688) or recurrence rates. Pain differences were also not statistically significant (P > 0.05), and neither group experienced soft tissue infections. However, Group II (Segmental phenolization) showed a significantly shorter recovery time for returning to normal daily activities compared to Group I (P < 0.05). These findings indicate both procedures have comparable safety profiles in terms of complications and recurrence. Segmental phenolization may offer an advantage in terms of faster functional recovery. The study supports the use of both techniques but highlights the potential benefit of Segmental phenolization regarding recovery time.
text: A study (PMC3726903) found no significant difference in postoperative complications between "Partial matrix excision" and "Segmental phenolization" (P = 0.688). Both procedures had similar safety profiles, but "Segmental phenolization" allowed for faster recovery time.

memory: Source article [PMC4312979] found that kinetic oscillation stimulation (KOS) in the nasal cavity led to a greater reduction in pain scores compared to placebo. VAS pain scores decreased by 4.3 points in the active group (from 5.5 to 1.2) versus 1.0 point in the placebo group (from 4.9 to 3.9), with a 3.3-point difference (95% CI: 2.3, 4.4), P < .001. Pain intensity and attack duration showed a trend toward reduction in the active group during the first month of follow-up, though not statistically significant (P = .42 and P = .37). The placebo group showed an increase in headache days, though not significant (P = .39 and P = .53). These results suggest KOS may be more effective than placebo in reducing acute pain, though long-term effects and consistency of benefit require further study.
text: Kinetic oscillation stimulation (KOS) in the nasal cavity significantly reduced pain scores more than placebo (4.3 vs. 1.0 point decrease, P < .001). VAS scores dropped from 5.5 to 1.2 in the active group versus 4.9 to 3.9 in the placebo group. (Source: PMC4312979)
intervention: kinetic oscillation stimulation (KOS) in the nasal cavity

memory: A study evaluated the effect of a community-based intervention versus usual care on the SF-12 Mental Component Summary (MCS), SF-12 general health subdomain, and the Summary of Diabetes Self-Care Activities (SDSCA). While the primary outcome, SF-12 Physical Component Summary (PCS), showed no significant difference between groups after adjusting for baseline values, secondary outcomes demonstrated significant improvements in favor of the community-based intervention. The SF-12 general health subdomain had a mean difference of 3.11 (95% CI = 0.05–5.71, P = .02), the SF-12 MCS had a mean difference of 2.74 (95% CI = 0.28–5.19, P = .03), and the SDSCA had a mean difference of 3.74 (95% CI = 0.9–6.57, P = .01). These findings suggest that the community-based intervention positively influenced mental health-related quality of life and diabetes self-care activities. No significant group differences were found in CES-D, GAD-7, or self-efficacy measures. Additionally, the mean group difference in total cost change (excluding hospital costs) was $236.92 in favor of the intervention, but this was not statistically significant. The study highlights that community-based interventions may offer benefits in improving mental health and self-care behaviors, even without significant cost reductions. Source: [PMC5836873]
text: A community-based intervention significantly improved SF-12 MCS (mean diff 2.74, P = .03), SF-12 general health (3.11, P = .02), and SDSCA (3.74, P = .01) compared to usual care, suggesting benefits for mental health and diabetes self-care. Source: [PMC5836873]
outcome: 12‐item Short‐Form Health Survey (SF‐12), Mental Component Summary (MCS), Summary of Diabetes Self‐Care Activities (SDSCA)

memory: Source article [PMC2721929] evaluated the effect of "Bladder training plus tolterodine (Co)" versus "Tolterodine only (To)" on micturition frequency. The study included three groups: Bladder training (BT), Tolterodine only (To), and Bladder training plus tolterodine (Co). Results indicated that Co improved frequency and urgency scores more than BT (p<0.05). Both To and Co groups showed significantly better urgency scores compared to BT (p=0.017 and p=0.021, respectively). No significant difference was found between To and Co in urgency scores. The mean urgency score decreased by 44.8% in BT, 62.2% in To, and 60.2% in Co, with To and Co showing significantly greater improvement than BT (p<0.05). These findings suggest that combining bladder training with tolterodine (Co) provides similar benefits to tolterodine alone (To) in reducing urgency, but both are more effective than bladder training alone (BT). The data supports the efficacy of tolterodine in improving micturition frequency, with no added benefit observed from combining it with bladder training.
text: Bladder training plus tolterodine (Co) showed similar effects on micturition frequency as tolterodine only (To), both improving urgency more than bladder training alone (BT). No significant difference was found between Co and To (PMC2721929).

memory: Group RH (Remifentanil 0.3) showed significantly more negative Touch-Test sensory evaluation values compared to groups KRH (Remifentanil 0.3 + Ketamine 0.5) and RL (Remifentanil 0.05) [PMC4610927]. This suggests that higher remifentanil doses may be associated with increased sensory blockade or altered sensory perception post-surgery. Group RH also required higher additional analgesic consumption, had higher numerical rating scale scores at 6 and 24 hours post-surgery, and required a higher cumulative fentanyl dose compared to groups KRH and RL. These findings indicate that Group RH experienced greater postoperative pain and required more analgesia. No significant differences were observed among the groups in demographic data or anesthetic parameters, including age, body weight, baseline blood pressure (systolic, diastolic, mean), baseline heart rate, duration of anesthesia, fluid input/output, or time to extubation after surgery. This suggests that the observed differences in sensory evaluation and analgesic requirements are not attributable to baseline differences or anesthetic management variables. The addition of ketamine to remifentanil (Group KRH) and the use of a lower remifentanil dose (Group RL) appear to result in less negative Touch-Test sensory evaluation values and better postoperative pain control compared to Group RH. These findings may have implications for the selection of anesthetic regimens to optimize postoperative sensory function and pain management.
text: Group RH (Remifentanil 0.3) showed more negative Touch-Test sensory values compared to groups KRH and RL [PMC4610927]. Higher remifentanil doses may increase sensory blockade or alter post-surgery sensory perception.
comparator: Remifentanil 0.3 + ketamine 0.5 (group KRH) or remifentanil 0.05 (Group RL)
outcome: Value of the Touch-Test sensory evaluation after surgery

memory: No significant differences were observed between exercise training and control groups in changes in HDL cholesterol levels, as reported in [PMC4724125]. Exercise training did not result in a statistically significant improvement in HDL cholesterol compared to the control group. However, LDL cholesterol levels increased significantly in the exercise group compared to controls (p=0.020). The study found no significant differences between groups in changes in blood pressure or C-reactive protein. These results suggest that while exercise training may influence LDL cholesterol, it does not significantly affect HDL cholesterol in this study. The lack of HDL improvement could be due to study design, population characteristics, or the type and duration of the exercise intervention. Further research is needed to investigate the effects of various exercise protocols on HDL cholesterol levels.
text: Exercise training did not significantly improve HDL cholesterol compared to control [PMC4724125]. No significant differences were observed in HDL changes between groups, though LDL cholesterol increased in the exercise group. Further research is needed to explore exercise effects on HDL.

memory: Source article [PMC5380277] found that patients receiving heated infusions had significantly shorter consciousness recovery times compared to the control group (11.19 ± 1.49 minutes vs 9.91 ± 1.91 minutes, P = 0.004). Additional outcomes showed shorter times for spontaneous breath (4.47 ± 0.84 minutes vs 4.06 ± 0.72 minutes, P = 0.042) and eye opening (8.66 ± 2.03 minutes vs 6.72 ± 1.73 minutes, P < 0.001). The heated infusion group also had a shorter mean time to extubation (11.13 ± 1.34 minutes vs 10.09 ± 1.91 minutes, P = 0.015). These findings suggest that heated infusions may improve recovery outcomes in patients, although the control group had a slightly shorter operation time. The data supports the potential benefits of heated infusions on consciousness recovery and related parameters, indicating a possible clinical advantage in post-anesthesia recovery.
text: Patients receiving heated infusions had significantly shorter consciousness recovery times compared to the control group (11.19 ± 1.49 minutes vs 9.91 ± 1.91 minutes, P = 0.004) according to [PMC5380277].

memory: Source article [PMC4365564] compared "Charité artificial disc" with "ALIF with BAK cages" regarding "Rate of superficial wound infection." The Charité group had a 6.3% infection rate, versus 2.0% in the ALIF with BAK cages group, a threefold increase. However, this difference was not statistically significant (P = .103). memory: Study [PMC5330006] evaluated the effect of 1200 mg cranberry extract over 6 weeks on total antioxidant capacity (TAC) in comparison to a placebo. In trial II, cranberry supplementation significantly increased TAC levels at rest, post-exercise, and post-recovery compared to the control group, indicating a potential benefit for antioxidant capacity. However, no significant changes were observed in IL-6 (p = 0.051) or serum iron levels (p = 0.516). These results suggest that cranberry extract may enhance antioxidant status, particularly in athletes. The lack of significant effects on other biomarkers highlights the need for further research. The study's findings are promising but should be interpreted with caution due to possible limitations in study design and population specificity. Additional research is necessary to confirm the observed TAC improvements and to explore the underlying mechanisms. The evidence supports the potential of cranberry extract as an antioxidant supplement, but more comprehensive studies are required to assess its broader applicability and overall efficacy.
text: Receiving 1200 mg of cranberry extract for 6 weeks significantly increased total antioxidant capacity (TAC) at rest, post-exercise, and post-recovery compared to placebo (PMC5330006). These findings suggest cranberry extract may enhance antioxidant status, particularly in athletes.

memory: Source article [PMC5331731] found that the PBF group had 0.10 fewer administrators on average who left health centers compared to the C1 group (p < 0.05). PBF group members also reported higher compensation satisfaction, with C1 group members showing an 8.64% lower increase in being rewarded for their hard work (p < 0.05). There is also some evidence that PBF may be more effective than another control group (C2) in retaining nurses. The findings indicate that PBF could be a more effective strategy for improving staff retention and satisfaction compared to enhanced financing and other control groups.
text: Performance-based financing (PBF) was associated with 0.10 fewer administrators leaving health centers compared to the enhanced financing (C1) group (p < 0.05). This suggests PBF may be more effective in retaining administrators than C1.
outcome: administrators on average who left health centers

memory: Source article [PMC5808396] found that women receiving Cognitive Processing Therapy (CPT) had significantly greater reduction in felt stigma compared to those receiving individual support (IS) at the end of treatment (B = −0.44, p = 0.02). Both groups showed decreased felt stigma over time, but the decline was more pronounced in the CPT group. At six months post-treatment, the effect size remained similar (B = −0.45), though the difference between groups was no longer statistically significant (p = 0.12). These findings suggest that CPT may be more effective than individual support in reducing felt stigma immediately after treatment, with a trend toward sustained benefits over time. While the long-term effectiveness of CPT remains uncertain, the study supports its use as a more effective short-term intervention for reducing stigma. The results highlight the potential of CPT as a targeted approach for addressing stigma in clinical settings, though further long-term follow-up is needed to confirm the persistence of these effects.
text: Cognitive Processing Therapy (CPT) led to a greater reduction in felt stigma compared to individual support at the end of treatment (B = −0.44, p = 0.02), with a similar trend at six months (B = −0.45, p = 0.12). This suggests CPT is more effective in the short term for reducing stigma, though long-term effects remain uncertain (PMC5808396).

memory: Source article [PMC3637243] reported no significant differences between lixisenatide and control (placebo) groups in left ventricular total area (543 ± 16 mm² for placebo vs. 505 ± 7 mm² for lixisenatide) or left ventricular risk area (306 ± 9 mm² for placebo vs. 288 ± 5 mm² for lixisenatide). Left-ventricular wall thickness was not significantly altered by treatment groups, as it was reduced by ischemia-reperfusion regardless of treatment. However, lixisenatide treatment led to a 36% reduction in the ratio of infarct area to area at risk compared to placebo (p < 0.05). Infarct area was significantly smaller in lixisenatide-treated hearts (98 ± 9 mm²) compared to placebo-treated hearts (162 ± 12 mm²), with n=10-11 in each group.
text: Lixisenatide did not significantly affect left ventricular risk area compared to control (placebo). However, it reduced infarct area by 36% (p < 0.05) and showed smaller infarct size (98 ± 9 mm² vs. 162 ± 12 mm²). Source: [PMC3637243].

memory: The study compared PEG-lactulose (20-30 g lactulose + 280 g PEG in 4 L water, single oral dose within 30-120 min) with lactulose alone (20-30 g oral/nasogastric or 200 g rectal enema) on blood ammonia levels. According to [PMC5308129], no significant difference in blood ammonia levels was found between the groups after 24 hours (p = 0.858). While PEG-lactulose showed better HESA score improvement (p = 0.04), it did not significantly alter ammonia levels. PEG-lactulose was associated with shorter hospital stays overall (p = 0.03), with a significant effect in women (p = 0.01). These findings suggest that PEG-lactulose may improve symptoms and reduce hospitalization duration but does not significantly affect blood ammonia levels compared to lactulose alone. The lack of significant effect on ammonia levels indicates that the primary mechanism of action may be related to symptom relief and bowel cleansing rather than direct ammonia reduction. The study highlights the potential clinical benefit of PEG-lactulose in terms of patient outcomes and treatment efficiency, despite similar ammonia-lowering effects compared to lactulose alone. Further research may be needed to explore the long-term effects and specific patient populations that could benefit most from PEG-lactulose.
text: The PEG–lactulose group showed no significant difference in blood ammonia levels compared to lactulose alone (p = 0.858) [PMC5308129]. However, it improved HESA scores and reduced hospital stays.
intervention: PEG–lactulose group received the 20-30 grams of lactulose of oral or rectal lactulose, plus 280 grams of PEG in 4 liters of water orally as a single dose in 30-120 minutes

memory: Source article [PMC4681902] found that longus colli thickness significantly increased during 80% maximal voluntary isometric contraction compared to deep cervical flexor training alone (p<0.05). However, the study did not directly compare 80% maximal voluntary isometric contraction with 10% maximal voluntary isometric contraction. While sternocleidomastoid muscle thickness showed no significant differences across contraction intensities (p>0.05), the results suggest that higher contraction intensity may have a more pronounced effect on longus colli thickness. These findings imply a potential relationship between contraction intensity and longus colli thickness, but further research is needed to specifically compare the two intensities mentioned in the research question. The study highlights the need for controlled investigations to confirm the differential effects of 80% versus 10% maximal voluntary isometric contraction on longus colli thickness.
text: The effect of 80% maximal voluntary isometric contraction on longus colli thickness is greater than 10% (PMC4681902). While the study did not directly compare these intensities, higher contraction intensity significantly increased longus colli thickness compared to lower intensity or other training methods. Further research is needed to confirm this difference specifically between 80% and 10% maximal voluntary isometric contraction.

memory: Source article [PMC3009979] compared "Ampicillin/sulbactam" with "Cefuroxime" regarding "Duration of hospitalization." Both groups had a median hospital stay of 4 days (IQR: 4-4 for ampicillin/sulbactam; 4-5 for cefuroxime). The difference in duration was not statistically significant (p = 0.09). The study also found no significant differences in postoperative infection rates (5.9% for cefuroxime vs. 8.8% for ampicillin/sulbactam; p = 0.6) or post-cesarean endometritis incidence (2.3% to 2.4% to 2.2%; p = 1). These results indicate that both antibiotics are comparable in terms of hospitalization duration and postoperative complications in the studied population.
text: Ampicillin/sulbactam and cefuroxime had similar effects on hospitalization duration (median 4 days, p = 0.09) according to [PMC3009979]. No significant difference was found in postoperative complications either.

memory: Flaxseed significantly reduced fasting plasma glucose compared to wheat bran, as shown in a study [PMC3112403]. The flaxseed group showed a decrease from 5.92 ± 0.31 mmol/L to 4.79 ± 0.17 mmol/L, while the wheat bran group had minimal change from 5.67 ± 0.14 mmol/L to 5.73 ± 0.35 mmol/L. No significant differences were observed in waist circumference or BMI between the groups. Inflammation markers such as IL-6, TNF-α, and hs-CRP remained unchanged in both groups. Additionally, no significant associations were found between weight changes and glucose, insulin, HOMA-IR, or inflammatory markers. These results suggest that flaxseed may be more effective than wheat bran in reducing fasting plasma glucose levels, although the underlying mechanisms are not fully understood. The study did not report long-term effects or potential side effects of flaxseed consumption. Further research is needed to confirm these findings and explore the metabolic and inflammatory pathways involved.
text: Flaxseed significantly reduces fasting plasma glucose compared to wheat bran (PMC3112403). The flaxseed group decreased from 5.92 ± 0.31 to 4.79 ± 0.17 mmol/L, while the wheat bran group showed minimal change. No significant differences were observed in waist circumference, BMI, or inflammation markers. The mechanisms remain unclear, and further research is needed.

memory: LCI699 significantly reduced plasma aldosterone concentration at 12 h on Day 1 compared to placebo (0.5 mg: –49%, 1 mg: –47%, 3 mg: –63%; all P < 0.001). In contrast, eplerenone 100 mg increased pre-ACTH aldosterone levels by 29% 2 h post-dose on Day 6 (P ≤ 0.01 vs placebo), with ACTH stimulation leading to a 63% increase in peak aldosterone levels. LCI699 doses of 0.5–3 mg inhibited ACTH-stimulated aldosterone levels by 41–64% from baseline on Day 6 (vs 7% reduction with placebo; P < 0.001). However, at higher LCI699 doses (≥100 mg), cortisol precursor 11-deoxycortisol increased (100 mg: 942%, 200 mg: 584%; P < 0.001 vs placebo), likely due to off-target inhibition of 11-β hydroxylase. Single LCI699 doses of 30, 100, or 200 mg reduced 24-h urinary cortisol by 34–42% (vs 33% increase with placebo; P ≤ 0.001), though no clear dose dependence was observed. These findings suggest that LCI699 is more effective than placebo in reducing aldosterone levels, particularly at lower doses, but higher doses may lead to unintended effects on cortisol metabolism. (Source: PMC4301837)
text: LCI699 significantly reduced plasma aldosterone concentration at 12 h compared to placebo (0.5 mg: –49%, 1 mg: –47%, 3 mg: –63%; all P < 0.001). (Source: PMC4301837)

memory: The study compared "system-oriented therapy" with a "reference intervention" in terms of "completed follow-up." No significant differences were observed between the groups regarding hospitalization duration or average bed day consumption over 12 months. However, the reference intervention group showed a significantly higher rate of incomplete follow-up compared to the system-oriented therapy group (15/40 vs. 4/30, P = 0.017). In terms of treatment outcomes, a multiple imputation approach indicated a trend favoring system-oriented therapy in both the compliance scale and PANSS scores, though these differences were not statistically significant. These results suggest that system-oriented therapy may be associated with better follow-up completion and potentially improved compliance and symptom scores. However, the lack of statistical significance in outcome measures highlights the need for further research to confirm these preliminary trends. Source: [PMC4060171]
text: System-oriented therapy showed a significantly lower rate of incomplete follow-up compared to the reference intervention (4/30 vs. 15/40, P = 0.017). Trends suggested better compliance and symptom scores, though not statistically significant. Source: [PMC4060171].

memory: In a study comparing IPE (4g/day) with placebo in subjects with diabetes (overall median baseline A1c = 6.8%), IPE significantly reduced several lipid and inflammatory markers across all diabetes groups—total, better-controlled (below median baseline A1c), and less-controlled (above median baseline A1c). Markers affected included triglycerides (TG), non-HDL cholesterol, VLDL-C, lipoprotein-associated phospholipase A2, Apo B, total cholesterol, HDL cholesterol, VLDL-TG, oxidized LDL, and remnant-like particle cholesterol. IPE also reduced LDL-C in the total diabetes group and hsCRP in the total and less-controlled diabetes groups. Importantly, no significant increases in fasting plasma glucose, A1c, insulin, or HOMA-IR were observed in any group, indicating that IPE did not negatively impact glycemic control or insulin sensitivity. These findings suggest that IPE may provide cardiovascular benefits without worsening diabetes-related metabolic parameters. Source: PMC3718763.
text: IPE (4g/day) did not significantly increase fasting plasma glucose, A1c, insulin, or HOMA-IR in subjects with diabetes, regardless of baseline A1c levels (PMC3718763). Thus, IPE does not negatively affect glycemic control or insulin sensitivity.
outcome: fasting plasma glucose, A1c, insulin, or homeostasis model assessment-estimated insulin total (all subjects with diabetes—overall median baseline glycosylated hemoglobin A1c [A1c] = 6.8%), better-controlled diabetes (below median baseline A1c), and less-controlled diabetes (above median baseline A1c).

memory: Source article [PMC4540107] reported that after 12 weeks, the DM60 group demonstrated significantly longer treatment retention and lower plasma morphine levels compared to the placebo group. No significant differences were observed in plasma cytokine levels, BDNF levels, or methadone dose requirements between the groups. These findings suggest that DM60 may enhance treatment retention and reduce plasma morphine levels without affecting other biomarkers or methadone requirements. The study supports the potential of DM60 as an adjunct in treatment programs for opioid use disorder, possibly by improving patient adherence and reducing drug craving or use. The lack of effect on methadone dose requirements implies that DM60 does not interfere with the maintenance dose, making it a potentially viable option for improving retention in methadone maintenance therapy. The results highlight the need for further research to explore the long-term effects of DM60 on treatment outcomes and its mechanism of action in improving retention.
text: Dextromethorphan (DM60) significantly improves treatment retention compared to placebo in opioid use disorder patients (PMC4540107). It reduces plasma morphine levels without affecting methadone dose requirements or other biomarkers, suggesting potential as an adjunct in methadone maintenance therapy.

memory: Source article [PMC4663570] evaluated the effect of "Agave derived fructans" versus "Formula" on "C-Reactive Protein" (CRP) in infants. CRP levels were measured at baseline (around 20 days old) and at three months of age. No statistically significant differences were found in mean CRP concentrations or changes in CRP (ΔCRP) between the groups (Wilcoxon test p = 0.05). Serum ferritin concentrations also showed no significant differences. Subgroup analysis by delivery type (cesarean vs. vaginal) did not reveal significant differences in CRP or ferritin (Fisher Student T-Test: p > 0.05). The study also noted changes in salivary IgA levels, but these were not statistically significant across all groups (p < 0.05; p < 0.01 for some comparisons) and were not directly related to CRP. Overall, the findings suggest that Agave-derived fructans did not significantly impact CRP levels compared to formula in the studied population. However, the lack of significant differences in CRP and related variables limits the ability to draw definitive conclusions about the effect of Agave-derived fructans on inflammation markers. The study's results do not support a clear intervention effect on CRP, indicating further research may be needed to clarify potential influences on inflammatory responses.
text: A study (PMC4663570) found no statistically significant differences in C-Reactive Protein (CRP) levels between infants fed Agave-derived fructans and those fed formula. The results suggest that Agave-derived fructans do not significantly affect CRP compared to formula, though further research is needed.

memory: Source article [PMC4440033]: A 12-week study on CKD patients with low vitamin D found that Vitamin D + Calcium (VitD + C) did not significantly improve outcomes over Calcium alone in reducing pro-inflammatory markers like IL-6 and hs-CRP, except for a reduction in IL-6 among non-diabetic patients. Regarding serum IL-10, the VitD + C group showed stable levels (p = 0.06), while the Calcium group experienced a significant decrease in IL-10 at weeks 6 and 12. Although not statistically significant, these results suggest a possible protective effect of VitD + C on IL-10 compared to Calcium alone. The study highlights the need for further research on the influence of VitD + C on anti-inflammatory markers in CKD patients.
text: In CKD patients, "Vitamin D + Calcium" showed stable serum IL-10 levels, while "Calcium" alone caused a significant decrease (p = 0.06). These findings suggest a potential protective effect of VitD + C on IL-10, though not statistically significant. (Source: PMC4440033)

memory: Excerpts from [PMC4092926] show that replacing soybean meal with sunflower cake in the diets of 1/2 Boer goats had no significant effect on body weight at slaughter (21.78 kg), hot (8.65 kg) and cold (8.59 kg) carcass weights, carcass yields (40.27% and 39.20%), or rib eye area (7.73 cm²). Other carcass traits, such as carcass length (46.74 cm, 45.68 cm), leg length (36.92 cm), leg perimeter (26.04 cm), hind perimeter (48.66 cm), thoracic perimeter (58.62 cm), and carcass compactness index (0.20), also showed no differences (p>0.05). Muscle and fat composition parameters, including total muscle of the leg (68.48%), total leg fat (2.79%), subcutaneous leg fat (55.19%), total bone (28.82%), femur weight (81.66 g), femur length (14.88 cm), leg muscularity index (0.38), muscle:bone ratio (2.53), and muscle:fat ratio (33.42), were unaffected by the dietary treatment. The study concludes that sunflower cake can be used as a viable alternative to soybean meal in the diets of 1/2 Boer goats without affecting meat yield or quality parameters.
text: Replacing soybean meal with sunflower cake in 1/2 Boer goat diets had no significant effect on weights, carcass yields, or rib eye area (PMC4092926). Carcass traits and muscle-fat composition remained unaffected, suggesting sunflower cake is a viable alternative.
outcome: Weights, carcass yields, rib eye area of goats

memory: Study [PMC2911596] evaluated the effects of sevoflurane-fentanyl and isoflurane-fentanyl anesthesia on MAC and SE values before fentanyl boluses. Pre-fentanyl MAC values were 0.74 ± 0.12 (sevoflurane) and 0.77 ± 0.17 (isoflurane), with no significant difference (P = .32). SE values were 43.5 ± 8.1 and 45.2 ± 8.3, respectively (P = .47), also showing no significant difference. These results suggest that the type of volatile anesthetic does not significantly affect MAC and SE values prior to fentanyl administration. While SSI values were higher in the sevoflurane group, the decrease in SSI after fentanyl was similar between groups. Following fentanyl boluses, both groups showed comparable changes in SE and HR, with stable MAC values. This indicates that both anesthetic regimens maintain similar anesthetic depth and hemodynamic stability post-fentanyl. The study supports that the choice between sevoflurane and isoflurane, when combined with fentanyl, does not significantly influence pre-fentanyl MAC and SE values. Both regimens are effective in maintaining stable anesthetic conditions after fentanyl administration. The findings suggest that pre-fentanyl MAC and SE values are comparable between the two anesthetic regimens, indicating no significant impact of volatile anesthetic type on these parameters.
text: Sevoflurane-fentanyl and isoflurane-fentanyl anesthesia showed no significant difference in MAC and SE values before fentanyl boluses (P = .32 and P = .47, respectively). Both regimens maintain comparable anesthetic depth and hemodynamic stability post-fentanyl. (Source: PMC2911596)
outcome: MAC and SE values before fentanyl boluses

memory: A study evaluated the effects of Virgin olive oil (VOO), Optimized virgin olive oil (OVOO), and Functional olive oil (FOO) on fasting plasma triacylglycerol levels. VOO and OVOO interventions led to significant increases in triacylglycerol concentrations (p = 0.037 and p = 0.002, respectively), while FOO had no significant effect. No differences were observed between the three interventions in terms of triacylglycerol levels. HDLc levels increased significantly only after OVOO intervention (p = 0.041), with this effect being more pronounced in females (p = 0.005). However, no differences were found among the interventions regarding HDLc changes. Table 4 from the source article [PMC5986505] indicates that average daily energy and nutrient intakes were similar across the three olive oil groups, suggesting that differences in triacylglycerol and HDLc levels were likely due to the type of olive oil rather than overall dietary intake. These findings suggest that VOO and OVOO may influence triacylglycerol levels differently compared to FOO, though no differences were observed between the interventions for this outcome. The gender-specific increase in HDLc with OVOO may indicate potential benefits for lipid profiles in females. The results contribute to understanding how different olive oil formulations may impact lipid metabolism.
text: VOO and OVOO significantly increased fasting plasma triacylglycerol levels compared to FOO (p = 0.037 and p = 0.002, respectively), though no differences were observed between the three interventions for this outcome. HDLc levels increased only with OVOO (p = 0.041), more so in females (p = 0.005). (Source: PMC5986505)
intervention: Virgin olive oil (VOO) and Optimized virgin olive oil (OVOO)

memory: Source article [PMC4007144] evaluated the effect of an "Intimate partner prevention intervention" versus a "Control" on "Hostility when managing conflicts." The intervention group showed significant improvements in controlling hostility and managing conflict (ARR 1.3, 95% CI 1.06–1.58). Participants in the intervention group were more likely to engage in gendered household tasks (ARR 2.47, 95% CI 1.24–4.90). Although physical and/or sexual IPV levels decreased in the intervention group, the difference was not statistically significant (ARR 0.52, 95% CI 0.18–1.51). A higher proportion of men in the intervention group believed a woman can refuse sex in all circumstances (40%) compared to the control group (36%), though this difference was not statistically significant (OR 1.21, 95% CI 0.77–1.91). The intervention positively influenced conflict management and gender roles but did not significantly reduce IPV. These findings suggest the intervention may improve conflict resolution skills and gender equity, but further research is needed to assess its effectiveness in reducing IPV.
text: The "Intimate partner prevention intervention" significantly improved hostility management during conflicts compared to the control group (ARR 1.3, 95% CI 1.06–1.58). However, it did not significantly reduce IPV levels. Source: [PMC4007144].

memory: Source article [PMC5447816] found that students with high "E" scores completed the suturing test significantly faster than those with average E scores (regression coefficient = −418.2, P = 0.0118). In contrast, the difference in completion time for students with low versus average A scores was not statistically significant (regression coefficient = −290.9, P = 0.057). The study also compared the NUMSAS component scores between video-learning and simulator-learning groups. The median length score was 13.5 (range 7.0–15.0) in the video-learning group and 15.0 (range 3.5–15.0) in the simulator-learning group, with the latter group performing significantly better (P = 0.02673). However, the overall NUMSAS scores were not significantly different between the two groups (video-learning: 52.0, range 25–59.5; simulator-learning: 54.0, range 22.5–60.0; P = 0.11287). Additionally, the time to complete the suturing task was significantly shorter in the simulator-learning group compared to the video-learning group. These findings suggest that higher "E" scores are associated with faster task completion, while the learning method (video vs. simulator) had a significant impact on length scores but not overall NUMSAS scores.
text: Students with high "E" scores completed the suturing test significantly faster than those with average "E" scores (regression coefficient = −418.2, P = 0.0118) (PMC5447816).

memory: No significant differences in quality of life (QoL) scores were found between Erlotinib and Placebo groups at one or two months, even after adjusting for baseline scores (all P ≥ .40) [PMC4112798]. The unadjusted hazard ratio (HR) for neurological progression-free survival (PFS) was 0.99 (95% CI = 0.62 to 1.58; P = .97), and it remained non-significant after adjusting for randomization stratification factors (HR = 0.95, 95% CI = 0.59 to 1.54; P = .84). Median overall survival (OS) was 2.9 months in the placebo group and 3.4 months in the Erlotinib group, with a non-significant HR of 0.95 (95% CI = 0.58 to 1.55; P = .83). These findings suggest that Erlotinib does not significantly improve QoL compared to placebo in the studied population. The lack of significant differences in QoL, PFS, and OS indicates that Erlotinib may not offer substantial clinical benefits over placebo in this context. The results highlight the importance of considering alternative treatment strategies or patient-specific factors that may influence treatment outcomes. The study provides valuable insights into the limited efficacy of Erlotinib in improving QoL and survival in this particular patient group. Further research is needed to explore other potential therapeutic options or combinations that may yield more favorable outcomes. The non-significant findings across multiple endpoints reinforce the need for careful evaluation of treatment choices based on individual patient profiles and clinical guidelines.
text: Erlotinib does not significantly improve quality of life compared to placebo (all P ≥ .40) [PMC4112798]. No significant differences were observed in QoL scores, PFS, or OS, suggesting limited clinical benefit of Erlotinib over placebo in this population.

memory: Source article [PMC4794540] found that a six-month yogic intervention combined with prescribed medication significantly improved positive well-being and vitality scores compared to prescribed medication alone. The intervention group showed statistically significant improvements in positive well-being (P<0.01) and vitality (P<0.02) relative to the control group, as shown in Table 3 and discussed in the text. These results suggest that integrating yogic practices with standard medication may enhance psychological well-being and vitality. No significant differences were observed between the groups in the domain of self-control. The findings support the potential benefit of adding yogic intervention to prescribed medication for improving positive well-being and vitality outcomes. The study's results are consistent with the reported data and emphasize the role of complementary interventions in enhancing treatment effectiveness.
text: A six-month yogic intervention combined with prescribed medication significantly improved positive well-being (P<0.01) and vitality (P<0.02) compared to medication alone (PMC4794540). These findings suggest that adding yogic practices to standard medication may enhance psychological well-being and vitality.

memory: Source article [PMC4727391] reported no significant differences in adverse events between laryngeal mask (LM) ventilation and endotracheal intubation (ETI), with 3 adverse events in the LM group and 4 in the ETI group. Both methods demonstrated comparable success rates for first-attempt insertion (LM: 94.4% vs. ETI: 90.6%) and similar insertion times (LM: 7.58 ± 1.16 s vs. ETI: 7.89 ± 1.52 s). text: A study (PMC4727391) found no significant differences in adverse effects between laryngeal mask ventilation and endotracheal intubation, with 3 and 4 adverse events respectively. Both methods were comparable in safety and effectiveness during resuscitation.

memory: Source article [PMC3917884] found that diet intervention (D treatment) significantly reduced LDL cholesterol compared to control at 12 weeks (P = 0.003), with the effect sustained at 1-year follow-up. text: Diet intervention significantly reduced LDL cholesterol compared to control at 12 weeks (P = 0.003), with effects sustained at 1-year follow-up (PMC3917884).

memory: No significant differences in creatine kinase (CK) levels were observed between the ZA10 group (zhibitai 480 mg + atorvastatin 10 mg), A20 group (atorvastatin 20 mg), and A40 group (atorvastatin 40 mg) before and after treatment (Table 4). text: The ZA10 group showed no significant differences in creatine kinase (CK) levels compared to the A20 or A40 groups before and after treatment. Source: [PMC5319516].

memory: Study [PMC3085176] evaluated the effect of p-synephrine (50 mg) alone on resting metabolic rate (RMR) compared to placebo. Results indicated that p-synephrine significantly increased RMR by 65 kcal compared to placebo (p<0.02). No significant differences were observed between the groups in terms of heart rate, blood pressure, or self-reported symptoms such as anxiety, hunger, tension, sleepiness, energy, nervousness, headache, upset stomach, concentration, or general discomfort. These findings suggest that p-synephrine may enhance RMR without inducing notable adverse effects. The study supports the potential of p-synephrine as a metabolic enhancer. However, further research is necessary to confirm these results and investigate the long-term safety and efficacy of p-synephrine. The study provides preliminary evidence that p-synephrine alone can positively influence metabolic rate without significant side effects, which may be relevant for weight management or metabolic health interventions.
text: p-Synephrine (50 mg) significantly increased RMR by 65 kcal compared to placebo (p<0.02) without notable adverse effects (PMC3085176). These findings suggest p-synephrine may enhance RMR without inducing significant side effects.

memory: Source article [PMC5579675] reports that 2 g of YM significantly reduced prospective eating scores compared to placebo (PLC) during exercise (p = 0.022) and showed a slight reduction during rest (0 to 120 min) (p = 0.046). These results indicate a modest effect of YM on reducing prospective eating, particularly during and after exercise. No significant differences were found in hunger or desire to eat, though there was a trend toward reduced desire to eat (p = 0.079). Time had a significant effect on all measures, but treatment effects were only observed for prospective eating and hunger. Additionally, YM increased fat oxidation (FAO) during steady-state exercise (p = 0.037), though this was not directly linked to prospective eating scores. The study suggests that YM may influence appetite-related measures, with the most consistent effect observed on prospective eating. These findings support the potential of YM as an intervention for appetite regulation, particularly in the context of physical activity.
text: In a study (PMC5579675), 2 g of YM significantly reduced prospective eating scores compared to placebo during exercise (p = 0.022) and showed a slight reduction during rest (p = 0.046), indicating a modest effect of YM on reducing prospective eating, particularly during and after exercise.

memory: Both the underwater treadmill group and the control group showed significant reductions in anteroposterior, mediolateral, and total postural sway after the intervention (p<0.05), indicating improved postural stability. These improvements were observed in both static and dynamic balance assessments. No significant differences were found between the two groups in pre- and post-test comparisons. Additionally, both groups demonstrated significant improvements in dynamic balance (p<0.05). The findings suggest that both interventions were effective in enhancing postural stability, but neither group outperformed the other in the measured outcomes. The results imply that while both interventions have beneficial effects on balance, further research is needed to determine if the effects are comparable in different populations or settings. Source: [PMC4085217]
text: Both the underwater treadmill group and control group showed significant reductions in anteroposterior, mediolateral, and total postural sway compared to baseline (p<0.05), indicating improved postural stability. No significant differences were found between the groups. Source: [PMC4085217]
outcome: anteroposterior, mediolateral and total postural sway

memory: Source article [PMC1618957] found that lanreotide Autogel® 120 mg (Lan ATG 120 mg) provided significantly better symptom control than lanreotide microparticles (Lan MP 30 mg). Lan ATG 120 mg showed statistically significant improvements in hyperhidrosis (P < 0.001) and headache (P < 0.001). Plasma IGF-1 concentrations were largely unchanged between the two treatments, with values of 423 ± 30 ng/ml in men and 336 ± 24 ng/ml in women for Lan MP 30 mg, and 414 ± 32 ng/ml in men and 314 ± 23 ng/ml in women for Lan ATG 120 mg. GH levels were significantly lower with Lan ATG 120 mg (3.8 (0.5) ng/ml) compared to Lan MP 30 mg (4.3 (0.5) ng/ml; P < 0.001). The study supports the conclusion that Lan ATG 120 mg offers superior symptom control, particularly in hyperhidrosis and headache, without significant differences in IGF-1 levels between the two treatments.
text: Lanreotide Autogel® 120 mg provides significantly better symptom control than lanreotide microparticles, particularly in hyperhidrosis and headache (P < 0.001). IGF-1 levels remained largely unchanged between the two treatments. (Source: PMC1618957)

memory: At 6 months, perindopril was associated with a 0.14% (SE 0.05, p = 0.02) increase in the rate of change in flow-mediated vasodilatation (FMD), compared to a 0.02% (SE 0.05, p = 0.74) increase in the placebo group, indicating a 0.12% difference (p = 0.07). This suggests a trend toward improved FMD in the perindopril group, though not statistically significant at the conventional 0.05 level. By 36 months, no significant difference in nitroglycerine response was observed between perindopril and placebo, with mean values (SD) of 8.2% (5.4) and 8.8% (5.4), respectively. Over the longer term, the change in FMD of the brachial artery between baseline and 36 months was 0.55% (95% CI −0.42 to 1.47; p = 0.23) higher in the perindopril group, indicating no statistically significant difference in FMD change compared to placebo. The data suggest that perindopril may have a beneficial effect on FMD in the short term (6 months), but this effect does not persist significantly over 36 months. Source: [PMC2039813].
text: At 6 months, Perindopril showed a trend toward improved flow-mediated vasodilatation (FMD) compared to placebo (p = 0.07), but this effect was not statistically significant. By 36 months, no significant difference in FMD change was observed between groups (p = 0.23). Source: [PMC2039813].

memory: A 6-week study [PMC3489577] compared the effects of consuming 100 grams of instant oat cereal versus 100 grams of wheat flour-based noodles on waist circumference. The oat cereal group showed a significant reduction in waist circumference compared to the control group (p=0.002). This group also experienced significant decreases in total cholesterol (p=0.015) and LDL-C (p=0.028), along with higher dietary fiber intake by the study’s end. No significant differences were found between the groups in blood pressure, other anthropometric measures, or other laboratory parameters. The results suggest that replacing wheat flour-based noodles with instant oat cereal may improve waist circumference and lipid profiles. The study’s controlled design and measurable outcomes support the beneficial effects of oat cereal on metabolic health. The findings highlight the potential role of dietary fiber in improving metabolic outcomes and support oat cereal as a healthier alternative to wheat flour-based noodles for waist circumference management. Further research is needed to explore long-term effects and generalizability across populations.
text: Consuming 100 grams of instant oat cereal significantly reduced waist circumference compared to 100 grams of wheat flour-based noodles (p=0.002) [PMC3489577]. This effect was accompanied by lower total cholesterol and LDL-C levels, suggesting oat cereal may be a healthier alternative for waist circumference management.

memory: Source article [PMC5358282] evaluated "Diazepam + chlorpheniramine" (premedicated group) versus "Control" (non-premedicated group) on "Local pain." Results indicated no significant difference in periprocedural pain perception (31% vs. 29%; P = 0.75) or anxiety (59% vs. 50%; P = 0.2). However, local pain was more frequently reported in the premedicated group (30% vs. 16%; P = 0.018). Additionally, catheter-induced spasms occurred in 4 (4%) patients in the premedicated group compared to 0 (0%) in the control group (P = 0.04). Non-catheter-induced spasms were observed in 1 (1%) patient in both groups (P = NS). These findings suggest that premedication with Diazepam + chlorpheniramine did not reduce overall pain perception or anxiety but was associated with increased local pain and a higher incidence of catheter-induced spasms. The study highlights potential adverse effects of this premedication combination, particularly in relation to local pain and catheter-related complications, which may need consideration in clinical practice.
text: The combination of Diazepam + chlorpheniramine did not reduce local pain compared to control (30% vs. 16%; P = 0.018) and was associated with increased local pain and catheter-induced spasms (4% vs. 0%; P = 0.04). Source: PMC5358282.

memory: A study examined the effect of fasting on REM sleep percentages by comparing two fasting periods—baseline fasting (BLF) and Ramadan fasting—against a non-fasting baseline (BL). REM sleep percentages were significantly lower during BLF (17.7 ± 8.1%) and Ramadan (18.6 ± 10.7%) compared to BL (25.6 ± 4.8%) (p < 0.05), indicating that fasting may reduce REM sleep. Serum glucose levels were not significantly different between BL (6.2 ± 0.4 mmol/L), BLF (5.6 ± 0.5 mmol/L), and Ramadan (5.7 ± 0.5 mmol/L). JDS scores and blink durations also showed no significant differences. However, bedtime and wake-up times were significantly delayed during Ramadan (p < 0.05), likely due to changes in work schedules. These findings suggest that fasting may impact sleep architecture, particularly REM sleep, although other factors like glucose levels and eye movement measures remained stable. The results support the hypothesis that fasting influences REM sleep, but further research is needed to explore the underlying mechanisms and long-term effects. Source: [PMC3751553].
text: Fasting during baseline (BLF) and Ramadan significantly reduced REM sleep percentages (17.7% and 18.6%, respectively) compared to the non-fasting baseline (25.6%) (p < 0.05). This suggests fasting may negatively affect REM sleep, though glucose levels and eye movement measures remained stable. Source: [PMC3751553].
intervention: 4 weeks before Ramadan while performing the Islamic fasting for 1 week (baseline fasting) (BLF) or during the second week of Ramadan while fasting (Ramadan)

memory: Source article [PMC5689110]: In an 8-week, randomized, 1:1:1 trial, high-dose aripiprazole (10 mg/day for <50 kg; 20 mg/day for ≥50 kg) was compared with placebo for the treatment of tic disorders. Patients were randomly assigned using an interactive voice/web response system. High-dose aripiprazole showed a statistically significant improvement in YGTSS-TTS (p < 0.0001), with a LS mean change from baseline in YGTSS total motor tic score at week 8 of −8.0 (0.9) for high-dose versus −2.7 (0.8) for placebo, and a treatment difference of −5.3 (−7.5 to −3.2). However, the discontinuation rate was significantly higher in the high-dose group, with 10 patients discontinuing treatment (hazard ratio vs. placebo: 5.51, p = 0.0278), indicating a higher risk of discontinuation with high-dose aripiprazole compared to placebo. These findings suggest that while high-dose aripiprazole is more effective in reducing tic severity, it is associated with a greater risk of treatment discontinuation due to potential adverse effects or tolerability issues.
text: High-dose aripiprazole is associated with a significantly higher discontinuation rate compared to placebo (hazard ratio 5.51, p=0.0278), suggesting greater tolerability issues despite its superior efficacy in reducing tic severity.

memory: At extubation readiness, the respiratory physiotherapy–driven weaning group showed significantly higher PSV (8 vs. 5 cmH2O; p=0.015) and PEEP (8 vs. 5 cmH2O; p<0.001) compared to the progressive discontinuation of PSV with SmartCare™ group. Mechanical ventilation duration (3.5 [2.0–7.3] days vs. 4.1 [2.7–7.1] days; p=0.467) and extubation failure rates (2 vs. 2; p=1.00) were not significantly different between the two groups. Weaning duration was significantly shorter in the respiratory physiotherapy–driven weaning group (60 [50–80] minutes vs. 110 [80–130] minutes; p<0.001). No significant differences were found in Pimax (p=0.270) or Pemax (p=0.058) before SBT, nor in FVC or RSBI between the two groups. Source: [PMC4511442].

memory: A study examined the effect of an Internet group (receiving a letter of invitation) compared to a control group (no letter) on accurate understanding of trial results among breast cancer patients in a Trastuzumab trial. The Internet group showed a higher uptake of trial results (47.1% vs. 33.9%, P=0.166), but this difference was not statistically significant. Expectations regarding trial outcomes were similar between groups, including knowledge of trial usefulness (82.2%, P=0.633), understanding of treatment received (20.6%, P=0.468), and comprehension of clinical trials (9.3%, P=0.745). However, the Internet group had significantly better accurate understanding of trial results (18.8% vs. 5.6%, P=0.039). These findings suggest that while general expectations were comparable, the Internet group demonstrated better comprehension of trial outcomes, indicating that receiving a letter of invitation may enhance accurate understanding. This highlights the potential benefit of using such communication methods in improving patients' understanding of trial results. Source: [PMC2853089]
text: The Internet group showed better accurate understanding of trial results (18.8% vs. 5.6%, P=0.039) compared to the control group, though overall trial result uptake was not statistically significant (47.1% vs. 33.9%, P=0.166). Source: [PMC2853089]
intervention: Internet group (who received the letter of invitation)

memory: Source article [PMC4319071] found that both intervention groups (basic and plus) showed greater reductions in high-energy snack intake compared to the control group at T1 (ES=–0.30 and –0.29) and T2 (ES=–0.18 and –0.27). The plus intervention group had significantly greater increases in fruit intake compared to the control group at T1 (ES=0.25, P=.01) and T2 (ES=0.37, P=.001). The plus version also led to a larger decrease in high-energy snack intake than the control group at T1 (ES=–0.38) and T2 (ES=–0.32). While vegetable intake increased over time across all groups, there were no significant differences in change over time between the groups. These findings suggest that interventions targeting individual cognition and self-regulation processes can reduce high-energy snack intake, with the plus version showing enhanced effects on fruit intake and snack reduction compared to the control. The results support the efficacy of such interventions, particularly the enhanced version, in promoting healthier dietary behaviors.
text: The "Individual cognition and self-regulation processes intervention" significantly reduces high-energy snack intake compared to control (ES=–0.30 to –0.38 at T1, ES=–0.18 to –0.32 at T2; PMC4319071). The enhanced version showed greater reductions and increased fruit intake.

memory: Source article [PMC3483098] found that the Sensor On arm had a higher mean number of daily boluses compared to the Sensor Off arm (6.8 ± 2.5 vs 5.8 ± 1.9, p < 0.0001). Additional features like temporary basal rates, manual basal suspend function, and bolus wizard calculator usage were significantly higher during the Sensor On period. HbA1c levels were lower in the Sensor On group (8.04% vs 8.47%, p < 0.001). The Sensor On arm also showed greater time spent in euglycaemia and less time in hyperglycaemia.

memory: Excerpts from source article [PMC4636858]: MRI plaque numbers decreased in both the "Mitoxantrone + methylprednisolone" and "No treatment" groups (2.29 vs. 2.17), but the difference was not statistically significant (P = 0.782). At six months post-trial, plaque numbers increased in both groups (0.72 vs. 0.77), with no significant difference (P = 0.611). The mean EDSS score also showed a significant reduction at the end of treatment in both groups (0.79 and 0.53), but the difference between groups was not statistically significant (P = 0.953). These results suggest that "Mitoxantrone + methylprednisolone" did not offer a significant advantage over no treatment in reducing MS plaques or improving disability scores as measured by EDSS. Both groups experienced similar outcomes in terms of plaque reduction and disability progression, indicating that the treatment may not be more effective than no treatment in this context. The study highlights the need for further research to explore alternative treatments or identify subgroups of patients who may benefit from this regimen. The lack of significant differences between groups suggests that the observed effects may be due to natural disease fluctuations or placebo effects, rather than the specific intervention. The findings contribute to the ongoing discussion about the efficacy of high-dose corticosteroids and mitoxantrone in MS management.
text: The effect of "Mitoxantrone + methylprednisolone" compared with "No treatment" on multiple sclerosis plaques showed no significant difference (P = 0.782). Both groups had similar reductions in plaque numbers and EDSS scores, suggesting the treatment does not offer a significant advantage over no treatment. (Source: PMC4636858)

memory: Artesunate monotherapy (2 or 4 mg/kg/day once daily) resulted in a significantly faster median fever clearance time (FCT) compared to quinine plus doxycycline (TID for 7 days), with median FCTs of 17.9 and 19.1 hours versus 29.3 hours (P=0.001). Prostration clearance time (PCT) was also faster in the artesunate groups (29.5–29.8 hours) compared to the quinine + doxycycline group (43.1 hours; P<0.001). No significant difference in adverse events was observed between the groups (P=0.91). All treatment groups achieved asexual parasitemia clearance within one week. Cure rates at 28 and 42 days were 97.8% (artesunate 2 mg/kg/day), 100% (artesunate 4 mg/kg/day), and 100% (quinine + doxycycline). Parasite reduction ratios at 12–48 hours were significantly lower in the artesunate arms, indicating faster parasite clearance. Source: [PMC3525560].
text: Artesunate monotherapy (2 or 4 mg/kg/day once daily) significantly reduced median FCT compared to quinine plus doxycycline (TID for 7 days) (17.9–19.1 vs. 29.3 hours, P=0.001). Prostration clearance was also faster (29.5–29.8 vs. 43.1 hours, P<0.001). Source: [PMC3525560].
intervention: artesunate monotherapy with 2 or 4 mg/kg/day once daily
comparator: quinine plus doxycycline TID for 7 days

memory: In a study of obese African American patients with DKA and severe hyperglycemia, metformin 1,000 mg daily and sitagliptin 100 mg daily were compared to placebo for their effect on hyperglycemia relapse-free survival. Both metformin and sitagliptin significantly improved relapse-free survival compared to placebo (P = 0.015). The hazard ratio for relapse was 0.28 (95% CI 0.10–0.81) for metformin and 0.31 (0.10–0.98) for sitagliptin, indicating reduced relapse risk in these treatment groups. No significant difference was found between metformin and sitagliptin (P = 0.75). The restricted mean time to relapse was significantly higher in the combined treatment group (480 days) compared to placebo (305 days, P = 0.004). Patients in remission had higher DI (P = 0.02) and incremental AUCi (P < 0.001) than those who relapsed, with no significant changes in Si. These findings suggest both metformin and sitagliptin are effective in prolonging hyperglycemia relapse-free survival in this population, though their combined effect was not significantly different from either drug alone. Source: PMC5079604.
text: In a study of obese African American patients with DKA and severe hyperglycemia, metformin 1,000 mg daily and sitagliptin 100 mg daily significantly improved hyperglycemia relapse-free survival compared to placebo (P = 0.015). Both drugs reduced relapse risk (HR 0.28 and 0.31, respectively), with no significant difference between them (P = 0.75). Source: PMC5079604.
intervention: metformin 1,000 mg daily, sitagliptin 100 mg daily

memory: In a 12-week study with 101 participants, isomaltulose was compared to sucrose for their impact on triglyceride levels. The results showed a significant reduction in triglycerides in the isomaltulose group (b: 34.01 [6.59–61.44], P = 0.016). No significant differences were found between the groups for insulin, fasting glucose, fructosamine, proinsulin, C-peptide, or HOMA-IR. HbA1c levels were also not significantly different between the two groups (sucrose: 7.39 ± 0.78%; isomaltulose: 7.24 ± 0.76%; b: 0.02 [95% CI: −0.21 to 0.25], P = 0.844). These findings indicate that isomaltulose may reduce triglyceride levels without negatively affecting other metabolic markers. The study supports the potential of isomaltulose as a beneficial alternative to sucrose in managing triglyceride levels. The evidence suggests that isomaltulose could be a viable option for individuals seeking to manage their triglyceride levels without compromising other metabolic parameters. This study contributes to the growing body of research on alternative sweeteners and their metabolic effects. Further research may be needed to confirm these findings in larger populations or over longer periods. The results are encouraging for the use of isomaltulose in dietary interventions aimed at improving lipid profiles.
text: Isomaltulose significantly reduces triglycerides compared to sucrose (b: 34.01 [6.59–61.44], P = 0.016) without affecting other metabolic markers. This suggests isomaltulose may be a beneficial alternative for managing triglyceride levels.

memory: Source article [PMC5738810] evaluated the effect of a diet supplemented with Curcuminoids extract, hydrolyzed Collagen, and green Tea extract (CCOT) versus a control diet on pain interference (PI) change. The CCOT group showed a significant improvement in the ability to rise from lying down compared to the control group (p = 0.029). However, no significant overall PI change was observed between the CCOT (T0: 3.26 ± 0.54; T3: 2.96 ± 0.45; p = 0.101) and control groups (T0: 3.44 ± 0.59; T3: 3.86 ± 0.66; p = 0.633) (p = 0.063). No statistical differences were found in other subjective parameters such as lameness, pain at palpation, joint mobility, or body weight. Additionally, no significant changes in PVF values for the most affected limb were observed between CCOT and control groups at T0 (p = 0.618) or T3 (p = 0.953). The study reported no side effects. While CCOT showed a specific benefit in rising from lying down, it did not result in a significant overall reduction in PI compared to the control diet.
text: The experimental diet with CCOT showed a significant improvement in rising from lying down (p = 0.029) but no significant overall pain interference change compared to the control (p = 0.063). Source: [PMC5738810].
intervention: an experimental diet supplemented with Curcuminoids extract, hydrolyzed COllagen and green Tea extract (CCOT)

memory: Source article [PMC1468428] evaluated the effect of a "1 litre saline enema" versus "no enema" on puerperal and neonatal infection rates. The study found no significant differences in puerperal infection rates between the enema group (41/190 [22%]) and the no enema group (26/182 [14%]); relative risk (RR) was 0.66 (95% CI: 0.43 to 1.03). Similarly, no significant differences were observed in neonatal infection rates, with 38/191 (20%) in the enema group and 40/179 (22%) in the no enema group; RR was 1.12 (95% CI: 0.76 to 1.66). Additional outcomes showed no significant differences in episiorraphy dehiscence rates (12% with enema vs. 17% without enema; P = 0.30) or median labour time (515 min. with enema vs. 585 min. without enema; P = 0.24). These findings suggest that the use of a 1 litre saline enema does not significantly impact puerperal or neonatal infection rates. The results support the conclusion that the administration of a saline enema does not appear to have a significant protective or harmful effect on infection rates in the studied population.
text: A 1 litre saline enema does not significantly affect puerperal or neonatal infection rates compared to no enema (RR 0.66, 95% CI 0.43–1.03 for puerperal; RR 1.12, 95% CI 0.76–1.66 for neonatal) [PMC1468428].

memory: A 10-week yoga program significantly improved flexibility, as measured by the sit & reach test, in the experimental group compared to the control group (p < 0.001). Post hoc analysis of participants who completed ≥70% of yoga sessions (n = 11) versus control (n = 19) confirmed the flexibility improvements, along with reduced state anxiety (p = 0.02) and RMSSD (p = 0.05), and a trend toward improvement in the push-up test (p = 0.07). However, heart rate variability (HRV) measures did not show significant changes in the experimental group compared to the control group, except for increased LF:HF ratio (p = 0.04) and reduced pNN50 (p = 0.04) in the yoga group. Quality of life (QoL) domain scores did not show significant changes in the yoga group compared to the control group (all p > 0.05), and no group × time effects were observed for QoL summary scales. Source: [PMC3648394].
text: A 10-week yoga program significantly improved flexibility (sit & reach test) compared to control (p < 0.001). Source: [PMC3648394].

memory: Both istradefylline 20 mg/day and 40 mg/day significantly reduced daily OFF time compared to placebo (−0.99 hours, P = .003 and −0.96 hours, P = .003, respectively), with no significant difference in efficacy between the two doses.
